events.text: On your island every child learns to read the tide the way children elsewhere learn letters. Grandaunt Oru, who has no teeth and no fear, takes the little ones down to the flats at low water and makes you listen to the mud. It clicks. It sighs. It is, she says, telling you when the sea is coming back.

choices.text: Listen until you understand it

effects.log: You lie with your ear to the mud until the clicking turns into counting. When the sea returns you are the first child up the beach, and Oru nods at you once, which from her is a medal.

choices.text: Dig for the clams while the others listen

effects.log: You come home with a basket of clams and wet to the neck, because the tide came in while you were digging. Everyone eats well. Oru calls you Clam for a year.

choices.text: Ask Oru why the sea goes away at all

effects.log: Oru says the sea goes to visit the god who made it, at the edge of the world, and comes back to tell the islands what was said. You are not sure she is joking. Neither is she.

events.text: A spring tide, the lowest in twelve years. The flats run out so far that a reef nobody living has seen stands bare in the sun, and on it, a ring of standing stones, green with weed. The grown-ups argue on the beach about whether it is holy, or haunted, or just stones.

choices.text: Run out to the ring before the sea comes back

effects.log: You touch the tallest stone. Someone carved a wave on it, and a hand above the wave, open, as if blessing it. You run back with the tide at your heels and your heart in your mouth.

choices.text: Count the minutes the way Oru taught you, and warn the others

effects.log: You call the turn of the tide before any adult does. Two cousins who had wandered out come back in time because of you. The village talks of it all winter.

choices.text: Stay on the beach, where it is sensible

effects.log: From the beach the ring looks like a crown lying in the water. You draw it in the sand and the sea takes the drawing, gently, which feels like an answer.

events.text: Oru is dying, quite cheerfully, in a bed by the window where she can hear the water. She sends for you, of all the children. 'Tell me what the tide is doing,' she says, with her eyes shut. 'Not what you see. What you hear.'

choices.text: Tell her the truth: the sea is going out

effects.log: 'Good,' says Oru. 'So am I. It always comes back.' She dies before the turn, smiling. You read the tide for the whole island after that.

choices.text: Tell her the ring of stones had a hand carved on it

effects.log: Oru laughs, a dry little sound. 'So you went out. Good. Somebody made all this, child, and left a mark. Keep looking for the marks.' You promise. She holds you to it.

choices.text: Hold her hand and say nothing

effects.log: You sit with her until the light goes. She seems glad of the quiet. When the family comes in, they find you both asleep, her hand still in yours, and she does not wake.

events.text: The islands of {pw_world} trade in everything, but they count in shells: blue cowries from the warm south, white ones from the north. A trader named Benna Sixsails has a leaky boat, a good eye and no crew, and is looking for somebody young and foolish enough to sail the island round with her.

choices.text: Sign on with Benna

effects.log: You learn more swearing in the first week than in your whole life. You also learn the stars, and how to sleep in a boat that is trying to throw you out.

choices.text: Buy a share in her cargo instead

effects.log: You give Benna your savings and she gives you a scratched shell with her mark on it. 'That is a promise,' she says. 'I am good for it, mostly.'

choices.text: Wish her luck and stay ashore

effects.log: You watch the patched sail until it is a fingernail on the horizon. Some days, after, you look at that horizon longer than you mean to.

events.text: Six islands, six different ideas of a fair price. On Long Reef they want salt, on the Twins they want songs (really: a good song is worth a basket of fish), and on Hollow Island they want nothing at all, and look at your boat as if it were a new kind of weather.

choices.text: Sing for your supper on the Twins

effects.log: You sing a fishing song from home, badly, and they pay you anyway, out of pity and then out of enjoyment. Benna is speechless, then calculating.

choices.text: Try to sell to Hollow Island

effects.log: You sit on their beach for three days before an old man trades you a black pearl for a story about where you come from. You tell it well. It is a good pearl.

choices.text: Sell salt hard on Long Reef

effects.log: You haggle like a gull over a fish head. The Long Reefers respect it and buy everything, and you go to bed richer and slightly ashamed.

events.text: Benna Sixsails comes home at the end of the season with a hold full of blue shells and a face full of news. 'There is an island that is not on any chart,' she says, 'and it is moving. Westward. Like it is going somewhere.'

choices.text: Go with her to chase it

effects.log: You chase the moving island for a month and never reach it. But you see it once, at dawn, a green hump with a light on it, sailing against the wind. You never forget it.

choices.text: Take your share and buy a boat of your own

effects.log: You buy a small, honest boat and name it after Benna, who is insulted and flattered in equal parts. The sea is open to you now.

choices.text: Tell her she has had too much sun

effects.log: Benna snorts and sails off to chase it alone. She comes back a year later, thinner, and will not say what she found. She gives you a white shell carved with an open hand.

events.text: Off the Point, in water so clear it looks like air, there is a temple on the sea floor. It sank long before anyone remembers, and the divers say the statue of the god down there has its eyes open, which none of the temples on land do. Nobody dives deeper than the roof. The priests say the bottom is not for the living.

choices.text: Train your breath until you can reach the doors

effects.log: You practise all summer: a minute, two, three. Your chest learns to be patient. At the end of it you can hang in the green water and look straight down at the doors.

choices.text: Ask the oldest diver what is down there

effects.log: She tells you it is cold below the roof, and quiet, and that once she heard something like a bell ring when there was no bell. Then she charges you a fish for the story.

choices.text: Leave the dead their temple

effects.log: You row past the Point on calm days and look down at the white roof, and that is enough for you. The water keeps its secret, and you keep your breath.

events.text: A calm day, the calmest of the year. You go down the rope with a stone in your arms, past the roof, past the pillars, into the great hall. The god's statue sits with its hands open on its knees, and in the left hand there is something that is not stone: a small bronze bowl, green with age.

choices.text: Take the bowl and kick for the surface

ok.log: You break the surface with the bowl in your fist and your lungs on fire. Every boat on the Point cheers, and then goes quiet when they see what you hold.

fail.log: Your lungs give out halfway and you drop the bowl and claw upward. You are hauled into the boat blue and coughing. Below, the bowl settles back into the god's hand, as if put there.

choices.text: Look at the statue's face instead

effects.log: The eyes are open, as they said. The face is plain, almost kind, and it looks a little like someone you might have been. You come up dizzy and say nothing to anyone.

choices.text: Leave the bowl where it is

effects.log: You put your hand on the god's open hand, briefly, and let the stone pull you no further. It feels like shaking hands with someone very old.

events.text: Word reaches the island temple. The high priest comes down to the beach in his salt-white robe and asks to speak to you, alone, about what you saw at the bottom of the sea.

choices.text: Give the bronze bowl to the temple

effects.log: The priest holds it as if it might break. 'The Maker's own offering bowl,' he says. 'It was lost when the sea rose.' It sits on the altar now, and the island is proud of you.

choices.text: Keep the bowl and tell him nothing

effects.log: You keep it by your bed. When you fill it with seawater the water stays still, however the house shakes in a storm. You never tell anyone why that frightens you.

choices.text: Tell him the statue looks like you

effects.log: The priest looks at you a long time. 'Many people say that,' he says at last. 'Very few of them have been down there.' He leaves you a temple token, and his address.

choices.text: Say you saw nothing but fish

effects.log: The priest seems relieved. Some secrets are easier for a temple not to have. He blesses you, and you feel nothing, and that is fine.

events.text: In the storm season the islands cannot visit each other, so they hold the weddings before it: the whole archipelago at one beach, fires every twenty paces, and boats tied together into a floating dance floor. You are dancing badly on a raft when you collide with {npc}, who is dancing worse.

choices.text: Keep dancing, worse on purpose

mem.note: danced badly with me at the storm weddings

effects.log: You out-badly each other until the musicians stop to laugh. {npc} is from an island three days east, and leaves on the morning tide, and waves until you cannot see the wave.

choices.text: Apologise and ask {npc} to sit out the next one

mem.note: sat with me till the fires went out

effects.log: You sit on the edge of the raft with your feet in the warm sea and talk until the fires burn down. {npc} knows the names of stars you thought nobody else had noticed.

choices.text: Go back to your friends

effects.log: You shrug and go back to your cousins' fire. Later you see {npc} leave on an eastern boat, and feel, very briefly, that you have dropped something.

events.text: A message arrives by the first boat after the storms: a string of shells knotted in a pattern. On your island it means nothing. Your neighbour, who married an eastern islander, laughs out loud. 'It is from {npc},' the neighbour says. 'It says: did you survive the season? Here, I lived.'

choices.text: Knot a string back

effects.log: Your neighbour teaches you the knots. Yours says: I survived. Come back for the next weddings. It takes you all night and your fingers bleed a little. It is sent.

choices.text: Sail east yourself

mem.note: sailed three days to see me

effects.log: Three days in an open boat. You arrive salt-stiff and sunburnt on the beach of {npc}'s island, and {npc} drops a basket of fish at the sight of you.

choices.text: Let it go: the sea is too wide

effects.log: You put the string of shells in a box. It is a very beautiful string. You take it out, sometimes, and do not knot an answer.

events.text: The next storm weddings. {npc} is on the beach before your boat touches sand, and this time nobody is dancing. The island grandmothers have already noticed, and are pretending not to, very loudly.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to marry you on the floating floor

effects.log: You are married on the rafts with the whole archipelago watching and the first storm of the season on the horizon, like a guest that came too early. Nobody minds. It is a good omen here.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to wait one more season

effects.log: {npc} looks at you a long time and says one more season, then, and no more. The grandmothers sigh like a wind.

choices.text: Tell {npc} the truth: you belong to the sea, not to anyone

effects.log: {npc} nods slowly, as if this were a known kind of weather, and kisses your forehead and goes back to the dancing. You are both, after, a little lighter and a little sadder.

events.arc: The Lamp of the Last Island
events.text: At the edge of the charts, where the islands thin out, there is a lighthouse kept by priests. They say its lamp has burned since the god first lit the sun, and that it shows ships the way home and shows the god the way back. The priests are short one keeper. The last one, they say, simply walked into the sea.

choices.text: Offer to keep the lamp for a year

effects.log: You trim wicks, haul oil up four hundred steps, and talk to gulls. The priests teach you their prayer, which is very short: Here. We are still here.

choices.text: Bring them oil and go home

effects.log: You row over a barrel of fish oil and the priests bless your boat. On your way home their light is behind you all night, and you never once lose your way.

choices.text: Ask what happened to the last keeper

effects.log: 'He said he saw someone walking on the water, coming home,' the eldest priest says. 'He went to meet them.' She does not seem to think he was mad.

events.arc: The Lamp of the Last Island
events.text: A night of fog so thick the lamp shines into nothing. Somewhere out there a fishing fleet is trying to find the Last Island, and you can hear their horns, lost, moving the wrong way.

choices.text: Climb out onto the gallery and swing the lamp's shutter by hand, in the old signal

ok.log: You work the shutter until your arms shake: long, short, long. One by one the horns turn toward you. Eleven boats come in. The twelfth was never lost, only rude.

fail.log: The shutter jams and cuts your hand. You keep the light burning steady instead. Eight boats come in at dawn. Three found another island. None were lost, in the end.

choices.text: Ring the fog bell instead, all night

effects.log: You ring until dawn, and in the grey light the fleet creeps in on the sound. Your ears ring for a week, but every boat comes home.

choices.text: Pray the keepers' prayer and trust the lamp

effects.log: Here. We are still here. You say it all night. In the morning the fog lifts and the fleet is anchored in the bay, and nobody can say how they found it.

events.arc: The Lamp of the Last Island
events.text: Your year as keeper ends. On the last night, sitting on the gallery, you see it: far out, where the sea ends, a second light, very faint, answering yours. Long. Short. Long.

choices.text: Answer it

effects.log: You work the shutter: here, we are still here. The far light goes out, slowly, like an eye closing in contentment. The priests ask what you saw. You tell them, and they write it in the lamp book.

choices.text: Wake the priests

effects.log: By the time they come up, the far light is gone. But the eldest priest looks at your face and writes something in the lamp book anyway, and underlines it twice.

choices.text: Watch it until it goes out

effects.log: You watch until it fades. You do not know what it was. You find you are crying, and do not know that either.

events.text: The salt of your island is famous across {pw_world}: white, fine, with a faint taste of violets that nobody can explain. The salt pans belong to six families who have quarrelled about them for three hundred years. One family is selling its pan, because the last of them wants to go and see the mainland, if there is one.

choices.text: Buy the pan with everything you have

effects.log: You become the seventh party in a three-hundred-year quarrel. The other six are united for the first time in living memory, against you.

choices.text: Work the pans for wages

effects.log: You rake salt under a white sun until your skin is leather. The pay is bad and the salt is beautiful, and you learn where the violet taste comes from: a little purple weed that grows only here.

choices.text: Help the last of the family find a boat to the far islands instead

effects.log: You find a berth for the salt-maker on Benna Sixsails's boat. The salt-maker gives you a jar of the best salt, the kind kept for weddings.

events.text: The six families come to your pan at dawn, together, with rakes. Not to fight, it turns out. They want to know if you mean to sell to the mainland traders, who pay double and would ruin the price for everyone.

choices.text: Promise to sell only through the old families

effects.log: The eldest of the six spits in her hand and shakes yours. You are in the quarrel now, on the inside, which is where all the warmth is.

choices.text: Sell to whoever pays most

effects.log: You make a great deal of money and nobody on the island will sit next to you at the festival. Your salt is still excellent.

choices.text: Propose that all seven pans sell as one

effects.log: It takes a year of shouting. Then the Violet Salt of the Seven Pans is sold across {pw_world} at a price that makes everyone rich, and they argue only about whose idea it was.

events.text: A storm floods the pans with seawater and mud, all seven. When the water drains, the purple weed is gone. Without it the salt is only salt. The families sit in the mud, looking at each other.

choices.text: Search the whole island for the weed

effects.log: You find one patch, clinging to the cliff under the temple. You replant it root by root. In three years the pans are violet again. A small statue of you goes up, very ugly.

choices.text: Pray at the temple for the weed to come back

effects.log: You pray, and for once you mean it. In the spring the weed comes back on its own, everywhere, more of it than before. The priests say the god listens to salt.

choices.text: Sell the plain salt and say nothing

effects.log: Nobody on the mainland can taste the difference for a year. Then everybody can. The price falls. The island forgives you slowly, as islands do.

events.text: Every eleven years the great whales pass between the islands on their way to wherever whales go, and every eleven years the islands argue about whether to follow them. The old songs say the whales know the road to the edge of the world, where the god sat down when the making was done.

choices.text: Follow the whales in a small boat

effects.log: You follow them for nine days. They let you. At night you hear them singing under the hull, a sound like the world thinking.

choices.text: Fish the waters they stir up

effects.log: The whales churn the sea and the fish rise in silver clouds. You fill your boat three times. You eat like a lord all winter.

choices.text: Watch them from the cliffs with everyone else

effects.log: The whole island sits on the cliffs with bread and children. The whales spout like fountains in the sunset. It is the best day of the year, and the whales do not know it.

events.text: On the ninth night, the biggest whale, a pale old one with a back like a hill, rises beside your boat and simply stays there, one great eye above the water, looking at you.

choices.text: Look back at it

effects.log: You look into the eye. It is very old and not at all surprised. You have the strangest feeling that it remembers you, from before the islands, from before it was a whale.

choices.text: Reach out and touch its skin

effects.log: It is warm and rough and alive. The whale breathes out, a hot fishy fog, and sinks away gently, as if it had been waiting a long time for just that.

choices.text: Turn back for home

effects.log: You turn your boat around. The whale sings once, low, and the sea shivers. You are home in eight days, fast, as if the current were helping.

events.text: You come home sunburnt, thin, and different. The island priest wants your story for the temple book; a singer wants it for a song; Benna Sixsails wants to know if there is trade at the edge of the world.

choices.text: Give the story to the temple

effects.log: The priest writes it down word for word. Pilgrims come to hear you tell it for years after. You get tired of it, and then you get fond of it.

choices.text: Give it to the singer

effects.log: The song is wildly inaccurate. You are much taller in it, and the whale talks. It is sung on every island for a hundred years.

choices.text: Tell nobody about the eye

effects.log: You tell the story of the journey, and leave out the eye. That part is yours. On bad nights you remember it and are less afraid of dying.

events.text: The moving island has come close. You can see it from the cliffs now: green, low, with a single white tower, sailing slowly against the wind, steady as a promise. The island council sends a boat to hail it. You are in the boat, because you were standing nearest.

choices.text: Climb onto its shore first

effects.log: The ground is soft and moves gently under your feet, like a deck. There are no people. There are gardens, kept, and a tower with an open door.

choices.text: Hail it from the boat, politely

effects.log: Nobody answers. But the island slows, for the first time anyone knows, and stays beside your boat for an hour, like a horse waiting to be mounted.

choices.text: Mark its course on a chart

effects.log: You chart its path carefully. It is going in a perfect straight line toward the place where the sea ends. The council does not know what to do with this information. Neither do you.

events.text: In the tower of the moving island there is one room, and in the room one chair, and on the chair a cloak of grey cloth folded as if someone had just taken it off. It is dry. It is warm.

choices.text: Put the cloak on

effects.log: It fits you exactly. That is the frightening part. You take it off and fold it the way you found it, and your hands know the fold.

choices.text: Leave everything as it is

effects.log: You back out and close the door. The island turns its back on you, slowly, and walks on toward the edge of the world.

choices.text: Take the cloak to the council

effects.log: The cloak goes cold the moment you leave the tower, and by the time you reach the boat it is only cloth. The council puts it in a box. You keep thinking about it.

events.text: The moving island is out of sight now, on its way. On clear nights you still see a faint light where it went, like a lamp in a window left on for someone who is late.

choices.text: Build a boat to follow it, one day

effects.log: You start a boat in your yard. It takes you years. You are not sure you will ever launch it. The building is the point.

choices.text: Light a lamp of your own at the cliff, every night

effects.log: You keep a lamp on the cliff. The island children call it your star. Some nights, very faintly, you think the far light flickers back.

choices.text: Let it go

effects.log: It was not yours. Or it was, once, and you gave it away. Either way it is going home. You sleep better than you have in years.

events.text: Once a year the Long Caravan comes through: four hundred wagons, a thousand oxen, and a dust cloud you can see for two days before it arrives. It crosses the whole of the continent, coast to coast, and takes three years to do it. The caravan master, an enormous calm woman called Hesper Wheel, is hiring.

choices.text: Join as an ox-driver

effects.log: Your first week you learn that oxen have opinions. Your second, that the caravan is a town on wheels, with its own bakers, its own feuds and its own temple, a cart with a bell on it.

choices.text: Sell the caravan bread and water

effects.log: You bake for two days without sleeping and sell everything at the roadside. The drivers pay in coins from cities you have never heard of. You keep one of each.

choices.text: Ask Hesper Wheel what lies at the far coast

effects.log: 'The other sea,' she says. 'And a city where they think we are the legend.' She looks at you as if measuring you for a wagon seat.

events.text: A year on the road. The plains go on so long that the caravan has a word for the feeling: grass-drunk, when the horizon has not changed for a month and the mind starts to float. Half the drivers have it. A wagon wheel cracks in the middle of nowhere.

choices.text: Mend the wheel with what you can find

effects.log: You splint it with a tent pole and rawhide and it holds for six hundred miles. Hesper Wheel calls it ugly and gives you a second wagon to drive.

choices.text: Start the caravan singing to break the grass-drunk

effects.log: You start a counting song and it runs down the line of wagons like a fire, four hundred wagons singing the same silly verse. Nobody is grass-drunk for a week.

choices.text: Walk ahead alone to see what is over the rise

effects.log: There is nothing over the rise but more grass, and a stone marker with a carved hand on it, very old, pointing on. You touch it. It is warm in the cold wind.

events.text: You reach the far coast. There is a sea here, grey instead of blue, and a city that has never seen the caravan's dust before because nobody in it is old enough. Its people stare at you as if you had come out of a story.

choices.text: Stay in the far city

effects.log: You stay. You are the most interesting person in the city for about a year, and after that you are just a neighbour, which is better.

choices.text: Ride the caravan home again

effects.log: Three more years to go back. You are a different person by the time the dust cloud reaches your own village, and your village is a different village.

choices.text: Ask the far city's priests about the carved hands on the road

effects.log: 'The Maker walked the whole continent once,' they say, 'to see if it was big enough. The hands mark where it rested.' You have touched one. It still feels warm.

events.text: The Grass Riders live on horseback in the middle of the continent, where no city has ever stuck. They come to the edge of your farmland every spring to trade colts for iron. This year their headwoman, Yarrow, points at you and says something in the riders' tongue that makes all of them laugh.

choices.text: Ask what she said

effects.log: It means, roughly, that one has legs like a foal. You are offended. Then you are offered a foal. You are less offended.

choices.text: Challenge her to a race on foot

effects.log: You lose by a great deal, to a woman of sixty. The riders lose their minds with joy and give you a riding lesson out of sheer goodwill.

choices.text: Trade fairly and keep your dignity

effects.log: You trade iron for a sturdy brown colt with an evil eye. It bites you. You love it immediately and hopelessly.

events.text: The riders come again and ask if you will ride with them for a summer. They follow the grass, which follows the rain, which follows, they say, the Maker's old footsteps across the continent.

choices.text: Ride with them

effects.log: A summer of grass to the horizon, sleeping under the sky, milk tea and wind. You come back sunburnt, bow-legged and unable to sleep under a roof.

choices.text: Stay and farm, and keep the colt

effects.log: The colt grows into a horse that pulls a plough as if it is personally insulted by the soil. Your field is the best ploughed in the valley.

choices.text: Ask Yarrow about the Maker's footsteps

effects.log: She takes you to a hill and points: the grass on the plain below grows in a faint long line, greener, as if someone walked there once and the land never forgot.

events.text: The Great Ride: every rider band races once a generation, across the plain from the Green Hill to the Bone Stone, three days without stopping. Yarrow is too old to ride it. She asks you to ride for her band.

choices.text: Ride the Great Ride

ok.log: You ride until you are part of the horse. On the third dawn you touch the Bone Stone first, and the plain howls your name. You are a rider of the grass for life.

fail.log: You fall at the river crossing and finish last, soaked and laughing. The riders say finishing at all is what counts. They are lying, kindly.

choices.text: Ride it for the joy and not for the stone

effects.log: You let the fast bands go and ride the plain at your own pace, singing. You come in on the fourth day. Yarrow says it was the best Great Ride she ever watched.

choices.text: Decline, and help her watch

effects.log: You sit with Yarrow on the Green Hill for three days. She tells you every Great Ride she remembers. It turns out to be the history of the whole plain.

events.text: Tobin Quill, map-maker to {pw_kingdom}, has spent his life mapping the continent and has a problem: his maps do not close. Walk far enough in any direction, he swears, and the coast is always a little further than it was last time. He needs an assistant with good legs and no imagination.

choices.text: Take the job, and pretend to have no imagination

effects.log: You carry chains and pegs across a hundred miles of country. Your imagination survives, quietly. Your legs become extraordinary.

choices.text: Tell him the world is probably just big

effects.log: 'Big is not the problem,' Tobin says. 'Growing is the problem.' He shows you two maps, ten years apart. The second coast really is further.

choices.text: Buy one of his old maps

effects.log: It is beautiful, wrong and cheap. You hang it on your wall, and over the years you notice that the world keeps not matching it, in exactly the way Tobin said.

events.text: On the western coast, Tobin's chains measure the shore twice in one week, and the second time it is a hand's width further out. There is new land, wet and grey, as if the world has been stretching in its sleep.

choices.text: Step onto the new land

effects.log: It is soft and warm and smells like rain on stone. Your foot leaves a print. By morning a small green shoot has come up in it.

choices.text: Help Tobin write it down properly

effects.log: You help him write a careful report for the court of {pw_kingdom}: the world is growing, one hand a week, westward. The court laughs. Tobin sends a second copy to the temple, who do not.

choices.text: Tell him to stop measuring before it notices

effects.log: Tobin looks at you strangely, and then he laughs, and then he stops laughing. He measures more quietly after that, like a man in a sleeping house.

events.text: Tobin Quill dies old, still mapping, and leaves you his last map. It is not finished. At its western edge, where the coast should be, he has written in a shaking hand: Still being made. Whoever made it, thank you.

choices.text: Finish the map

effects.log: You finish it, as far as the world goes this year. Next year it will be wrong. You write at the edge, under his line, in your own hand: Yes. Still.

choices.text: Give the map to the temple

effects.log: The priests hang it behind the altar. Pilgrims come to read the line at the edge. Some of them cry. Tobin would have been embarrassed and delighted.

choices.text: Keep it, and start your own maps

effects.log: You become a map-maker. Your maps are always a little wrong, westward, and you leave a gap at the edge of each one, out of respect.

events.text: Your village sits in the middle of the wheat sea: fields so wide that at harvest the wind makes waves in them all the way to the sky. Every child is told the same warning: never go into the wheat alone in the last week, when it is taller than you, because the wheat sea is the only sea that can drown you dry.

choices.text: Go in anyway, just a little way

effects.log: Three steps in, the world is gold and whispering and you cannot see the village. You come out backward, heart thumping, and never tell anyone.

choices.text: Climb the grain tower to look at it instead

effects.log: From the tower the wheat sea goes on forever, and the harvesters look like boats. You stay up there till dark and get told off and do not mind.

choices.text: Make a wheat-straw doll for the harvest

effects.log: Your doll is lopsided and has one eye. It is put on the first sheaf for luck anyway, because it was made by the youngest hand.

events.text: Harvest. The whole village goes into the wheat with sickles and songs, and the youngest children are given the most important job: running water out to the cutters, and listening for the Wheat Mother, who lives in the last sheaf and must be caught.

choices.text: Run water all day without stopping

effects.log: You run until your legs are jelly. Every cutter in the village knows your name by evening, and says it gratefully.

choices.text: Hunt the Wheat Mother in the last corner of the field

effects.log: You crawl into the last standing wheat and hear something rustle away from you, laughing, small. When you tell the grown-ups they look at each other and say: good, she is well.

choices.text: Fall asleep in the stubble

effects.log: You fall asleep in the shade of a stook and dream that the field is the sea and you are a fish. Someone carries you home. It is the best day.

events.text: The last sheaf is bound with ribbons and carried to the temple of the Maker. Every year one child is chosen to carry it in. This year the old priestess looks over all the children and picks you.

choices.text: Carry it in with great seriousness

effects.log: You walk so carefully that the whole village goes quiet. You lay the sheaf at the statue's feet and, for a moment, the statue seems to smile.

choices.text: Tell the priestess you heard the Wheat Mother laugh

effects.log: The priestess bends down to you. 'Then she chose you, not me,' she whispers. 'She only laughs for people the Maker likes.' You glow for a year.

choices.text: Give the honour to your smallest friend

effects.log: The smallest friend carries it in with tears of pride. The priestess gives you a nod across the temple that is worth more than the honour.

events.text: Your town sits on the river that divides two kingdoms of {pw_world}. On this bank they bow twice to the Maker; on that bank, three times. Over this, three wars have been fought. The bridge has been broken for forty years, and both banks are very proud of not mending it.

choices.text: Row across and buy bread on the other side

effects.log: The bread is better over there. You say so, loudly, at home. You are not invited to the next wedding.

choices.text: Learn to bow three times, in private

effects.log: It feels different, slower, more like a conversation. You do not know which way is right. You suspect the Maker never said.

choices.text: Stay on your bank and mind your business

effects.log: You mind your business. The river runs on between the kingdoms and does not bow at all.

events.text: A flood. The river rises in one night and the low streets of both banks go under. On the far side, an old woman is on her roof with a goat, and nobody on her bank has a boat.

choices.text: Row across the flood to fetch her

ok.log: You bring back the woman and the goat. Both banks watch you do it. Nobody says anything about bowing for a month.

fail.log: The current pushes you downstream and you only just make it to the far bank, where people from that side haul you out and dry you by their fire. They are perfectly nice.

choices.text: Shout across to her to hold on, and fetch the town

effects.log: Both banks, shouting at each other, finally agree to throw a rope across. It is the first thing the two towns have done together in forty years.

choices.text: Pray for the river to fall

effects.log: You pray, and the river does fall by morning. The old woman is fine. The goat ate her roof. Both banks thank the Maker, separately.

events.text: There is talk now, on both banks, of mending the bridge. Nobody will say it first. Someone has to stand up at the river festival, on one side or the other, and say: we will bow however you like, only give us back the bridge.

choices.text: Stand up and say it

effects.log: You say it. There is a dreadful silence. Then the old woman with the goat, on the far bank, stands up and says it back. The bridge is mended in a year.

choices.text: Suggest the bridge have both: two bows going, three bows coming

effects.log: Everyone laughs, and then nobody can think of a reason against it. The bridge has a bowing rule painted on it to this day.

choices.text: Leave it to the young

effects.log: You let the young ones do it. They mend the bridge without asking anyone, one night, and both kingdoms pretend to be outraged and are secretly delighted.

events.text: The Walking Market never stops. It moves across the continent at the speed of a slow ox, a whole town of stalls on wheels, and to buy anything you must walk alongside it while you haggle. Old traders here have one leg longer than the other from always walking on the left of the road.

choices.text: Buy something while walking

effects.log: You haggle for a copper kettle over two miles. You get it for half price because the trader is out of breath. You are out of breath too. It is a good kettle.

choices.text: Rent a stall for a season

effects.log: You sell pickles from a cart that never stops. By autumn you know every road on the continent and four new swear words.

choices.text: Sit by the road and watch it go by

effects.log: It takes the whole afternoon to pass. You see a fortune-teller, a dentist, a goat on a wagon roof, and a temple cart ringing its bell. It is better than a festival.

events.text: Disaster: the Walking Market has stopped. For the first time in two hundred years, every wheel in it is still, because at the head of the road a single tortoise is crossing, and the oldest law of the Market is: you do not run over a tortoise.

choices.text: Pick up the tortoise and carry it across

effects.log: There is a gasp from a thousand throats. Then a cheer. You are carried along the market on shoulders, while the tortoise looks deeply unimpressed.

choices.text: Use the stop to sell to everyone

effects.log: A market that cannot move is a market that wants pickles. You sell out in an hour.

choices.text: Wait, like a proper member of the Market

effects.log: You wait four hours with everyone else, sharing tea, telling stories. It is the friendliest four hours in the Market's history, and the tortoise gets across.

events.text: The Market elders give you a token for the tortoise affair: a small bronze wheel. It means, they say, that the Market will always slow down for you.

choices.text: Ask them to slow down for an old friend who walks badly

effects.log: The Market crawls past your friend's door for a whole morning so your friend can buy everything, at walking pace. Your friend weeps into a bag of figs.

choices.text: Keep it for a day you need it

effects.log: You keep the bronze wheel on a cord. Years later, old yourself, you will use it, and the Market will stop at your door, and you will buy one kettle, very slowly.

choices.text: Ask them how the Market began

effects.log: 'The Maker said the people should meet,' the eldest says. 'Nobody said where. So we decided: everywhere.' It is the most sensible thing you have ever heard a priest-free person say about a god.

events.text: On a sky island everyone knows somebody who fell. That is why the nets: great ropes strung under the edges of every island, mended every spring by the net-keepers, who are the most respected people in {pw_world}. You are chosen for net-keepers' school because you are small enough to crawl along the ropes.

choices.text: Crawl out along the ropes on the first day

effects.log: The sky goes down forever between your knees. You do not look. Then you look. It is the most beautiful and terrible thing you have ever seen, and you keep crawling.

choices.text: Learn the knots first, on the safe ground

effects.log: You learn eleven knots before you set foot on a rope. The old net-keeper says you will live long. From her that is the highest praise.

choices.text: Refuse: the edge is not for you

effects.log: You go back to the middle of the island, where the sheep are. Nobody blames you. The sheep are glad of you.

events.text: A gale. A whole family's washing, a cart and a boy go over the edge of the next island, and the boy lands in your nets, bounces, and hangs there screaming, three hundred feet out over nothing.

choices.text: Go out along the net to him

ok.log: You reach him, tie him to you, and crawl back with the net bucking under you like a horse. Both islands watch. The boy's family names a goat after you, which is a great honour.

fail.log: A rope snaps near your hand and you hang by one arm until the other keepers reach you both. You are all saved. Your shoulder is never quite the same.

choices.text: Throw him a line and talk him in

effects.log: You throw the line and talk, calmly, about nothing, about sheep, about his dinner, until he has crawled to you. Afterwards you shake for an hour.

choices.text: Run for the net-keepers

effects.log: You run faster than you have ever run. The keepers bring him in. You are given a keeper's cord for your speed, which is not nothing.

events.text: The old net-keeper retires. In the island's tradition she cuts a single strand from the oldest net, the one that hung there when the islands were made, and gives it to whoever will take her place.

choices.text: Take the strand, and the place

effects.log: You become the keeper of the nets of your island. You never sleep through a gale again. Every child who falls and lives is, in some way, yours.

choices.text: Ask her where the oldest net came from

effects.log: 'Nobody tied it,' she says. 'It was here at the making. The Maker did not want anyone to fall. Not even then.' She presses the strand into your hand anyway.

choices.text: Give the place to someone braver

effects.log: You give it to the boy from the gale, grown now, who has never stopped looking at the nets. He is a fine keeper. You are proud of yourself for once.

events.text: Two islands drift close together for one month every year, close enough for a rope bridge to be thrown across. For that month the islands are one town: markets, feuds, and a great many romances that end when the islands drift apart. On the bridge, on the first day, {npc} drops a basket of plums on your head.

choices.text: Help pick up the plums

mem.note: chased plums with me on the bridge

effects.log: You chase plums across the bridge, laughing, while the islands sway. {npc} gives you the bruised ones as a reward, which is honest at least.

choices.text: Complain loudly

mem.note: argued with me on the bridge

effects.log: {npc} complains back, louder and funnier. A crowd gathers. It becomes the best argument of the month, and you both enjoy it far too much.

choices.text: Walk on

effects.log: You walk on with plum juice in your hair. You think about {npc} for the rest of the day, which is annoying.

events.text: The last night of the bridge month. Tomorrow the islands drift apart and will not touch again for a year. {npc} is on the bridge, at the exact middle, where everyone goes to say what they mean before the ropes are cut.

choices.text: Meet {npc} at the middle of the bridge

mem.note: met me at the middle of the bridge

effects.log: You talk until the ropes creak. When the keepers come to cut the bridge, they look at you two and go away again for an hour.

choices.text: Send a kite after the islands part

mem.note: sent me a kite across the sky

effects.log: You wait until morning and fly a kite with a message across the widening gap. It lands on {npc}'s roof. The answer comes back on another kite, three days later.

choices.text: Stay on your island

effects.log: The ropes are cut at dawn. You watch the other island float away with {npc} on it, getting smaller, until it is a cloud among clouds.

events.text: The islands meet again. This time {npc} is waiting with a bag packed. On sky islands, whoever marries crosses the bridge for good, and one island loses a person and the other gains one, and there is a song for both.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to cross to your island and marry you

effects.log: {npc} crosses with the bag and the whole of your island sings the gaining song. The other island sings the losing one, and means it kindly.

choices.text: Cross to {npc}'s island yourself, and marry there

effects.log: You cross the bridge with everything you own. The ropes are cut behind you. You are home in a new place, and married, and a little dizzy.

choices.text: Say it is better once a year

effects.log: {npc} considers this, seriously, and agrees. Every year after, for one month, you are the happiest pair in {pw_world}. The rest of the time you write.

events.text: Under every sky island the roots hang down into the clouds like beards, and among the roots, upside down, live the Root Folk: people who walk on the underside of the world and think that those who live on top are the strange ones. One of them has climbed up to your island to complain about your drains.

choices.text: Apologise and fix the drains

effects.log: You fix the drains. The Root Folk send up a gift: a jar of honey made by bees that fly upside down. It tastes faintly of cloud.

choices.text: Argue that the drains were there first

effects.log: The root-dweller argues that the roots were there first, and wins. It turns out to be very hard to argue with someone hanging by their feet.

choices.text: Ask what the world looks like from underneath

effects.log: 'Like a ceiling with a sky on the other side,' the root-dweller says. 'We pray to the Maker as well. Up. Which for us is down.' You think about that for a week.

events.text: The Root Folk invite you down. You climb over the edge on a root ladder, turn over at the root-line, and suddenly the clouds are your floor and your island is a great dark roof full of hanging gardens.

choices.text: Stay a month and learn their crafts

effects.log: You learn root-weaving, cloud-fishing and how to sleep hanging. You come back up and fall over for three days.

choices.text: Visit their upside-down temple

effects.log: Their temple hangs from the deepest root, a carved Maker facing down into the cloud. From underneath, you realise, the statue's open hands are catching, not giving.

choices.text: Climb back up quickly, dizzy

effects.log: You last an hour. The Root Folk are very understanding about it, and give you a root charm against falling, which you wear forever.

events.text: A drought on top: no rain for a season, and your island's cisterns are dry. The Root Folk, underneath, live inside the clouds and have all the water they could want. Your island council wants you to ask them.

choices.text: Ask the Root Folk as a friend

effects.log: They send up water in root-buckets for the whole season and refuse payment. 'Drains,' they say, meaningfully. Your island never forgets.

choices.text: Offer the council's silver for their water

effects.log: They take the silver politely, and send the water, and you sense it would have come anyway. The council looks a little foolish. So do you.

choices.text: Ask the Maker for rain at their upside-down temple

effects.log: You pray facing down into the cloud. That night it rains on top for the first time in a season. The Root Folk say the god has always been easier to reach from below.

events.text: Your island is drifting. Slowly, a finger's width a day, it is moving away from the others, toward the empty blue where nothing lives. The islanders say the anchor stones, deep in the island's heart, have gone to sleep. Someone has to go down and wake them.

choices.text: Volunteer to go down

effects.log: You go down the old stair with a lamp and a rope, past the cellars, past the wells, into rooms of warm rock that hum.

choices.text: Help the island tie ropes to its neighbours

effects.log: Ropes as thick as trees, thrown across the gap and tied to the next island's trees. It slows the drift. It also starts a lawsuit about the trees.

choices.text: Pack your things, just in case

effects.log: You pack your things and sit on them. Your neighbours mock you. You notice they are also, quietly, packing.

events.text: In the heart of the island there are three great stones set in a ring, each carved with a word in a script nobody can read. They hum. One of them has stopped humming.

choices.text: Put your hand on the silent stone

effects.log: Under your palm the stone warms, and you understand the word on it, the way you understand your own name: STAY. It begins to hum.

choices.text: Sing to it, the way the old wives sing to bread

effects.log: You sing a rising song, badly, to a stone. The stone, which has heard worse, begins to hum along. The island shivers and stops drifting.

choices.text: Fetch the priests

effects.log: The priests come down and chant for three days. The stone wakes on the third. Nobody is sure if it was the chanting. The priests are.

events.text: The island is back in its place among the others. The priests want to know what happened down there, and the council wants to know how to make sure it never happens again.

choices.text: Tell them the stone said STAY

effects.log: The priests write it on the temple door, and it becomes the island's motto. Children say it to each other when they go away. It is a very good word for an island.

choices.text: Suggest someone visit the stones every year

effects.log: A stone-singer is chosen every spring now, to go down and sing to the anchors. It becomes the island's favourite job and fiercest election.

choices.text: Say nothing and go back to work

effects.log: You go back to work. Sometimes at night you feel the island humming through your floor, and it feels like being held.

events.text: There are no rivers on a sky island. Water comes from the clouds, milked with long combs of fine wire on the windward edge every morning, by cloud-milkers who are proud, damp and unbearable at parties. The head milker is looking for an apprentice who does not mind being wet forever.

choices.text: Apprentice yourself to the cloud-milkers

effects.log: You are wet from the first day to the last. You learn to tell a good cloud from a bad one by smell. A good cloud smells like a clean sheet.

choices.text: Invent a better comb

effects.log: Your comb catches twice as much water and three times as many birds. The milkers are not grateful. The birds are less grateful.

choices.text: Stay dry and buy water like a sensible person

effects.log: You buy your water by the jug like everyone else, and listen to the milkers boast at the inn. They boast about clouds the way other people boast about horses.

events.text: A thundercloud, black and heavy, comes drifting straight at the island. Old milkers say a thundercloud milked carefully gives a year's water in one morning. Milked carelessly, it gives you a very new hairstyle.

choices.text: Milk the thundercloud

ok.log: You comb it slowly, gently, talking to it like an angry goat. The cisterns fill to the brim. The milkers carry you round the island on a water barrel.

fail.log: Lightning finds your comb. You are fine, eventually. Your hair stands straight up for a month and the island children follow you around to look at it.

choices.text: Warn everyone to get indoors

effects.log: You ring the cloud bell and the island takes cover. The storm passes over with a lot of noise and no harm. The milkers grumble about wasted water.

choices.text: Watch it from your window with tea

effects.log: It is a magnificent storm. You drink your tea and feel enormously wise.

events.text: The island's cisterns are full, thanks in part to you. The head milker, who has never praised anyone, comes to your door with a cloud-comb of old silver and does not say anything at all for a long time.

choices.text: Accept the old comb

effects.log: It is the comb the first milker used, the head milker says at last, the one the Maker left on the windward edge when the islands were made. You feel it hum in your hand.

choices.text: Tell her she should keep it

effects.log: She looks relieved and offended at once. You both have a drink. It turns into a very long and very wet friendship.

choices.text: Ask for a raise instead

effects.log: She laughs for the first time anyone can remember, and gives you one.

events.text: Two islands are going to collide. Not yours, quite, but the one beside yours, Lark, and the one beside that, Pell. They have hated each other for a century. In three weeks they will meet with a sound like the world clapping, and the astronomers say they will stick.

choices.text: Go to Lark and help them prepare

effects.log: You help tie down roofs and move the old and the goats to the far side. Lark's people are frightened and very rude. You like them anyway.

choices.text: Go to Pell and help them prepare

effects.log: You help Pell build padding walls of straw along their edge. Pell's people are frightened and very proud. You like them anyway.

choices.text: Sell padding straw to both

effects.log: You sell straw to both sides at the same price. Both sides think you are cheating them. You are the only honest merchant in the matter.

events.text: The collision. A deep, long sound, and the two islands grind together and stop. Nobody is hurt. Two towns that have not spoken in a century are now joined by a ridge of crumpled meadow, and everybody is standing on it, staring at everybody else.

choices.text: Walk to the middle of the ridge and introduce yourself

effects.log: You shake hands with the first person from the other side. Then, because everyone is watching, everyone has to. It takes all afternoon.

choices.text: Start the cleanup together

effects.log: You pick up a fallen fence and hand one end to a stranger from the other side. Work is the only language both islands speak.

choices.text: Keep to your side and see what happens

effects.log: Nothing happens for a week, and then two dogs make friends, and then two children, and then it is too late for anyone to stop it.

events.text: The joined island needs a name. Lark wants Lark, Pell wants Pell, and the council meetings have been going on for a year. They ask you, because you helped both, to choose.

choices.text: Call it Larkpell

effects.log: Pell hates it. Lark hates it. Everyone uses it within a year. It is a good name, for a place made of two quarrels.

choices.text: Name it after the Maker, who brought them together

effects.log: There is an uncomfortable silence, and then the priests of both islands nod together for the first time. The island is called Maker's Meeting.

choices.text: Refuse: they have to choose it themselves

effects.log: They are furious with you, and then with each other, and then, finally, they choose together. It is a dreadful name. It is theirs.

events.text: In your valley, if you shout across to the far cliff, the echo comes back. Everyone's does. But the old people say that once in a lifetime, if you shout the right thing, the echo comes back different: an answer.

choices.text: Shout your name

effects.log: Your name comes back. Then, very faintly, after it, a second time, as if someone on the far cliff were trying it out. You run home without stopping.

choices.text: Shout a question: who made the mountains?

effects.log: The question comes back to you, the same. Then silence. Then a sound like a laugh, or a rockfall. Your friends swear it was a rockfall.

choices.text: Shout something rude

effects.log: It comes back ruder. Your friends fall over laughing. You decide the mountains have a sense of humour, and you like them better for it.

events.text: Winter. The valley is snowed in, and the children are bored enough to climb to the Echo Ledge, which is forbidden, to have a contest: whoever gets an answer wins all the winter sweets.

choices.text: Climb to the ledge with them

effects.log: You climb, cold and giggling. Everyone shouts. Nothing answers. Then you shout, and the valley goes quiet the way it does before snow, and stays quiet, listening.

choices.text: Tell an adult, and get everyone in trouble

effects.log: Everyone gets in trouble. Nobody falls off the ledge. You lose your friends for a week and you keep their lives, and you decide, at nine, that this is a fair trade.

choices.text: Shout from the bottom instead, where it is safe

effects.log: From the bottom, your shout goes up and up and comes back down like snow, very soft. The others above hear it and think it is an answer. You never tell them otherwise.

events.text: You are older now, and you go back to the Echo Ledge alone, to try once more before you are too grown-up to believe in it.

choices.text: Shout: I am here

effects.log: The mountains say it back. Then, after a long time, in a voice that is a little like yours and a little like the wind, they say: I know. You do not tell anyone, ever.

choices.text: Shout: thank you

effects.log: It comes back thank you, thank you, thank you, rolling along the whole range. You feel ridiculous and happy. Somewhere a goat looks up.

choices.text: Say nothing, and just listen

effects.log: You listen. The mountains are full of small sounds: water under ice, a bird, wind. It is like hearing someone breathe in their sleep.

events.text: Between the valleys of {pw_world} there are no roads, only goat-tracks, and the post is carried by goat-runners: people who can run along a path the width of a hand above a drop the depth of a sky. Old Hamm, the fastest runner of his day, is looking for someone to carry his route.

choices.text: Learn the routes from Hamm

effects.log: He makes you carry a bucket of water along a ledge without spilling it. It takes a month. Then he gives you the post bag.

choices.text: Buy a goat and learn from it instead

effects.log: The goat teaches you nothing, eats your coat, and is the best friend you will ever have.

choices.text: Write letters, and let someone else carry them

effects.log: You become the best letter-writer in the valley, which is a different kind of runner: one who sends people's hearts across the mountains.

events.text: A letter must cross three valleys by tomorrow: a healer is needed for a child with fever, and the healer is on the far side of the Knife, a ridge where the goat-track is so thin that runners call it praying with your feet.

choices.text: Run the Knife

ok.log: You run the Knife at dusk with the wind pulling at you. The healer comes the next day. The child lives. The valley carves your name on the runners' post, under Hamm's.

fail.log: You slip, catch a root, hang over nothing, and haul yourself up. You arrive late, bleeding, but you arrive. The child lives anyway. You are shaking for a week.

choices.text: Take the long way round, and run all night

effects.log: The long way takes all night. You arrive at dawn, staggering. The healer is in time, just. You sleep for two days.

choices.text: Light the signal fires instead

effects.log: You light the old signal fires along the ridges, a chain of flame across the valleys. The healer sees them and comes. Nobody had used the fires in fifty years.

events.text: Hamm is dying, and wants to run his first route one last time. He cannot walk to the door. He asks you to carry him along it, on your back, the way runners carry the post.

choices.text: Carry him the whole route

effects.log: You carry him along the ledges at a walk. He names every stone. At the last valley he says: good, and then nothing more, and you carry him home.

choices.text: Carry him to the first ridge, where he can see it all

effects.log: He sees the whole route from the ridge, every valley, every track, all of it his. 'The Maker made these for goats,' he says. 'We just borrowed them.' He laughs and closes his eyes.

choices.text: Bring the goats to him instead

effects.log: You bring every goat in the valley to his window. He laughs until he cries. It is the best death in the valley that year.

events.text: In the Cliff of a Thousand Faces, each generation of carvers adds one face of the Maker to the rock. No two are alike, because nobody has ever seen the Maker. The guild of carvers is choosing its next apprentice by asking every candidate the same question: what does the god look like?

choices.text: Say: like everyone

effects.log: The masters look at each other. You are taken. 'That is the only right answer,' the eldest says, 'and it is wrong every time.'

choices.text: Say: like no one

effects.log: You are not taken. But the eldest carver walks you out and says you should come back when you have seen someone who looks like no one.

choices.text: Say nothing and draw a face in the dust

effects.log: You draw without thinking. The eldest looks at the drawing a long time, and then at you, and then very hard at you. You are taken.

events.text: Your face. Ten years of practice, and now a ledge has been given to you, high up, near the oldest faces. The rock is waiting. All the carvers will judge it.

choices.text: Carve the face you saw in a dream

effects.log: You carve for a whole summer. When you step back, the others go quiet. It looks like you, a little, and like someone much older than you, a lot.

choices.text: Carve the face of someone you love

effects.log: You carve the face of someone dear to you, and call it the Maker. Pilgrims touch it for luck. The person is mortified and secretly thrilled.

choices.text: Carve a face with its eyes closed, resting

effects.log: A sleeping god. Some carvers are scandalised. The children of the valley love it best of all, and leave it blankets of flowers.

events.text: A blind pilgrim comes to the Cliff and asks to be led to the face that is truest. The carvers argue. Then they send her to you.

choices.text: Lead her to your own face

effects.log: She puts her hands on the stone, then turns and puts them on your face. She is very quiet. Then she says: oh, it is you. And bows.

choices.text: Lead her to the oldest face

effects.log: The oldest face is worn almost smooth by ten thousand hands. She touches it and smiles. 'Everyone has touched this,' she says. 'That is what makes it true.'

choices.text: Lead her to a stranger in the crowd

effects.log: You put her hand in the hand of a random pilgrim. She laughs out loud. 'Yes,' she says. 'That one too.' The carvers argue about it for twenty years.

events.text: In the high valleys every house has a bell on a long rope, and the rule is simple: if you hear the mountain crack, you ring, and everyone below runs uphill and sideways. This winter, the snow is deeper than anyone has seen, and the mountain is making small noises at night.

choices.text: Take a turn on the night watch

effects.log: You sit up in the cold with a lantern, listening. The mountain creaks like an old house. It is the longest night of your life, and nothing happens.

choices.text: Dig an escape trench above the village

effects.log: You dig in the snow with three neighbours for a week. They call you mad. You feel mad. The trench is very good.

choices.text: Ask the priest to bless the slope

effects.log: The priest blesses the slope, at length. The mountain does not seem to notice. Still, it makes everyone sleep a little better.

events.text: It comes at dawn. A crack like the sky breaking, and a white wave starting down the far slope toward the lower houses, where people are still asleep.

choices.text: Ring the bell with everything you have

effects.log: You ring until the rope burns your hands. Doors open below. People run, in nightclothes, uphill and sideways, the way the rule says.

choices.text: Run down to wake the lowest house

ok.log: You get them out, a family of five and their dog, and you all reach the trench as the snow goes past below you like a white river.

fail.log: The snow catches the edge of you and rolls you down the slope. You are dug out, bruised and blue, by the people you went to warn.

choices.text: Run uphill, as the rule says

effects.log: You run uphill and sideways and live, and you are ashamed of nothing: the rule is the rule because it keeps the most people alive.

events.text: Spring. The avalanche has scoured the lower slope and torn the old bell-tower down. In its wreckage the villagers find something no one knew was there: a bell much older than the village, of a bronze that does not tarnish.

choices.text: Hang the old bell in the new tower

effects.log: It rings with a voice that carries across three valleys. The mountain is quiet for a hundred years after. The priests say it was the Maker's own bell.

choices.text: Give it to the temple

effects.log: The temple keeps it on the altar. On the anniversary of the avalanche, it rings once, by itself. Nobody can explain it. Everybody stops what they are doing.

choices.text: Melt it down for the rebuilding

effects.log: The bronze buys new roofs for every house the snow took. Some say it was a sacrilege. The people with roofs mostly do not.

events.text: Your valley farms in terraces cut into the mountainside, a staircase of fields from the snowline to the river. Water comes down from the top, field by field, and the oldest law of the valley is the water-share: every terrace gets its hour. The family at the top has started keeping theirs for two.

choices.text: Climb up and talk to them

effects.log: The top family is old and frightened; their spring is failing. They are keeping water because they think they will die without it. Nobody had asked.

choices.text: Call the water council

effects.log: The council meets in the threshing barn and argues for nine hours. Nothing is decided except that the top family is selfish. This does not help.

choices.text: Open the channel yourself at night

effects.log: The water comes down to your terrace. In the morning the whole valley knows who did it. You are right, and nobody likes you for it.

events.text: The spring at the top of the valley is failing, the first time in living memory. The old people say it comes from the god's own well, high up in the snow, and that someone must go and see.

choices.text: Climb to the snow and find the god's well

effects.log: You climb for two days. At the top there is a ring of stones and a spring, choked with a fallen rock. You move the rock. The water sings.

choices.text: Dig a new channel from the next valley

effects.log: It takes the whole valley a summer. The new water tastes different. The old people say it is the wrong water. The crops do not seem to mind.

choices.text: Help the top family move down, where the water is

effects.log: The top family comes down to live among the rest. Their old terrace goes wild, and wildflowers grow on it, and nobody fights over water that summer.

events.text: The water runs right again, every terrace in its hour. At the harvest festival the valley wants to thank someone, and is looking at you.

choices.text: Tell them about the stones at the god's well

effects.log: The priests climb up to see. They come back pale. The ring of stones, they say, is carved with the water-share, word for word, older than the valley.

choices.text: Thank the top family instead, for giving way

effects.log: The old couple from the top are seated at the head of the feast, very embarrassed. The valley learns that being thanked is a cure for a great many quarrels.

choices.text: Thank the mountain

effects.log: You raise your cup to the mountain. Everyone does. It is the only toast in the valley's history that nobody argued with.

events.text: The highest peak of {pw_world} has never been climbed. The priests say it is where the Maker stood to look at the finished world, and that on the summit there is a single footprint in the rock. Every generation someone tries. Every generation the mountain sends them home, or keeps them.

choices.text: Begin training for the climb

effects.log: You climb lesser peaks for two years. You learn the cold, the thin air, the way the mind gets slow and stupid above the clouds.

choices.text: Ask the families of those who tried

effects.log: They give you letters, maps, a broken ice-axe, and a great deal of grief. You learn the mountain's moods from the dead.

choices.text: Decide that some places should stay unclimbed

effects.log: You leave the peak alone. It looks down on your life, white and patient, and you never feel that it disapproves.

events.text: The climb. Above the last camp the air is so thin that every step is a decision. The summit is in sight, and so is a storm, coming in from the west, fast.

choices.text: Go for the summit before the storm

ok.log: You reach the top with the storm at your heels. There, in the rock, is a footprint, bare, a little bigger than yours. You put your foot in it. It fits better than it should.

fail.log: The storm catches you below the summit and you dig into the snow and wait it out. You come down alive, with frozen toes and nothing to show but the living.

choices.text: Turn back and live

effects.log: You turn back. It is the hardest thing you have ever done. Below the clouds, the air tastes like bread, and you are glad to be alive.

choices.text: Wait out the storm in the last camp

effects.log: You wait three days in a tent the size of a coffin. When the sky clears, you are too weak to go up. You go down, slowly, and the mountain lets you.

events.text: You are home. The priests want to know if the footprint is there. The whole valley wants to know.

choices.text: Tell them it is there, and that it fits you

effects.log: There is a silence in the temple like the silence on the summit. The high priest looks at your feet, then your face, and then he sends for the oldest book they have.

choices.text: Tell them it is there, and leave it at that

effects.log: You tell them it is there. Pilgrims will try to climb for a thousand years to see it. Most will turn back, as you taught them.

choices.text: Tell them you do not know

effects.log: You tell them what is true: the mountain is very high and very cold and very beautiful, and you came home. It turns out to be what the valley needed to hear.

events.text: The first fire of {pw_world}, the one the Maker gave, has never gone out. It burns in the Ember House in the oldest city, and every hearth in the world was lit from it once, carried in a clay pot by somebody walking. Once a year every town sends a pot to be relit. This year your town sends you.

choices.text: Carry the pot the whole way on foot, as is proper

effects.log: Forty days there, forty back, with a coal in a clay pot you must feed with dry moss every hour. You learn more about patience than in your whole life before.

choices.text: Take a cart, and feed it on the way

effects.log: The cart is faster and the coal nearly dies twice in the rain. You learn that fire does not care how you travel, only whether you pay attention.

choices.text: Ask why a town cannot just make its own fire

effects.log: 'It can,' says the old woman who chose you. 'But then it would just be fire.' You do not understand her for twenty years, and then you do.

events.text: The Ember House: a round hall, a great fire, and the keepers in grey who feed it and never let anyone else near. When you hold out your pot, the eldest keeper looks at you, then at the fire, which has leaned toward you as if a door had opened.

choices.text: Step closer to the fire

effects.log: It does not burn you. It is warm the way a hand is warm. The keepers stop what they are doing. One of them drops a log.

choices.text: Hold out the pot and look at the floor

effects.log: The keeper fills your pot quickly and sends you away. Behind you, you hear the keepers whispering.

choices.text: Ask the keeper what just happened

effects.log: 'The fire knows who it belongs to,' the keeper says, and then looks as if she wishes she had not said it. 'Go home. Keep it burning.'

events.text: Home again, the town relit from your pot. Years later a letter comes from the Ember House, sealed with soot. The keepers ask, very politely, whether you would come and tend the first fire. They have never asked anyone before.

choices.text: Go and become a keeper

effects.log: You tend the first fire of the world for the rest of your days. It never goes out. On cold nights it leans toward you, and the other keepers have stopped pretending not to see.

choices.text: Stay home and keep your own hearth

effects.log: You write back that one hearth is enough for you. The keepers send a coal anyway, wrapped in moss, and your hearth never goes out in your lifetime.

choices.text: Visit once, to thank them

effects.log: You visit and sit by the first fire for a night. It crackles at you like an old friend telling a joke you have heard before and still like.

events.text: {pw_world} is a world of rivers, the Maker's first gift, and the rivers have ferries, and the ferries have the Ferry Guild: the oldest, slowest and most argumentative body in the land. A ferry-woman named Lisbet Pole is retiring and selling her raft, her pole and her place in the Guild, which comes with a seat and a vote.

choices.text: Buy the raft and the vote

effects.log: You become a ferry-keeper. You learn the river's moods, the Guild's moods, and which of the two is more dangerous.

choices.text: Work the raft for her a season first

effects.log: Lisbet teaches you the river for a season, unpaid, and you learn more from her silence than from most people's talk.

choices.text: Cross on the ferry and wish her well

effects.log: She ferries you across one last time and tells you the river's name, which is a secret only ferry-folk keep. You have no idea why she told you.

events.text: The Guild meets once a year on a raft lashed together from a hundred rafts in the middle of the widest river. This year the vote is whether to build a bridge. A bridge would end the ferries. It would also end people drowning.

choices.text: Vote for the bridge

effects.log: You vote for the bridge, and lose by one vote, and half the Guild never speaks to you again, and the other half buys you tea.

choices.text: Vote against, and propose ropes across the deep crossings

effects.log: Your rope plan passes. The ferries stay. The drownings fall to almost nothing. You are a hero to everybody for about a month.

choices.text: Watch the meeting from the bank

effects.log: From the bank, a hundred rafts arguing in the middle of a river is the funniest thing you have ever seen. You laugh until you have to sit down.

events.text: In a dry summer the widest river drops lower than ever, and in the mud of its bed, where the Guild meets, something shows: a great flat stone, carved with a wavy line running from one end to the other, and at the end, an open hand.

choices.text: Trace the line with your finger

effects.log: It is a map, you realise: every river in the world, running to the sea, drawn by someone who knew them all before they had water in them.

choices.text: Tell the Guild

effects.log: The Guild argues about the stone for three days and votes, narrowly, that it belongs to the river. The river takes it back with the autumn floods.

choices.text: Say the river's secret name over it

effects.log: You whisper the name Lisbet told you. The water at your feet, low as it is, turns once around the stone, like a dog settling. You decide not to tell anybody.

events.text: The World Tree stands at the middle of {pw_world}, so tall its top is lost in the sky, so wide a city lives in its roots. Once a century it drops a single leaf, as big as a sail, and wherever it lands that town is blessed. This year the Leaf is coming down, slowly, turning, and every child in the world is watching the sky.

choices.text: Follow the Leaf as it falls, running

effects.log: You run for a day under the falling Leaf with a hundred other children. You do not catch it. You have never been so happy to be tired.

choices.text: Climb a hill and work out where it will land

effects.log: You watch the wind and guess. Your guess is right. Your town is the next one over. You are furious and proud.

choices.text: Pray that it lands somewhere poor

effects.log: It lands on a poor fishing village that has had three bad years. You decide, at eight, that the Maker listens.

events.text: The Tree-Climbers are a guild who live in the great branches, harvesting the fruit that grows there and the rain that pools in the bark. They take new climbers once a year, from anyone who can climb the first hundred feet of bark without a rope.

choices.text: Climb the first hundred feet

ok.log: You reach the first branch, which is as wide as a road. The climbers clap you on the back. You can see the whole world from here, and it is very small.

fail.log: You slip at sixty feet and slide down the bark, burning your hands. The climbers say try again next year, and mean it.

choices.text: Sell fruit from the roots market instead

effects.log: The fruit of the Tree tastes different every season. You learn to tell them all apart and sell them by their flavours. You are rich in a small, sweet way.

choices.text: Sit against the trunk and listen

effects.log: Put your ear to the trunk and the Tree is full of sound: water rising, a slow deep hum like a voice too big to make words.

events.text: The Tree-Climbers speak of the Crown: the very top of the Tree, above the clouds, where no climber has been in a thousand years. There, they say, the Maker planted the seed and sat to watch it grow.

choices.text: Climb to the Crown

effects.log: Days of climbing, nights roped to the bark. At the top, above the clouds, there is a hollow worn smooth in the wood, like a seat. You sit in it. The Tree sighs, all through, like someone glad to be home.

choices.text: Leave the Crown to the birds

effects.log: Some places are not for people. You harvest the middle branches all your life, and the Tree is good to you, and the top stays in the sky.

choices.text: Plant one of the Tree's seeds at home

effects.log: The seed grows. It is not a World Tree, only a tree. But it is the best tree in your village, and children climb it, and that is enough.

events.arc: The Courtship of Sun and Moon
events.text: The sun and the moon of {pw_world} were the Maker's first gift, and everyone knows the story: they are in love, and can only meet at an eclipse, and the rest of the time they chase each other round the sky. The great eclipse, the one that comes once a lifetime, is this summer, and every town is preparing the Wedding of the Sky.

choices.text: Build a paper sun for the parade

effects.log: Your paper sun is bigger than the house and catches fire twice. It is in the parade anyway, slightly singed, and everyone cheers it.

choices.text: Build a paper moon for the parade

effects.log: Your paper moon is beautiful, pale, and keeps blowing away. You chase it through the town three times. It becomes a whole part of the festival.

choices.text: Ask the astronomer whether they are really in love

effects.log: The astronomer sighs. 'They are lumps of light on fixed paths,' she says. 'And yes. Obviously. Look at them.'

events.arc: The Courtship of Sun and Moon
events.text: The eclipse. The whole town on the hill at noon, and the moon sliding across the sun, and the light going strange and silver and cold, and the birds going to sleep, and a ring of fire in a dark sky.

choices.text: Look at it through smoked glass, as you were told

effects.log: Through the glass the ring of fire is perfect. You feel, very clearly, that somebody arranged this, and arranged it to be beautiful.

choices.text: Watch the people instead

effects.log: Everyone's face is turned up, open, silver. You see your whole town for a moment as someone might who loved it from very far away.

choices.text: Shout the wedding toast with everyone

effects.log: The whole hill shouts: long may they chase! It echoes across the valley. Somewhere a dog joins in.

events.arc: The Courtship of Sun and Moon
events.text: After the eclipse, an old woman of the town tells you a version of the story you have never heard. In hers, the Maker did not make the sun and moon in love. The Maker made them, and they fell in love on their own, and the Maker was so surprised it wept, and the tears are the stars.

choices.text: Tell her you like her version best

effects.log: She pats your hand. 'So did the Maker,' she says. 'That is why it let them keep chasing.' You never hear it told that way again.

choices.text: Ask how she knows

effects.log: 'I asked,' she says, and will not say who. That night you dream of a sky with no stars at all, and then, one by one, stars.

choices.text: Laugh, and tell her the astronomer's version
