effects.log: She laughs too. 'Both,' she says. 'Lumps of light, and in love. Most things are both.' You think that is the wisest thing anyone has ever said to you.

events.text: In {pw_world} it is always spring. Nobody has ever seen snow. But there is a rumour, among travellers, of a place at the edge of the world where white feathers fall from the sky and are cold. Most people think it is a story for children. A traveller in the market says she has a jar of it.

choices.text: Pay to see the jar

effects.log: The jar holds water. 'It was snow when I bottled it,' she says, offended. You are not sure she is lying, which is the worst feeling.

choices.text: Laugh at her

effects.log: She laughs back. 'Wait till you see it,' she says. 'Then you will not laugh. Or you will laugh differently.'

choices.text: Ask her to describe it

effects.log: She describes it for an hour: cold, white, silent, falling. Every child in the market gathers to listen. Nobody believes her, and nobody leaves.

events.text: A strange morning: the air is colder than anyone remembers. Old people put on second shirts. And then, for the space of a few breaths, something white and soft falls out of the sky onto the blossoming trees.

choices.text: Catch some on your tongue

effects.log: It is cold and tastes of nothing and is gone at once. You stand with your mouth open in the street like a fool, and you are not alone.

choices.text: Run for the traveller and her jar

effects.log: She is in the square, laughing, holding the jar up to catch it. 'Told you,' she says. 'Told every one of you.'

choices.text: Run to the temple to ask what it means

effects.log: The priests are as baffled as you. The eldest finally says: the Maker is showing us something we were spared. You think about that for a long time.

events.text: It never snows again. But your town now has a Snow Day festival, once a year, where everyone throws white petals in the air and pretends to shiver. Children who were not born then ask you what it was really like.

choices.text: Tell them it was cold and beautiful and brief

effects.log: You tell them. They are disappointed it was so short. You tell them the best things usually are, and they roll their eyes, and you were the same at their age.

choices.text: Tell them it was enormous, and lasted a week

effects.log: They believe you entirely. The story grows. In fifty years the Snow Day is a three-day festival and you are a legend who survived the Great Cold.

choices.text: Take them to the hills to look for a cold place

effects.log: You find a cave where the air is cool. It is not snow. They love it anyway, and spend the whole day shivering on purpose.

events.text: In your town the year has four doors: at each change of season the whole town walks through a carved gate at the edge of the fields, the Spring Door, the Summer Door, the Autumn Door, the Winter Door, as if the season were a house to be entered. Children get to choose which door they love best, and that is their door for life.

choices.text: Choose the Spring Door

effects.log: Spring children are said to be hopeful and unreliable. You become both, cheerfully.

choices.text: Choose the Winter Door

effects.log: Winter children are said to be patient and hard to know. People stop telling you secrets and start telling you their troubles.

choices.text: Refuse to choose: you want all four

effects.log: The elders are scandalised and then amused. You walk through all four doors every year, and it becomes a little joke of the town.

events.text: The Winter Door has cracked in a frost. The carvers say it cannot be mended, only made again. The town argues: should the new door be carved like the old, or should it be new, for a new age?

choices.text: Argue for carving it like the old

effects.log: The new door is a careful copy. Old people weep to walk through it. The young think it is boring, and walk through it anyway.

choices.text: Argue for something new

effects.log: The new Winter Door has a carving of the town itself, with all its people. Your face is on it somewhere, very small. You find it every year.

choices.text: Volunteer to help carve it

effects.log: You carve a corner of the new door, a small bird. It is the best thing you will ever make, and nobody knows it is yours.

events.text: You are old enough now to walk through the doors slowly, and the young ones wait for you, out of courtesy and impatience. At the Winter Door, this year, you stop.

choices.text: Walk through, as always

effects.log: You walk through. Another winter, another door. You are glad of all of them, even this one.

choices.text: Tell the children the story of the doors

effects.log: The doors, you tell them, were carved by people who thought the Maker made the seasons as rooms in one house, so nobody would ever be outside. The children go quiet.

choices.text: Walk through your own door twice, for luck

effects.log: You go back and walk through it again. The children laugh. You do it every year after, and they start doing it too.

events.text: The winters of {pw_world} are long, and the longest night is very long indeed: a night of three days. To survive it, everyone goes out onto the frozen lake and holds the Long Night Fair, with fires on the ice and lanterns, and nobody is allowed to sleep alone.

choices.text: Run a stall of hot chestnuts

effects.log: Three days of chestnuts. By the second night you can roast them blind. You make a small fortune and burn every finger you own.

choices.text: Carve an ice sculpture for the contest

effects.log: You carve an ice whale. It melts a little at the fire and looks like it is crying. It wins second prize, for feeling.

choices.text: Keep an old neighbour company all three nights

effects.log: You sit with old Ansel under a blanket for three days, telling stories. He tells better ones. He is very glad not to be alone.

events.text: On the third night of the Long Night, the lights in the sky come out: green and violet, rippling, like a curtain someone is drawing back. The fair goes quiet. In {pw_world}, they say the Maker draws the curtain to look in.

choices.text: Wave at the sky

effects.log: You wave. Half the fair laughs, and then half the fair waves too. The lights ripple. It may be the wind. It may not.

choices.text: Look up and wish for a short winter

effects.log: The winter that year is the shortest in a generation. You are careful never to tell anyone you wished for it.

choices.text: Ask Ansel what he thinks the lights are

effects.log: 'An old friend checking we are still here,' says Ansel, 'in the dark.' He salutes the sky with his tea.

events.text: The Long Night ends. The sun comes up over the frozen lake like something remembered, and the whole fair cheers, hoarse, half-asleep. You have one last chestnut, cold, in your pocket.

choices.text: Give it to the smallest child at the fair

effects.log: The child eats it as if it were the sun itself. You remember that face for many winters.

choices.text: Eat it yourself, watching the sunrise

effects.log: It is the best chestnut you have ever eaten, because of the sunrise and the three days and the cold.

choices.text: Bury it in the ice for next year

effects.log: You bury it in the ice. Next year you will look for it, and not find it, and that will be a story too.

events.text: In {pw_world} the great rains come every year and stay for months. Towns are built on stilts, and every town has its Rain Counters, who sit in towers and count the days and the depth and ring a bell when the river is about to come into the houses. The counters are short a pair of young eyes.

choices.text: Join the counters

effects.log: You learn to read the colour of the river, the sound of rain on different roofs, and the exact smell of a flood an hour before it comes.

choices.text: Help build a boat-house instead

effects.log: Your boat-house floats when the rains come, and three families shelter in it. You are a builder from then on, in your town's eyes.

choices.text: Splash in the puddles and enjoy it

effects.log: The rains are long and warm and you are young. You spend a whole season wet, happy and slightly mossy.

events.text: One night the rain changes its sound. Nobody else seems to notice. You are on watch alone in the counting tower, and the river below you looks, for a moment, as if it is breathing in.

choices.text: Ring the bell now

effects.log: You ring. Half the town grumbles out of bed and up to the high houses. An hour later the river comes in like a wall. Nobody is lost.

choices.text: Wake the head counter and ask

effects.log: The head counter listens and goes white and rings the bell herself. Afterwards she says you have the ears for it. You decide to be proud.

choices.text: Wait to be sure

effects.log: You wait a quarter of an hour. Then you are sure, and ring. It is enough, just. You never wait to be sure again.

events.text: The rains end. In the mud they leave, near the old counting tower, a stone shows that nobody had seen: a post carved with notches, hundreds of them, with a little open hand at the top. The first rain-count of the world.

choices.text: Add a notch of your own

effects.log: You cut a notch for this year's rains, under the first counter's last. It feels like signing your name in a book kept since the making.

choices.text: Count the notches

effects.log: There are exactly as many notches as years of the world, until a hundred years ago, when they stop. You start them again. Someone should.

choices.text: Tell the temple

effects.log: The priests carry the post into the temple, singing. It becomes the Rain Post, and pilgrims touch it before the rains. Your town is famous for it.

events.text: In {pw_kingdom} every blade remembers the hand that forged it. Hold a knife up in a crowd and it will lean, very slightly, like a dog straining at a leash, toward the smith who made it. So smiths are the most careful people in the land: every edge they sell is a witness that will point at them forever. Haldra Ironwell, whose forge is the loudest building in town, needs an apprentice who does not mind being pointed at.

choices.text: Take the apprenticeship

effects.log: Haldra works you like a bellows. By the end of the first year your arms are rope, and your first knife, ugly and honest, leans toward you whenever you walk past the rack. It is the most flattering thing that has ever happened to you.

choices.text: Ask why anyone would want to be pointed at

effects.log: 'Because a blade that remembers its maker remembers to behave,' Haldra says. 'Mostly. Sweep the floor.' You sweep it, and think about that for years.

choices.text: Go and sell bread instead; bread forgets everyone

effects.log: You bake. Loaves are wonderfully discreet. Still, when the town watch parades past with every sword leaning toward Haldra's forge like flowers to the sun, you feel a small pang.

events.text: A purse-cutting at the spring fair. The thief got away but dropped the little blade, and when the watch captain holds it up it swings round, slow and certain, and points at Haldra's forge. The law of {pw_kingdom} is very old and very simple: the hand that forged a blade answers for it, until the hand that misused it is found.

choices.text: Search Haldra's sales ledger for the buyer

effects.log: Haldra writes down every knife she sells, in a hand like barbed wire. You find it on the third night: sold to the cheese-seller's nephew, a year ago. The purses are under his mattress. The watch is impressed with you, and slightly afraid of the ledger.

choices.text: Hold the knife up at the fair and watch which face goes pale

ok.log: You raise the blade over the crowd like a lantern. A young man at the honey stall goes white as wax. The purses are in his hat. The fair applauds, and so, grudgingly, does the watch.

fail.log: Everyone goes pale, because everyone has something to hide. You frighten a priest, two grandmothers and a goat, and catch nobody.

choices.text: Stand witness for Haldra before the watch

effects.log: You tell the watch captain that Haldra would sooner eat her anvil than cut a purse. The captain laughs, and agrees, and lets her go home, and Haldra gives you the afternoon off, which has never happened before.

events.text: Haldra is old now, her hands shake, and she wants to finish one last thing: a blade for the temple of the Maker, who, the priests say, forged the first edge in {pw_world} and left it unclaimed. 'A blade for the god,' she says, 'ought to remember somebody worth remembering.'

choices.text: Forge it yourself, and let it remember you

effects.log: You work nine days and nights. The temple blade comes out of the quench singing, and on the altar it leans, forever after, toward your house. Pilgrims come to see which way it points, and then to see you.

choices.text: Let Haldra strike the last blow

effects.log: You hold the tongs and Haldra strikes once, with all she has left. She dies that winter. On the altar the blade leans toward the hill where she is buried, and the town calls it Haldra's Finger, fondly.

choices.text: Forge it together, two hands on one hammer

effects.log: The priests are scandalised: the blade cannot decide whom to remember, and hangs on the altar pointing at the empty air between your two houses. Haldra says it is the best thing she ever made.

events.text: When a smith dies, every blade they ever made begins, very slowly, to go home. Lost knives creep across floors at night; old swords inch out of ditches; all of them make for the grave of the hand that forged them. {pw_kingdom} keeps an Office of Wandering Blades to stop the roads filling up with cutlery, and the Office is hiring.

choices.text: Take the job

effects.log: On your first day you are given a sack, a pole with a hook, and the North Road, where three hundred kitchen knives are migrating toward the grave of Old Tibbet the cutler at the speed of a tired snail. You fill eleven sacks by noon.

choices.text: Ask what happens to a blade nobody stops

effects.log: The clerk takes you to the window. On the hill above town is Tibbet's grave, under a glittering shell of four thousand knives, like a hedgehog made of silver. Pilgrims leave flowers. The knives seem pleased.

choices.text: Go and visit Tibbet's grave

effects.log: It shines like a frosted bush. A widower is there, apologising to a carving knife for losing it in the garden. The knife, as far as you can tell, forgives him.

events.text: A crisis: Tibbet's grandson wants to move the old man to the family plot across the river, and the knives will not cross water. There are a great many of them. They are very slow. They are, the Office agrees, extremely determined.

choices.text: Build them a bridge

effects.log: You build a plank bridge, one knife wide, all the way across the ford. It takes a month for the procession to cross, and the town makes a festival of watching it, with pies. You are the Bridge Clerk now, forever.

choices.text: Persuade the grandson to leave the grave where it is

ok.log: 'He liked the hill,' you say. 'And he liked company.' The grandson weeps, laughs, and leaves the grave alone. The knives settle down with a contented clink.

fail.log: He moves the grave anyway, and for a year the riverbank bristles with knives sulking at the water's edge. The fishermen complain bitterly, mostly to you.

choices.text: Have the strays melted down; a new blade remembers a new hand

effects.log: The smiths melt two thousand knives into one bell for the town. It is a good bell. When it rings, you would swear it rings toward the hill.

events.text: In the deepest vault of the Office lies the oldest blade in {pw_world}: a plain grey knife with no hilt and no mark, found, the clerks say, in the first furrow of the first field. For all the {pw_years} years of the world it has lain perfectly still, pointing at nothing, because its maker never died. When you carry the lamp in, it turns over on its velvet, slowly, and points at you.

choices.text: Pick it up

effects.log: It sits in your hand as if it had been waiting for exactly that palm. Something in you remembers a forge made of starlight and a very long first day. The Office records it in the ledger it keeps for impossible things.

choices.text: Step aside and see if it follows

effects.log: It follows you exactly, like a compass needle finding north. The senior clerk drops the lamp. You leave the vault with a great deal of explaining to do and nothing to explain it with.

choices.text: Back out and lock the door

effects.log: You lock the vault and keep the key. Some nights you dream of a grey knife lying in the dark, patient as a mountain, waiting for you to come back.

events.text: In {pw_kingdom} no oath sworn on steel can be broken, which is why children are not allowed knives at supper until they can keep their mouths shut. You are not there yet. On a feast day, faced with a bowl of boiled turnips, you seize a butter knife and announce to the whole table: 'I swear on this I will never eat a turnip as long as I live.'

choices.text: Mean it with your whole heart

effects.log: The knife goes warm in your fist. The table goes silent. Somewhere down it an old woman says, 'Well. That is that, then,' and passes you the bread. You will never eat a turnip again. You feel tremendous.

choices.text: Giggle and drop the knife before the end

effects.log: You drop it on the word 'live' and the oath falls with it, unfinished. The grown-ups breathe out. You eat the turnips. They are horrible, but at least they are optional.

choices.text: Swear on the wooden spoon instead, just in case

effects.log: Wood keeps no oaths. Everybody laughs, the turnips sit on your plate a while, and you learn the most important lesson in {pw_kingdom}: always check what you are holding.

events.text: Years later you are a guest in the hall of the Lord of the Marches, a great honour, and the great dish of the evening, carried in with trumpets, is the Lord's famous turnip pie. The whole hall waits for you to taste it.

choices.text: Explain about the oath

effects.log: The Lord of the Marches roars with laughter and shows you his own: a fork he swore on at nine, never to wear yellow. The hall bursts into confessions of childhood oaths. It is the best party in years.

choices.text: Try to eat it anyway

effects.log: Your hand will not lift the spoon. Your jaw will not open. You sit there turning purple while the Lord watches with growing interest. Steel does not care about manners.

choices.text: Eat a large slice and praise it

effects.log: It is, astonishingly, delicious. The Lord gives you the recipe, written on a napkin, which you keep for the rest of your life and never once use.

choices.text: Admire the pie loudly without tasting it

effects.log: You praise its crust, its height, its trumpets. The Lord is so pleased by the praise that nobody notices your slice going quietly to the dog under the table.

events.text: Your turnip story gets about. Now people come to you before they swear anything on steel: merchants, lovers, a nervous young guard. They want the words checked first. In {pw_kingdom} an oath-wright is half lawyer, half poet, and entirely necessary.

choices.text: Set up as an oath-wright

effects.log: You spend your days rewording promises until they can be kept. 'I will love you forever' becomes 'I will try, every morning.' Your oaths are famous for never trapping anyone.

choices.text: Refuse; let people make their own mistakes

effects.log: You send them away. A year later a merchant swears on his scales never to lower a price, and is ruined by it, and you feel worse about it than you expected.

choices.text: Write a little book of safe oaths and give it away

effects.log: The book is copied in every market. Children learn it with their letters. Turnip eating in {pw_kingdom} quietly rises.

events.text: Almost nobody in {pw_kingdom} marries on steel. A steel vow cannot be broken, and nobody sane wants a promise they can never get out of; so weddings are sworn on a loaf of bread, which can be broken, and is, and eaten, with jam. You meet {npc} at the bakers' hall, where you are both trying to buy the last wedding loaf for two different friends.

choices.text: Split the loaf

mem.note: split the last wedding loaf with me

effects.log: You cut it down the middle and both friends marry on half a loaf. The priest says it is irregular but legal. {npc} catches your eye across both weddings.

choices.text: Let {npc} have it

mem.note: let me have the wedding loaf

effects.log: {npc} looks at you as if you had done something much braver than give up bread. A week later a loaf arrives at your door with no name on it.

choices.text: Outbid {npc} shamelessly

effects.log: You win the loaf. {npc} laughs out loud, which is not what you expected, and says you would be a terrible person to marry. It does not sound like a complaint.

events.text: You and {npc} have been walking out for a year. On the old bridge {npc} stops and takes a small iron nail from a pocket, the sort carpenters drop, and turns it over and over. 'My grandmother married on steel,' {he} says. 'Sixty years, and never one night of doubt.'

choices.text: Say you would never be afraid of a promise to {npc}

mem.note: said a promise to me would not frighten them

effects.log: {npc} closes a hand on the nail and says nothing for a long time, and then laughs, shakily, and holds your arm all the way home.

choices.text: Admit that steel frightens you

effects.log: {npc} nods. 'It frightens everyone. That is the point of it.' You walk on, a little closer and a little more honest.

choices.text: Throw the nail in the river, laughing

mem.note: threw the nail in the river

effects.log: It sinks. {npc} watches it go with an odd look, as if you had answered a question {he} had not asked aloud.

events.text: The day comes. The priest of the Maker stands at the temple door with a loaf of bread on one cushion and, because {npc} asked, a plain steel ring on the other. The whole street has turned out to see which one you reach for.

choices.text: Swear on steel, forever

effects.log: The ring goes warm in your hand. The street gasps, then cheers like a storm breaking. It is a promise you will never be able to break, and you find, to your surprise, that you never want to.

choices.text: Swear on bread, like everyone

effects.log: You break the loaf together and eat it on the temple steps with the neighbours. It is a good, ordinary, breakable marriage, and you both mean to keep it anyway.

choices.text: Ask for one more year before any vow

effects.log: {npc} takes the steel ring back, slowly. 'Not on steel, then. Not yet.' The street goes home disappointed and gossiping, and the priest eats the bread.

events.text: In {pw_world} every seed that falls finds soil. Drop an apple pip on bare stone and by morning there is a cupful of dark earth under it and a green shoot. So the cities of {pw_kingdom} are gardens whether they like it or not: oaks on the roofs, beans in the gutters, a cherry tree in the high priest's bath. The Seedwardens patrol with nets and brooms, and they are always short of hands.

choices.text: Join the Seedwardens

effects.log: You get a broom, a net, a green sash and the legal right to confiscate dandelions. The children hate you. The gardeners buy you supper.

choices.text: Plant a garden on your own roof on purpose

effects.log: You scatter a handful of beans on the tiles and by summer your house wears a green wig. The neighbours complain about the shade, and then eat your beans.

choices.text: Ask a priest why the Maker made seeds so stubborn

effects.log: 'Because the Maker was lonely before the world was full,' the priest says, 'and could not bear for anything to be wasted.' You look at the weeds on the temple steps differently after that.

events.text: Dandelion season. Someone in the market square has blown a dandelion clock, a whole fat one, and the wind is carrying a hundred and twelve seeds over the capital. Every one of them will find soil. The bells ring the alarm.

choices.text: Chase the seeds with a net

ok.log: You catch ninety-one in a single glorious afternoon, leaping over carts. The city counts the rest by their flowers: twenty-one, in very awkward places, including the judge's hat.

fail.log: You catch eleven and fall in a fountain. By midsummer the capital is gold with dandelions, and the city decides, all together, that it is rather pretty.

choices.text: Find whoever blew it

effects.log: It was a very small girl who wanted to make a wish. You do not report her. You ask what she wished for. 'More flowers,' she says. Well.

choices.text: Let them fly; a city should be a little wild

effects.log: The Seedwarden captain glares at you. But next spring, when the dandelions come up through the cobbles, the whole city stops to look, and the captain stops too.

events.text: One morning a seed falls into your open palm as you sit on the step: a winged maple key, spinning down out of a cloudless sky. Before you can shake it off there is a pinch of warm soil in the hollow of your hand, and a root, thin as a hair, testing your skin.

choices.text: Hold still and let it grow

effects.log: You hold still for an hour, then carry it cupped to the hill and plant it. People call it your tree. It grows unnaturally fast and very straight, and in its shade people find it hard to lie.

choices.text: Shake it off onto the street

effects.log: It lands between two cobbles and finds soil there instead. In ten years a maple splits the street in two, and the carts go round it, and nobody blames you, much.

choices.text: Carry it to the temple

effects.log: The priests plant it in the courtyard and write in their book: a seed chose a living hand for soil. They look at you strangely for weeks.

events.text: Every child in {pw_kingdom} has tried it: drop a seed somewhere silly and watch the soil come to meet it. Your friends have grown radishes on a fence post and a daisy on a sleeping goat. You have a pocket full of melon seeds, and there is an old pond turtle called Biscuit sunning himself on a rock.

choices.text: Drop a seed on Biscuit's shell

effects.log: By evening Biscuit is wearing a tiny cap of soil and a single melon sprout, and looks deeply offended, and then, after a while, rather proud.

choices.text: Plant them in the proper garden

effects.log: Your melons are excellent and completely ordinary. You win the children's prize at the harvest fair: a ribbon and a very small cake.

choices.text: Drop one on your own head

effects.log: You wake with a melon shoot in your hair and soil behind your ears, and the whole street laughs for a week. You laugh too. It is that kind of street.

events.text: Biscuit has wandered off. A turtle with a garden on its back is not hard to track: a trail of melon rinds and very satisfied crows leads into the reed marsh, where Biscuit sits in the mud under a vine that has grown into a small green tent.

choices.text: Carry Biscuit home

effects.log: You carry him home, staggering, with the vine trailing behind like the train of a gown. The melons ripen on the windowsill. Biscuit is famous.

choices.text: Leave Biscuit to the marsh

effects.log: You sit with him till sunset and then go home without him. He lifts his head when you go, which is turtle for goodbye.

choices.text: Make a map of the trail

effects.log: Your map is wobbly and has a drawing of every crow. The temple teacher pins it on the wall, which nobody has ever done for you before.

events.text: Something is coming up the river road, slowly, and the whole town has gone out to look. It is a turtle the size of a cart, and on its shell grows an orchard: melon vines, an apple tree, a plum, a bird's nest, and a little stone bench somebody once put there. It stops at your gate.

choices.text: Say his name

effects.log: 'Biscuit,' you say, and the great old head swings round and blinks at you, slow as a season. You sit on the bench in the orchard on his back and eat a plum, and the whole town cheers.

choices.text: Feed the turtle and let it go on its way

effects.log: You bring it a bucket of greens. It eats every leaf, leaves a melon on your step, and goes on up the road toward the hills.

choices.text: Ask the temple what it means

effects.log: The priests say that in the oldest stories the Maker's first gardener was a turtle, carrying the first orchard on its back across an empty world. They give you a blessing you do not quite understand.

events.text: In {pw_world} the dead may speak once to those who loved them. Just once: a sentence, a word, at a moment of their choosing. Some speak at the graveside. Some wait thirty years and say 'Close the window' in the middle of the night. Old Tessaly Fenn, who has ferried you across the river every morning for years and never once let you pay, is dying, and has asked for you.

choices.text: Go and sit with her

effects.log: She is propped up on pillows, cheerful and rude. 'I have been thinking what I will say,' she says. 'You will not like it. Or you will. I have not decided.' She dies a week later, and says nothing yet.

choices.text: Take over her ferry while she rests

effects.log: You pole her boat across the river every morning, badly. She watches from her window and shouts corrections until the day she stops shouting.

choices.text: Stay away; you hate goodbyes

effects.log: You do not go. She dies on a bright morning. Afterwards you wait for a word and none comes, and you are not sure whether that is a judgement.

events.text: Years go by. Everyone else Tessaly loved has had their word: her nephew got 'Sell the boat', her old rival got 'You cheated at cards, I always knew.' You are the last. People ask you about it in the market, kindly, the way they ask about an illness.

choices.text: Stop waiting

effects.log: You stop listening for her. You find you are happier, and also that you sometimes set out a second cup without meaning to.

choices.text: Ask a priest whether the dead can forget

effects.log: 'They never forget,' says the priest. 'They choose. The longer they wait, the more it matters to them.' This is not comforting, exactly. It is something better.

choices.text: Keep her ferry running, just in case

effects.log: You keep the ferry running, and you never take a coin, because she never did. The town notices. The children start calling it your ferry.

events.text: A night like any other. You are reaching for the flour jar, thinking about nothing at all, when a voice you have not heard in years says, perfectly clearly, right in your ear: 'Not that one. The blue one. Behind it.'

choices.text: Look behind the blue jar

effects.log: Behind the blue jar, wrapped in oilcloth, are forty silver coins and a note in Tessaly's terrible hand: Hid this here years ago when you were not looking. For the ferry. Do not argue. You laugh until you cry, and then cry until you laugh.

choices.text: Say goodnight to her, out loud

effects.log: You say it. There is no answer, and there never will be another. But the kitchen is warm, and for a moment it smells of river water and pipe smoke.

choices.text: Tell her the ferry still runs

effects.log: You tell the empty kitchen that the ferry runs every morning and nobody pays. You could swear the lamp flame bows. That year the river is gentle as milk the whole season long.

events.text: Because the dead speak once to those who loved them, {pw_kingdom} has no wills. It has the Hall of Last Words, where priests called Listeners record what the dead said, and to whom, and where, every single week, somebody lies about it. The Hall needs a junior Listener. The pay is poor and the stories are extraordinary.

choices.text: Become a Listener

effects.log: You learn the oath, the ledger and the hardest skill of all: telling a grieving face from a greedy one. The senior Listener says you have the sort of face people confess to.

choices.text: Watch a hearing from the gallery

effects.log: A widow swears her late husband's word to her was 'Sorry.' His sister swears it was 'Sorry' to her as well. The Listeners spend a whole afternoon deciding which of them is lying, since a dead man only gets the one word for each.

choices.text: Laugh at the whole business and walk on

effects.log: You walk on. Behind you, through the open doors, someone is shouting that a dead aunt definitely said the orchard was theirs. The Hall will be busy forever.

events.text: The richest wool merchant in {pw_kingdom} has died, and five heirs stand in the Hall, each swearing old Corvane spoke his one word to them. The custom is simple: the goods go to those the dead man spoke to, because he can only have spoken to those he loved.

choices.text: Question each heir about the exact words

ok.log: Four of them say something grand: 'You were always my favourite.' The fifth, a stable hand nobody counted, says Corvane told him the bay mare needs new shoes. That is the true one. Nobody lies that boringly.

fail.log: They all have perfect answers. You give the estate to the most convincing, and learn a year later that he was simply the best liar of the five.

choices.text: Ask whether Corvane loved anyone at all

effects.log: The room goes very quiet. Then the merchant's old dog, lying under the bench, thumps its tail, and everyone understands at once. After much argument the wool goes to a trust for the care of dogs.

choices.text: Leave it to the senior Listeners

effects.log: They take a month and give the wool to the stable hand. You never find out how they knew, and it bothers you for years.

events.text: One evening, alone in the Hall, you hear a voice. Not one voice: thousands, faint as wind in barley, all speaking the one word they have saved, all at once, all to you. You have never met them. And yet the dead of {pw_world} have waited, some of them for {pw_years} years, to say it to someone they loved.

choices.text: Listen to what they say

effects.log: They say thank you. Thousands of them, in every accent of {pw_world}, for the rivers and the bread and the mornings. You understand, with a cold and enormous clarity, who in this world all of them could have loved. The Hall's lamps burn blue until dawn.

choices.text: Answer them

effects.log: You say: I loved you too. All of you. You did not know you were going to say it. The voices go quiet, like children who have finally been tucked in, and a great weight you never knew you carried is gone.

choices.text: Write it in the ledger as a mistake

effects.log: You write: voices heard, source unknown, no estate affected. The senior Listener reads it in the morning, says nothing, and starts treating you with a careful, frightened courtesy.

events.text: In {pw_world} silence is never empty. Sit in a truly quiet room and you will hear what is in it: the last thing said there, or the thing nobody said, or something stranger. Up in the hills is the House of the Hush, where people go to hear the silences, and come down different. The keepers take anyone who can sit still a whole day without humming.

choices.text: Try to sit still for a whole day

ok.log: You last until sunset. In the last hour the silence of the stone room says, in a woman's voice three hundred years old: 'I left the bread in.' You are accepted.

fail.log: You hum. Only a little, at noon, but they hear it. The keepers send you home with a jar of their silence as a consolation. Opened at night, it whispers rain.

choices.text: Buy a jar of silence at the gate

effects.log: The keepers sell it sealed with wax: the quiet of the inner hall, bottled. At home you open it and hear, faintly, a choir nobody alive has heard. You keep it on the shelf.

choices.text: Go home; silence sounds like hard work

effects.log: You go back to your noisy street with its dogs and its arguments. It is, you decide, exactly the right amount of noise for a person.

events.text: The keepers send you to the deepest place: a cave beneath the House where no sound has been made since before {pw_kingdom} had a name. Novices go in with a candle and come out at dawn. Most say they heard their own heartbeat. A few will not say what they heard.

choices.text: Go in and listen

effects.log: The silence down there is old and heavy and full. It holds a song, very low, the kind someone hums while working with their hands. You know the tune. You cannot think how.

choices.text: Go in and speak first

effects.log: You say your name into the dark. The silence gives it back a moment later, in a voice that is not yours, softly, as if correcting how you said it.

choices.text: Refuse; some quiet should stay unbroken

effects.log: The eldest keeper nods slowly. 'That is also an answer,' she says, and gives you the keys to the gate instead.

events.text: Years later you are a keeper of the Hush yourself. A child pilgrim asks you the question every child asks: 'What is in the very first silence? The one before the world?'

choices.text: Hum the song from the cave

effects.log: You hum it, and the child's eyes go wide, and so do yours, because now you remember where you learned it: you hummed it yourself, long ago, while you were making the hills. The House is very quiet for a very long time.

choices.text: Say: someone who was about to speak

effects.log: The child thinks about this very seriously, and nods. Your answer is painted on the wall of the House, where pilgrims read it for centuries.

choices.text: Say nothing, and let the child listen

effects.log: You sit together in the quiet. After a while the child laughs softly at something only the child can hear, and you never ask what it was.

events.text: In {pw_kingdom} an awkward pause is a real danger, because silence is never empty: leave a gap in a conversation and the silence fills it, out loud, with whatever everyone at the table was thinking. Weddings hire talkers. Funerals hire talkers. You have, it turns out, a gift for talking about nothing at all for a very long time.

choices.text: Hire yourself out as a talker

effects.log: Your first job is a betrothal supper. You talk for four hours about the weather, cheese and a goose you once knew. Not one secret thought escapes. You are paid in silver and gratitude.

choices.text: Let one silence happen, on purpose

effects.log: In the middle of haggling at the fish stall you simply stop talking. The silence says, in the fishmonger's voice: 'I would take half.' You pay half. The fishmonger is furious and impressed.

choices.text: Learn to be comfortable in quiet

effects.log: You practise alone in your room, and the silence tells you only small things: the floor needs sweeping, you are lonelier than you admit. Both are true. You sweep the floor.

events.text: The great job: treaty talks between {pw_kingdom} and the river towns. Six days, two delegations who loathe each other, and if the room ever goes quiet the silence will announce exactly what each side really wants. You are hired to keep the talk flowing.

choices.text: Talk for six days straight

effects.log: You talk about rivers, roads, a dream about a giant pear and the history of spoons. On the sixth day both sides sign, mostly to make you stop. You lose your voice for a month.

choices.text: Let the silence fall at the right moment

effects.log: On the third day you stop talking. The silence says, in both delegations' voices at once: 'We just want the bridge fixed.' Everyone stares at each other. The treaty is two lines long.

choices.text: Ask for double pay

effects.log: You get it, talk adequately, and the talks collapse anyway when a cough leaves a gap. You are blamed, unfairly, and paid, fairly.

events.text: Older now, you sit on a bench by the temple with an old friend. Neither of you says anything. Neither of you is afraid to.

choices.text: Let the silence speak

effects.log: The silence says, in your friend's voice: 'I am glad it was you.' And then, in yours, the same. You both laugh, embarrassed, and sit on until the lamps are lit.

choices.text: Start talking out of habit

effects.log: You talk about the weather and cheese and that goose. Your friend listens to all of it again, smiling, which is its own kind of silence.

choices.text: Teach the temple children the kind pause

effects.log: You teach them to leave little gaps for good things to fill. Ten years on, the silences of {pw_kingdom} are noticeably nicer.

events.text: Every age leaves one moment that does not pass. In the market square of the old capital the moment of the last age still hangs in the air: a juggler, mid-throw, five painted balls above her hands like a little constellation, her face caught in pure delight. She has been like that for three hundred years. Pilgrims leave flowers at her feet. Children dare each other to touch the balls, which are warm.

choices.text: Touch a ball

effects.log: It is warm and perfectly still, like touching the middle of a held breath. For a second you can hear the old crowd cheering. Then only the pigeons.

choices.text: Ask who she was

effects.log: Nobody knows her name. The priests say that is the point: the Maker keeps one moment from every age, and never the one the kings expect.

choices.text: Leave a flower at her feet

effects.log: You leave a daisy among the roses. It seems to you, though it cannot be, that her smile is a hair wider when you look back.

events.text: The moment of this age has not yet been chosen, and {pw_kingdom} knows it. Everyone is trying to be it. The king was crowned at noon with nine hundred trumpets. A poet has stood on a bridge with one hand raised for eleven years. A baker pulls the same perfect loaf from the same oven every dawn. None of it has stuck.

choices.text: Try to make a moment of your own

ok.log: You climb the temple roof at dawn and sing. It is a beautiful moment and everyone agrees, and then the sun comes up and it passes like any other. Still, people remember it.

fail.log: You fall off the temple roof into a hay cart. That moment, everyone also agrees, deserved to last forever. It did not.

choices.text: Bring the poet on the bridge some soup

effects.log: He drinks it without lowering his arm. 'It is very hard,' he admits, 'to be eternal.' You keep bringing soup. He tells you everything he knows about time.

choices.text: Laugh at all of them

effects.log: You laugh and go about your day. Nobody laughs at you, because you are not trying to be anything. It is, you discover, very restful.

events.text: It happens on a nothing afternoon. A stranger, dusty from the road, asks you for water at the well, and you hand over the dipper, and a bit of sunlight catches the water as it spills, and the whole square goes silent, because the water has stopped in the air.

choices.text: Step back and look

effects.log: You step out of it, and there it hangs: a stranger's hand, your hand, a ribbon of water full of light. It is the moment of this age. Within a week there are pilgrims. Within a year there are songs, and in all of them your face is wrong.

choices.text: Fetch the poet from the bridge

effects.log: The poet lowers his arm for the first time in eleven years, and comes, and looks, and weeps. 'Of course,' he says. 'Of course it was this.' He writes the best thing he ever wrote, and then goes home and sleeps for a week.

choices.text: Thank the Maker for choosing something small

effects.log: You bow to the hanging water. Somewhere behind your eyes something old and tired smiles, as if pleased that someone understood. The priests carve your words on the well.

events.text: The moment the age before last left behind is, unfortunately, the magistrate of Upper Gallow in the middle of an enormous sneeze. He has been mid-sneeze in the council hall for six hundred years: eyes shut, mouth open, handkerchief halfway up. The council meets around him. Visitors are asked not to stand in front.

choices.text: Stand in front anyway

effects.log: Nothing happens, because nothing ever happens. But you get the uneasy feeling of a sneeze about to land, and it lasts for days. The council clerk says that is normal.

choices.text: Tuck your own handkerchief into his hand

effects.log: The town finds this so funny that it becomes a custom. There are now nine hundred handkerchiefs on the magistrate, a soft white mountain with a nose in it.

choices.text: Suggest the council meet somewhere else

effects.log: They look at you in horror. Move? From the Sneeze? Their grandparents sat here. You are not invited to the council supper.

events.text: A scholar named Ysolde Marrow arrives in Upper Gallow with a theory and a ladder. A still moment, she says, can be entered: step inside and you live that one instant forever, from the inside, and come out a heartbeat later. She needs someone brave or foolish to go first.

choices.text: Volunteer

effects.log: You step into the sneeze. For one endless instant you are inside the magistrate's head six hundred years ago, the sneeze is coming, it is glorious, and you understand everything there is to know about pepper. You stagger out a heartbeat later, changed.

choices.text: Hold the ladder

effects.log: Ysolde goes in herself and comes out a heartbeat later laughing so hard she cannot stand. 'He was thinking about lunch,' she gasps. 'Six hundred years, and he was thinking about lunch.'

choices.text: Warn her it is disrespectful

effects.log: She goes in anyway. When she comes out she is very quiet, apologises to the magistrate, and goes home. You never learn what she saw, only that she sends him flowers every year.

events.text: Word spreads. Pilgrims come to step into the Sneeze. The council charges admission. The temple objects. The magistrate, of course, has no opinion, but in the very corner of his eye there is now, for the first time in six hundred years, the faint beginning of a tear.

choices.text: Tell everyone what it is like inside

effects.log: You tell them: it is not holy, it is only a man about to sneeze on a summer afternoon, and it is the happiest thing you have ever felt. Pilgrim numbers double. The temple gives up and sells handkerchiefs.

choices.text: Argue to close the hall to visitors

effects.log: You win, narrowly. The Sneeze is left in peace. Some say the tear went back. Some say that even a moment that never passes deserves its privacy.

choices.text: Sell a cheaper view through the side window

effects.log: You make a small fortune at the side window. The council finds out, admires your nerve, and makes you treasurer.

events.text: In {pw_world} no hearth goes out while someone tends it. Fuel helps, but attention is what keeps a fire alive: watch it, poke it, mean it, and it will burn on a single stick through the longest night. The hearth of your village meeting hall has been tended without a break for nine hundred years, in shifts, and this winter your name is on the rota.

choices.text: Take the night shift

effects.log: Midnight to dawn, alone with the flames. Around three you find yourself telling the fire about your day, and it leans toward you, bright, as if listening. You take every night shift after that.

choices.text: Take the easy noon shift

effects.log: Noon is full of children warming their hands and old men arguing about the old days. The fire burns well on gossip. You learn everybody's business.

choices.text: Trade your shift to a neighbour for a pie

effects.log: The neighbour tends the fire and you eat the pie. It is a good pie. The hearth does not seem to notice, and you are faintly disappointed that it does not.

events.text: The Long Freeze: a winter so cold that birds fall asleep on the branches. Every fire in the valley is fed and watched, but the hearths at the poor end of the village are dying, because the people there work double to survive and fall asleep beside them.

choices.text: Go house to house tending other people's fires

effects.log: You go from hearth to hearth all night, a poke here, a word there. Not one fire goes out. By spring the poor end of the village calls you by a name that means, roughly, the one who stays awake.

choices.text: Bring everyone to the meeting hall's hearth

effects.log: Two hundred people sleep around the old fire for six weeks. It has never burned so high. Several marriages and one fistfight come of it.

choices.text: Tend your own fire and keep your door shut

effects.log: Your house is warm all winter. In spring two houses at the poor end stand cold and empty. Nobody says anything to you, which is worse.

events.text: The oldest tender of the meeting hall, a man called Orrin who has sat by the fire for seventy years, is dying, and asks for you. 'The hearth needs one who loves it,' he says. 'Not a rota. One.'

choices.text: Promise to be the one

effects.log: You sit by that fire for the rest of your life, a little each day, every day. It burns blue on the night Orrin dies, and gold on the day you laugh again. Travellers warm their hands at it and leave less cold inside.

choices.text: Tell him the rota is better

effects.log: Orrin thinks about it and laughs. 'You are right. A fire that needs one person dies with them.' The rota goes on, and the fire never goes out.

choices.text: Ask him what the fire says

effects.log: 'It says thank you,' he whispers. 'Every night. Nine hundred years of thank you.' He dies before dawn with his hand toward the flames, and the flames lean back toward him.

events.text: The Ember and Kettle inn on the north road has a hearth that has not gone out in four hundred years, because someone of the innkeepers' line has always been awake to tend it. The latest is {npc}, who is falling asleep at the bar on the night you arrive, snow on your boots, with the fire dropping low.

choices.text: Tend the fire so {npc} can sleep

mem.note: kept my fire alive while I slept

effects.log: You poke the embers and talk to the flames all night. At dawn {npc} wakes with a start, sees the hearth still burning and you still at it, and stares at you as if you had walked out of a song.

choices.text: Wake {npc} before it goes out

mem.note: woke me before the fire died

effects.log: {npc} jerks upright, swears at the fire and has it blazing in a moment. Then {he} pours you a cup on the house, and the two of you talk until the snow stops.

choices.text: Find a bed and leave it to the inn

effects.log: In the morning the fire is still burning, barely, and {npc} looks wrecked. You pay and move on. The north road feels colder than it did.

events.text: You find reasons to come back up the north road. Then the festival of Longest Dark arrives: the one night when, by custom, every hearth in {pw_kingdom} is tended by two people together, and the old songs say whatever you tell each other by the fire that night stays lit.

choices.text: Tend the inn's hearth with {npc}

mem.note: tended the fire with me on Longest Dark

effects.log: You sit side by side, feed it one stick at a time and tell each other true things until dawn. The fire burns a colour nobody at the inn has ever seen. The regulars pretend not to notice. They are terrible at it.

choices.text: Tend it, but keep the talk light

effects.log: You talk about the road and the weather and the regulars. It is a pleasant night. {npc} seems to be waiting for something, politely, and you do not quite give it.

choices.text: Spend Longest Dark elsewhere

effects.log: You tend a fire with friends in town. It is a good night. On the north road, they tell you later, the Ember and Kettle's hearth burned low and lonely.

events.text: {npc} asks you out into the yard, where the snow is blue under the stars and the inn chimney breathes warm smoke. 'The hearth needs two keepers,' {he} says. 'It always has. I just never found the other one.'

choices.text: Stay, and keep it together

effects.log: You are married by the hearth with the regulars as witnesses and the fire roaring its approval. In all the years after you never once let it go out, and neither does {npc}.

choices.text: Say yes, if you may still travel

effects.log: {npc} laughs. 'I will keep it lit for you.' You are married in the yard in the snow, and every journey you ever take after ends at that fire.

choices.text: Say you cannot stay in one place

effects.log: {npc} looks at the chimney for a long time. 'Then come back, sometimes. It will still be burning.' It always is.

events.text: Every river in {pw_world} reaches the sea, and so does everything you put in one. That is how the poor send letters: fold it, seal it in wax, drop it in any stream, and sooner or later it washes up on the Letter Shore, the long grey beach where all the rivers end. The Post of Drifts sorts them there, and you have just been hired to sort.

choices.text: Sort carefully, every name

effects.log: You learn to read handwriting softened by a thousand miles of water. Most letters are ordinary: buy flour, the goat is better, come home. A few make you sit down on the sand.

choices.text: Read the letters with no address

effects.log: The undeliverables are kept in a hut. People write to the dead, to the moon, to the Maker. One just says: Is anyone else awake? You write back. You have no idea where to send it.

choices.text: Comb the beach for coins instead

effects.log: People send coins too, for luck. By evening your pockets are full of green old coins, and a supervisor is watching you with folded arms.

events.text: A letter washes up sealed in blue wax and addressed in careful capitals: To whoever finds this on the Letter Shore. Inside, a girl in the high mountains asks if the sea is real, and if it is, could someone please tell her what colour it is today.

choices.text: Carry an answer up the river yourself

effects.log: Letters only go down to the sea, so you walk up. A month of asking at every village, and at the top of the world, in a stone house, a girl reads your letter and runs to tell the whole valley the sea is grey-green and in a bad mood.

choices.text: Pin it on the wall of the Post

effects.log: Within a week every sorter has added a line: grey, green, silver at dawn, black at night, gold at sunset. The Post sends the whole sheet upriver on a trader's boat. Somebody, somewhere, gets a very long answer.

choices.text: File it with the undeliverables

effects.log: It goes in the hut with the letters to the moon. On quiet evenings you take it out and look at the sea and think: grey-green today.

events.text: In the end everybody writes one letter to the river. Yours you have carried for years, folded small. You stand on the bank of a stream that will reach the sea in its own time.

choices.text: Write to someone you lost

effects.log: You drop it in. Some day a sorter on the Letter Shore will read it, and put it in the hut, and keep it safe. That is enough. It is more than enough.

choices.text: Write to the Maker

effects.log: You write: whoever made the rivers, thank you, they are good rivers. A year later a sorter tells you of a letter that washed up still dry, that every hand on the Shore swore was warm. It was yours.

choices.text: Read it aloud to the stream and keep it

effects.log: You read it to the water and fold it back into your pocket. Rivers reach the sea. Some things want to stay up here, with you.

choices.text: Keep it unread and unsent

effects.log: You put it back in your pocket. You are not ready, and the river, which has all the time in the world, does not mind.

events.text: Disaster: a spring has opened in your cellar. In most worlds you would bail it out and complain. In {pw_world} every river reaches the sea, the sea is ninety leagues away, and the new river has clearly made up its mind.

choices.text: Try to block it with a barrel

effects.log: The water goes politely round the barrel, under the door and out into the lane, where it starts carving a course toward the coast with the patience of a priest. The barrel floats after it.

choices.text: Open the cellar door and let it out

effects.log: It pours up the steps, across your kitchen, out of the front door and away down the street, humming. By evening your house has a river through the middle of it. The cat is appalled.

choices.text: Charge the neighbours to see it

effects.log: Half the town pays a copper to watch a river being born in a cellar. You make a tidy sum. The river does not care, and leaves anyway.

events.text: The new river has reached the mayor's house. The mayor stands in the doorway with a broom, ordering it to go round. Every river in {pw_world} reaches the sea, and in all of history not one of them has gone round a mayor.

choices.text: Help the mayor dig a channel around the house

effects.log: You dig for three days with half the street. The river, satisfied that someone made an effort, takes your channel. The mayor gives you a sash, and the river a name: yours.

choices.text: Tell the mayor the river has right of way

effects.log: It is the oldest law there is, older than mayors. The mayor goes pale and moves in next door. The river flows through the old parlour, which becomes a very popular place to fish.

choices.text: Hide in the bakery

effects.log: You hide among the loaves for two days. When you come out the river is through the mayor's house and halfway to the next town, and everyone has decided it was the mayor's fault.

events.text: Years on, the river from your cellar is a proper river, ninety leagues long, with mills, ferries, two towns and a fish market. There is a temple at its mouth. And everybody calls it the river of {name}.

choices.text: Take the credit

effects.log: You accept every free supper. You give speeches about your cellar. Children are told you dug it with a spoon. You do not correct them.

choices.text: Sail it to the sea

effects.log: You take a little boat from your own cellar steps all the way to the coast, past every mill and ferry and fish market your river made. At the mouth the sea tastes, very faintly, of your kitchen.

choices.text: Fix the hole in your kitchen floor at last

effects.log: You lay new boards over the river where it runs through the house, with a trapdoor left for fishing. It is the best kitchen in {pw_kingdom}. You catch breakfast through the floor.

events.text: In {pw_world} storms come only where they are owed. Lightning does not wander: it is a debt, collected. A stingy landlord can live under rain for a year; a village that cheats a stranger hears thunder by supper. And this spring, out of a clear sky, a storm has parked itself over your village and will not move.

choices.text: Ask the weather-reckoner what is owed

effects.log: The reckoner climbs the bell tower with a brass ledger and a wet finger. 'Old,' she says. 'Very old. Older than anyone here. Someone was never paid.'

choices.text: Search your own conscience first

effects.log: You go through your life with a candle. You did borrow a ladder once and never return it. You return the ladder. The storm does not care, but the neighbour is delighted.

choices.text: Sell umbrellas

effects.log: You make umbrellas from oilcloth and sticks and sell every one by noon. You are the only person in the village glad of the storm, which earns you some very wet looks.

events.text: The temple records say it plainly: a hundred and forty years ago a well-digger named Hollis Crane dug the village well, the one everyone still drinks from, and the council of the day paid him in promises. His descendants live two valleys over, poor and unaware.

choices.text: Collect the debt from every house

ok.log: You go door to door, and grumbling turns to shame and shame to generosity. You carry a chest of coins and a cart of preserves two valleys over. The Cranes do not know what to say.

fail.log: Half the doors slam. You collect half a debt, and the storm thins to a sulky drizzle, which everybody blames on you.

choices.text: Pay it yourself

effects.log: You empty your savings into a purse and walk it two valleys over. The storm follows you halfway, grumbling, and then simply breaks apart into a sunny afternoon.

choices.text: Wait it out; it is not your debt

effects.log: The storm waits too. It is very good at waiting. By midsummer the hay is ruined, and in the end somebody else goes to the Cranes.

events.text: The sky over the village is blue for the first time in a season, and the Crane family has come over the hills to see the well their ancestor dug. A small girl among them climbs onto its wall to look down into the water, and a small white cloud gathers overhead and rains, very gently, on the well alone.

choices.text: Hold a feast for the Cranes

effects.log: The whole village feasts by the well. The little cloud hangs overhead all evening like a guest who knows it is welcome, and rains warm rain on the dancing at midnight.

choices.text: Help the reckoner write it down

effects.log: The reckoner writes it in the brass ledger: debt paid, storm released, a hundred and forty years. Then she shows you the rest of the ledger. There are so many debts. You start helping her.

choices.text: Go home and sleep

effects.log: You sleep for a whole day. When you wake the sky is clear and smells of rain and new bread, and that, too, is a kind of payment.

events.text: You wake one morning with a cloud over your head. Just yours. It is the size of a sheepskin, grey, and it drizzles steadily on you and nobody else, which in {pw_world} can only mean one thing: you owe somebody something, and the weather has come to collect.

choices.text: Make a list of everyone you might owe

effects.log: The list is longer than you hoped. You start at the top. The cloud follows you from house to house, dripping on doorsteps, like an embarrassing dog.

choices.text: Go about your day as if nothing is wrong

effects.log: You go to market. Everyone gives you a wide berth and a knowing look. A grandmother hands you a towel without a word.

choices.text: Try to outrun it

ok.log: You sprint across three fields and lose it behind a hedge. You are dry for nearly an hour. Then it finds you again, sulking, and rains harder.

fail.log: It keeps up easily. You fall in a ditch. Now you are wet from both directions.

events.text: On the fourth day the cloud rumbles: a small, pointed rumble, aimed, you realise, at the house of Widow Pennick across the lane, from whom you borrowed a soup pot three winters ago.

choices.text: Return the soup pot

effects.log: You dig it out from under the stairs and give it back. Widow Pennick looks at the pot, then at the cloud, and laughs until she has to sit down. The cloud rains one fat drop on your nose and is gone.

choices.text: Return it full of your best soup

effects.log: The cloud evaporates instantly, and a small, very pretty rainbow appears over Pennick's roof, which she says is the cloud showing off.

choices.text: Insist she gave it to you

effects.log: The cloud thunders, quite loudly, right over your head. Your hair stands on end. You return the pot.

events.text: After the soup pot, people come to you. They have little clouds of their own: a forgotten favour, an unreturned book, an apology owed since the age of nine. You are, it turns out, the town's expert in personal weather.

choices.text: Hang out a sign: Small Clouds Cleared

effects.log: Business is steady. You clear a borrowed comb, three books, and an apology a hundred years overdue between two families. You are never rich, but your street has the best weather in {pw_kingdom}.

choices.text: Help anyone who asks, for nothing

effects.log: You help and take nothing. Over the years, whenever you walk under a clear sky, people say that is the weather saying thank you.

choices.text: Teach Widow Pennick's grandchildren the trick

effects.log: They become the most fearsome debt-finders in the region. Clouds, it is said, flee before them.

events.text: In {pw_world} the mountains do not move. Not an inch, not a pebble. A pick bounces off them like a spoon off a bell. In {pw_kingdom} the mountain called Old Stillback sits squarely where the king's new highway is meant to go, and you have just been hired onto the road survey.

choices.text: Measure the mountain honestly

effects.log: You measure for a month. Old Stillback is exactly as big as the oldest maps say, to the finger. Not one stone has fallen in a thousand years. You find this more moving than you can explain.

choices.text: Try a pick on it, just once

effects.log: The pick rings, leaps out of your hands and lands in a cabbage field. The other surveyors cheer. Everybody tries it on their first day.

choices.text: Ask the shepherds who live on it

effects.log: The shepherds laugh at the highway. 'Kings come and go,' says one. 'Stillback sees them off.' They give you cheese, which is excellent, and very still.

events.text: The king's engineer arrives with seven hundred workers and a great deal of confidence. The plan is to tunnel through. The mountain does not move. After a month the tunnel is the depth of a teacup.

choices.text: Propose a road around it, by your measurements

effects.log: Your road curves around the mountain like an arm around a shoulder. It is three leagues longer and twice as beautiful, and travellers stop at the bend to look. The engineer takes the credit, and you let him.

choices.text: Tell the engineer the truth

effects.log: You tell him: in {pw_world} you cannot move a mountain, you can only change your mind. He stares at the teacup tunnel a long time, and then laughs, which saves everyone a great deal of time.

choices.text: Keep digging; the pay is good

effects.log: You dig with the rest for a season and the tunnel gets nowhere. Your arms are magnificent and your pay is excellent. Old Stillback is unchanged.

events.text: The king himself comes to see the mountain that refused his highway. He is old, and he stands at the foot of Old Stillback a long time, and then asks you, of all the survey, a question: 'Why did the Maker make one thing that will not move?'

choices.text: So there would be one thing to come home to

effects.log: The king nods slowly. He never builds another road through a mountain. The bend in the highway is named for you, and couples meet there to make their promises.

choices.text: So that kings would have something to lose to

effects.log: The courtiers gasp. The king laughs until he cries, gives you a purse of gold for saying it, and then banishes you to the bend for a year, as a joke, more or less.

choices.text: Say you do not know

effects.log: 'Good,' says the king. 'Neither do I. I just wanted someone to say so.' You stand side by side and look at the mountain, which looks back, unmoved.

events.text: On the mountains of {pw_world} nothing moves, and that includes fevers. A sickness carried up the Still Slope simply stops where it is, and gets neither worse nor better until you come down. So when you catch the spotted fever one autumn, they carry you up the slope to wait for the healers' cure, and tuck you into the mountain hospice among the stones.

choices.text: Make friends with the old man in the next bed

effects.log: His name is Teodric and he has been waiting sixty-one years for a cure. As long as he stays on the mountain he is in perfect health. He teaches you nine card games and how to cheat at four of them.

choices.text: Watch the clouds, which do move

effects.log: From the Still Slope the whole sky goes by like a river. You learn the names of clouds. The nurses say you lie stiller than the mountain.

choices.text: Try to sneak down the slope

effects.log: You reach the last flat stone before your fever wakes up and pounces. You crawl back up, very sorry, and the mountain takes the fever back into stillness, gently, like a held breath.

events.text: The cure comes in spring: a bitter green syrup that tastes of nettles. You can go home. Teodric's cure was never found; his is a wasting sickness so rare it has no name. He walks you to the edge of the stillness and stops, the way he has stopped for sixty-one years.

choices.text: Promise to come back with his cure

effects.log: He laughs and shakes your hand like an equal. 'I will be right here,' he says. 'I am very good at it.' You go down the mountain with a promise in your pocket.

choices.text: Give him your favourite pebble

effects.log: He holds it up to the light like a jewel. 'A thing from the moving world,' he says. Years later you see it on a string around his neck.

choices.text: Run home without looking back

effects.log: You run all the way down, and it feels wonderful to move. At the bottom you look back, and there he is, waving, very small, perfectly still.

events.text: Years later the healers' college of {pw_kingdom} announces a cure for the nameless wasting sickness. You hear it in the market and drop a basket of eggs. Teodric is still on the Still Slope. He would be ninety now, if time moved for him up there. It does not.

choices.text: Carry the cure up the mountain yourself

effects.log: You climb with the vial wrapped in wool. Teodric is exactly as you remember, holding a hand of cards. He drinks it, makes a face, and walks down off the mountain with you into the moving world, laughing like a boy.

choices.text: Send word to the hospice

effects.log: The nurses send back his answer: thank you, and he will come down when he has finished his game. Six years later, he does.

choices.text: Climb up and ask whether he wants to come down at all

effects.log: He thinks about it for a whole day. 'Down there I would be old,' he says. 'Up here I am only waiting.' He keeps the cure by his bed, unopened, like a door he likes knowing is there.

events.text: In {pw_world} every word spoken carries a little further than it should. A whisper reaches the next room. A sigh reaches the next house. A shout on a still morning arrives in the next town, slightly annoyed. Nobody in {pw_kingdom} has ever kept a secret by saying it, which is why everyone learns finger-speech, and why the baker of your street has just heard you call his rye bread a doorstop.

choices.text: Go and apologise

effects.log: The baker listens with his arms folded, then admits the rye has been off since spring, and gives you a loaf of the new batch. It is very good. You say so, loudly, and it carries to the end of the street.

choices.text: Learn finger-speech properly

effects.log: You practise for months. Soon you can gossip in perfect silence with your hands under the table. It is the most useful thing you ever learn.

choices.text: Praise the baker very loudly from your doorstep

effects.log: You praise his buns to the morning. The words sail past the baker to the next town, where three people come over the hill to buy buns. He forgives you.

events.text: Love in {pw_kingdom} is a public matter, because confessions carry. Your friend Pell has been trying to tell the miller's daughter something for three years, and every time he clears his throat the whole lane leans out of its windows. He comes to you for help.

choices.text: Teach Pell finger-speech

effects.log: Pell learns in a week, out of desperation, and confesses in perfect silence across a crowded market. The whole market, which also knows finger-speech, bursts into applause.

choices.text: Tell him to just say it

effects.log: Pell says it at the mill, quietly. It carries to the whole village and two farms. The miller's daughter says yes, loudly, and that carries further still. The wedding is very well attended.

choices.text: Shout it for him from the hilltop

effects.log: You shout it from the hill. It carries to the mill, and also to the next valley, where a different Pell's sweetheart hears it and is delighted. There are now two weddings and a great deal of confusion.

events.text: The king of {pw_kingdom} is passing through town and the council needs someone to give the speech of welcome. They choose you, because you are, it seems, the person in town best known for words that carry.

choices.text: Make it very short

effects.log: You say simply: 'Welcome.' It carries all the way to the capital, and the king, who is used to two-hour speeches, is so moved that he knights the town bridge.

choices.text: Whisper the whole speech

effects.log: Your whisper carries exactly to the back of the crowd and not one step further. The king is impressed and asks how you did it. You have no idea.

choices.text: Mention the rye bread, by accident

effects.log: Somehow, in the middle of it, you mention the rye. The baker at the back hears every word. So does the king, who asks to try it, and agrees with you.

events.text: On the Hill of Far Words outside town the wind takes whatever you say and carries it a very long way. People go up at night to say what they cannot say to a face. One night up there you catch a voice on the wind that is not yours: 'The one in the green scarf at the fair. I cannot stop thinking about it.' You wore a green scarf at the fair. Three days of asking leads you to {npc}, who sells honey two villages over.

choices.text: Go to the honey stall

effects.log: You buy a jar. {npc} goes the colour of the honey, then redder, and gives you a second jar free, and neither of you mentions the hill.

choices.text: Answer from the Hill of Far Words

effects.log: You climb the hill and say: 'The green scarf is thinking about you too.' Two villages over a jar of honey is dropped. The next day a jar arrives at your door with a tiny green scarf tied round it.

choices.text: Decide it was meant for someone else

effects.log: You let it go on the wind. There are other green scarves. Still, for a long while you buy your honey from a different village, out of something that is not quite shyness.

events.text: Courting in {pw_kingdom} is mostly done by wind. Every night you and {npc} take turns on your own hills and send each other the day: the price of eggs, a joke about a goat, the colour of the sky. The whole valley can hear it. The whole valley has opinions.

choices.text: Keep it to small things

mem.note: sent me the small things every night

effects.log: You send eggs and goats and skies. The valley finds it unbearably sweet. An old woman on the far farm starts sending commentary back.

choices.text: Send something true and frightening

mem.note: sent me the true thing on the wind

effects.log: You say the thing you meant to keep. It carries, of course, a little further than it should: to {npc}, the valley, and the next valley, where several strangers weep. {npc} answers with the same thing, only braver.

choices.text: Ride over and say it to {npc} in person

effects.log: You arrive dusty and out of breath and say it face to face, and even then it carries to the next farm. {npc} laughs and says the wind will never let the two of you keep anything private, and does not seem to mind.

events.text: {npc} climbs your hill one evening, which is not the custom, and stands beside you at the top with the wind blowing hard. 'If I ask you up here,' {he} says, 'all of {pw_kingdom} will hear the answer.'

choices.text: Say yes into the wind

effects.log: You say yes. It carries over every hill in {pw_kingdom}. By morning there are cakes on your doorstep from towns you have never visited. The wedding is the loudest in living memory.

choices.text: Say yes with your hands, in silence, for {npc} alone

effects.log: You answer without a sound, and for once the wind has nothing to carry. It is the only secret the two of you ever keep. The valley finds out the next day anyway, at the wedding.

choices.text: Say not yet, quietly

mem.note: said not yet on the hill

effects.log: Even quietly, it carries. The valley groans as one. {npc} smiles and says not yet is not no, and the wind takes that too, gently, as far as the sea.

events.text: In {pw_world} what is sown is reaped, in this life or the next, and the temples can read it. Every baby is born with a small mark somewhere, and the priests of the Maker read it like a bill. You have always had yours: a little pale key on the inside of your wrist. The priests said it meant you owed someone a door.

choices.text: Go to the temple and ask about it properly

effects.log: A very old priest looks at your wrist through a glass. 'A door you shut on someone, in the life before,' she says. 'Someone left out in the cold. You will meet them.' It is not a comfortable thought.

choices.text: Ignore it; this life is trouble enough

effects.log: You wear long sleeves and get on with things. The mark itches sometimes, on cold nights, whenever someone knocks.

choices.text: Become a carpenter; doors seem relevant

effects.log: You learn to hang doors and you are very good at it. Every door you hang closes softly and opens easily, as if it had something to make up for.

events.text: A storm night. Someone hammers on your door. On the step is a stranger soaked to the bone, an old woman whose lantern has gone out, and when your eyes meet the key on your wrist burns as if it had been in a fire.

choices.text: Bring her in and give her your bed

effects.log: You give her the bed, the fire and the soup. By morning the mark on your wrist has faded to a faint white line, like an old healed scar. She leaves before you wake, and the door is closed softly behind her.

choices.text: Give her a coat and directions to the inn

effects.log: She takes them and goes. The key stops burning, but it does not fade. Half a debt, the priests say later. Better than none.

choices.text: Keep the door shut

effects.log: You stand with your back against it, heart thumping. When you open it at dawn she is gone, and the mark on your wrist has darkened. The priests say the debt will come again. They do not say when.

events.text: Years later the temple asks you to come and see a baby born in the poor quarter, because the priests are puzzled by its mark. It is a key: a little pale key on the inside of its wrist, exactly like the one you used to have, except that it is turned the other way.

choices.text: Hold the baby and look closely

effects.log: The key faces outward, the priest explains: not a debt, but a door owed to this child by the world. Someone will open a door for this one, some day. You find, without any surprise, that you mean to be that someone.

choices.text: Ask the priest what it means

effects.log: 'It means the debt is moving,' she says. 'It always moves. Nobody ever finishes paying; they only pass it on, kinder or crueller.' You go home and think about every door in your life.

choices.text: Leave a purse for the baby and slip out

effects.log: You never see the child again. But years later a young stranger hangs a beautiful new door on your house, refuses payment, and will not say why.

events.text: {pw_kingdom} has very few prisons. Why would it? What is sown is reaped, in this life or the next, and the watch mostly just writes things down. So when a young thief snatches your purse at the spring market and you catch him by the collar, the watchman only sighs and opens his book. 'Do you want to sow,' he asks, 'or let it lie?'

choices.text: Let him go with the purse, and let the world settle it

effects.log: The watchman writes: let lie. The thief, a skinny lad with a split lip, stares at you as if you were mad, and runs. Your purse goes with him.

choices.text: Take your purse back and give him a coin from it

effects.log: The thief looks at the coin in his palm for a long moment. 'Why?' he says. You do not know. The watchman writes something you cannot read, and for once he smiles.

choices.text: Have the watch fine him double

effects.log: He pays it in coppers, counting them out, glaring at you the whole time. You feel you have won something, and are not sure what.

events.text: A bad year. Your house floods, the crops fail, your savings go. You are sitting in the ruins of your kitchen when a cart pulls up outside, loaded with timber and grain. The driver is a broad young carpenter with a scar on his lip, and he does not need to tell you who he is.
