choices.text: Ask him why he came

effects.log: 'You gave me a coin,' he says. 'I bought bread and a chisel. The chisel made me a carpenter.' He rebuilds your house in a month and will not take a single coin. The watchman comes to see, and writes it all down, grinning.

choices.text: Ask if he remembers the market

effects.log: 'I spent your purse on dice,' he admits, 'and lost it, and the world reaped me hard for years. I owe you a purse, and then some.' He unloads the cart.

choices.text: Ask if he has come to gloat

effects.log: 'I came to pay,' he says, and unloads the cart. 'You were right to fine me. It hurt. It worked. I hated you for years.' He helps you rebuild, and slowly you become friends.

choices.text: Accept his help without a word

effects.log: You work side by side for a month and never talk about the market. When the house is done he drives off waving, and you do not see him again for a long time.

events.text: The watchman who wrote in his book that day at the market is retiring, very old, and wants to show you a page. It is the page of your market. Under the entry, in his hand, across all these years, are notes: what was sown, what grew, what was reaped. It runs to six pages.

choices.text: Read every page

effects.log: You read about the carpenter, his apprentices, the houses they built and the people those houses sheltered. One choice at a market stall, and six pages of consequences. You go home and sit very still for a long time.

choices.text: Ask him why he kept it

effects.log: 'Because people never see the harvest,' he says. 'Only the sowing. I wanted one person to see the whole field.' He gives you the book.

choices.text: Close it unread

effects.log: 'I would rather keep sowing than count,' you say. The watchman nods as if that were the right answer, and burns the page.

events.text: No kingdom in {pw_world} rises without another resting. When {pw_kingdom} has a good century, somewhere a neighbour falls into a long, gentle drowse: fields go fallow, clocks slow, people nod off over their soup and wake, unharmed, years later. {pw_kingdom} is rising now. To the east, the kingdom of Ostmere has been asleep for forty years, and a merchant caravan is going in to look.

choices.text: Join the caravan

effects.log: You cross the border at dawn and the air changes, thick and sweet as honey. The people of Ostmere sleep in doorways and fields and kitchens, smiling, with flies too drowsy to land on them.

choices.text: Put money in the caravan, but stay home

effects.log: The caravan comes back with forty-year-old cheese, which is either a delicacy or a weapon, depending on whom you ask. Your share sells well.

choices.text: Ask why {pw_kingdom} must rise at someone else's cost

effects.log: A temple scholar explains that it is not a cost but a turn. 'The Maker made the world to breathe,' she says. 'In, and out. We are the in.' You think of it every time you breathe.

events.text: In the middle of sleeping Ostmere, in a palace overgrown with roses, you find one person awake: a young queen sitting on the steps, keeping watch over her drowsing people. She has been awake and alone for forty years and has not aged a day. 'Someone has to remember,' she says, 'so we know where we were when we wake.'

choices.text: Sit and keep watch with her a while

effects.log: You stay a month. She tells you every name in Ostmere and you write them in a book. When you leave she is crying a little, because she had forgotten what it was to talk.

choices.text: Ask her how to wake them

effects.log: 'You cannot,' she says. 'Only {pw_kingdom} can, by resting.' She looks at you with terrible patience. You go home carrying that sentence like a stone.

choices.text: Pick a rose and go home

effects.log: At home the rose blooms for forty days, then closes and sleeps, and will not open again however you water it.

events.text: The golden age of {pw_kingdom} is ending. Harvests slow. The council meets in a panic, and there is talk of new taxes, new conquests, anything to keep rising. Across the border, people say, the roses of Ostmere have begun to open.

choices.text: Speak to the council for a gentle rest

effects.log: You stand in the council and tell them what you saw: a whole people asleep, safe, waiting their turn. The vote to rest passes by one. {pw_kingdom} lies down gently, like a farmer after harvest.

choices.text: Ride to Ostmere to see its people wake

effects.log: You arrive as Ostmere yawns and stretches and sits up in its fields. The queen runs down the palace steps to meet you, finally able to say every name to a waking face. You hold the book while she reads them out.

choices.text: Fill your cellar with grain and wait

effects.log: You doze through the long rest in great comfort. When you wake, years later, your hair is a little longer and your grain a little musty. You feel marvellous.

events.text: Every twenty years the kingdoms of {pw_world} meet at the Balance Table to decide who will rise and who will rest. You have been hired as the youngest scribe. You expected desperate bargaining for greatness. Instead every delegation has arrived with pillows.

choices.text: Ask the delegates why

effects.log: 'Rising is exhausting,' says the delegate of the Salt Coast, yawning. 'Wars, taxes, monuments. Resting is lovely. You sleep, the weeds grow, nobody invades.' Every single delegate wants the nap century.

choices.text: Take careful notes

effects.log: Your notes are excellent. Day one: arguments over who is most tired. Day two: a delegate falls asleep in protest. Day three: pillows are thrown. You cannot write fast enough.

choices.text: Fall asleep at the table yourself

effects.log: You nod off. The delegates are deeply impressed. Your kingdom is briefly considered for the rest on your merits alone.

events.text: Deadlock. Nobody will rise. If nobody rises nobody can rest, and {pw_world} will simply muddle along forever, which the old texts call the Grey Age and everyone agrees sounds dreadful. The chair of the Table, at the end of patience, asks the scribe for an idea.

choices.text: Propose drawing lots

effects.log: The lot falls on {pw_kingdom}. It must rise. Your own delegation glares at you as if you had proposed a war. You have, in a sense, proposed eighty years of hard work.

choices.text: Promise the rising kingdom the best rest afterward

effects.log: A guarantee: whoever rises now rests next, first choice, with honours. Three kingdoms volunteer at once. The Balance Table has never ended so early. Everyone takes a nap.

choices.text: Suggest they all rise, just a little

effects.log: The old texts say this is impossible. It is. The delegates try it for one afternoon, rising slightly, and are all so tired by sunset that the matter settles itself.

events.text: Twenty years on, the Balance Table invites you back as its chair. The first to arrive is a small, very serious young scribe, who asks you nervously what the Table is really for.

choices.text: Say: to make sure everyone gets their turn

effects.log: The scribe writes it down very carefully. You suspect it will be quoted back at you for twenty years. It is.

choices.text: Say: to give everyone somewhere to sit and complain

effects.log: The scribe laughs, startled. It is the truest answer anyone gives at the whole meeting, and the scribe tells it to everybody.

choices.text: Hand the scribe a pillow

effects.log: The scribe accepts it solemnly. You are, the scribe will later write, the wisest chair the Table ever had.

events.text: Every dream in {pw_world} is a little true. Dream of a lost ring under the bed, and there is at least a button there. Dream of a friend in trouble, and they have at least stubbed a toe. Dream-readers sit in every market at little tables with sharp eyes. For years you have had the same dream: a high, cold throne above the clouds, and a whole world spread out beneath it, small and bright as a bowl of jewels.

choices.text: Pay a dream-reader to explain it

effects.log: The reader listens, goes white, and gives you your coins back. 'A little true,' she whispers. 'I do not want to know which little.' She packs up her table early.

choices.text: Write the dream down every morning

effects.log: You fill a book. The throne is always the same. The world below changes a little each time: a new river, a new town. You start finding them on maps.

choices.text: Try to dream something else

effects.log: You eat cheese at midnight on purpose and dream of a giant goose. The next day a goose chases you down the high street. A little true. You go back to the throne.

events.text: Tonight, in the dream, someone else is sitting on the throne. They are turned away from you, looking down at the world, and you know with the certainty of dreams that if they turn around you will see a face you know very well.

choices.text: Walk up and touch their shoulder

effects.log: They turn. It is your own face, older and colder and very tired, and it looks at you with enormous relief. You wake with frost on your eyelashes, in summer.

choices.text: Call out to them

effects.log: Your voice crosses the dream like wind. The figure lifts a hand without turning, as if to say: not yet. You wake with your own hand raised the same way.

choices.text: Wake yourself up

effects.log: You pinch yourself awake and lie in the dark with your heart pounding. The dream does not come back for a year, and you miss it terribly, which you had not expected.

events.text: A pilgrim from the high temples comes to your town asking door to door for anyone who dreams of the throne above the clouds. The priests say it is the truest dream in {pw_world}, and that there is a stair, somewhere, for whoever dreams it truly.

choices.text: Say you have seen the face on the throne

effects.log: The pilgrim kneels in the dust of your doorstep. 'Then the stair is open to you,' comes the answer, and a map drawn in silver, with one road on it that goes up.

choices.text: Tell the pilgrim only about the throne

effects.log: The pilgrim writes it down and looks at you a long time. 'A little true,' the pilgrim asks, 'or all true?' Before leaving, the pilgrim presses a silver token into your hand, marked with a stair.

choices.text: Send the pilgrim away

effects.log: You shut the door. That night, for the first time in your life, you dream of nothing at all, and wake feeling like an ordinary person, which is both a gift and a loss.

events.text: You dream that a dragon lives in the old well at the end of the lane: a great golden dragon with eyes like lamps. Every dream in {pw_world} is a little true. In the morning, peering down the well with your friends, you find a lizard. A very small lizard. It is, unmistakably, slightly golden.

choices.text: Name it and bring it breakfast

effects.log: You call it Sunrise and bring it crumbs every morning. It is the best-fed lizard in {pw_kingdom}, and when it looks at you its eyes, very faintly, glow.

choices.text: Dream about it again, bigger

effects.log: You try very hard to dream it bigger. The next morning the lizard is the size of a cat and grumpy about it. Your friends are terrified and delighted. The grown-ups are only terrified.

choices.text: Tell the temple teacher

effects.log: The teacher explains, kindly, how a little true dream works: the world meets you halfway. 'So be careful what you dream,' she says, 'and be kind.' You lie awake that night practising kind dreams.

events.text: Wendel, the boy next door, has bad dreams of fires and wolves every night, and every morning something small and true comes of them: a scorched pot, a dog that growls at him. He has stopped wanting to sleep at all.

choices.text: Teach Wendel to dream of Sunrise

effects.log: You tell him all about the little golden lizard until he falls asleep smiling. He dreams of dragons, and in the morning there is a warm golden scale on his pillow. He sleeps every night after that.

choices.text: Sit up with him and tell funny stories

effects.log: You tell stories until you both fall asleep. He dreams of a talking goose. In the morning a goose is honking at his window, rather rudely. It is an improvement.

choices.text: Tell him bad dreams only come a little true

effects.log: He thinks about that. 'A little wolf is just a dog,' he says, and goes to bed brave. In the morning there is a puppy on his step that nobody can explain.

events.text: You are grown now, and the town has noticed that your dreams come a little more true than most. Farmers ask you to dream of rain. A sick woman asks you to dream her well. The temple wants to know if you would dream for them, officially, in a little room with a very good bed.

choices.text: Become the temple dreamer

effects.log: You dream of rain for the farmers, health for the sick, lost things found. Each comes a little true, and the littles add up to a great deal. You are very well rested and very loved.

choices.text: Refuse; dreams should be free

effects.log: You go on dreaming for whoever knocks, for nothing, on your own pillow. The temple grumbles. The town brings you pies.

choices.text: Dream one last dream for Sunrise

effects.log: You dream the old lizard as big as the first dream was. In the morning the well at the end of the lane is empty, and in the sky over town something golden circles once, glinting, and is gone.

events.text: In {pw_world} no road is ever longer than the will to walk it. A courier who truly means it crosses {pw_kingdom} in a day; a bored tax clerk takes a week to cross the square. The pilgrimage to the Temple at the End of the Road takes the devout three days and the doubtful three years. You have decided, for reasons you cannot quite name, to go.

choices.text: Set out with nothing but the wanting

effects.log: You walk out of town at dawn with a stick and a loaf. The road seems to fold toward you. By noon you are in a country you have never seen, and you are not even tired.

choices.text: Go with a band of pilgrims

effects.log: The pilgrims sing and bicker and slow each other down; one of them keeps wanting to go home. The road stretches like dough. You learn more about people than about roads.

choices.text: Pay a courier to carry a letter there instead

effects.log: The courier runs off and is back by supper, sweaty and grinning, with the temple seal on your letter. You could have gone yourself. You know it.

events.text: Halfway. The road climbs through a pass where the wind smells of snow, and here it starts to lengthen: every doubt you carry adds a league. A man sits by the road at a fire. He has been trying to reach the temple for nineteen years. 'I want to want it,' he says. 'I just do not.'

choices.text: Help him find what he does want

effects.log: You talk all night. At dawn he admits that what he really wants is to go home to his garden. The road home, for him, is about four steps long. He waves from his own gate.

choices.text: Leave your doubts at his fire

effects.log: You sit and name them one by one and drop each in the flames. When you stand up the pass is a short walk, and the temple roof shows against the sky.

choices.text: Walk on before he slows you down

effects.log: You go on. The road is long and steep and you resent every step of it, and it takes you a week to cross a pass that should have taken a morning.

events.text: The Temple at the End of the Road is small, plain and very old. Beyond it, the priests say, the road goes on, but nobody has ever wanted anything enough to walk it. It climbs into the clouds as a stair.

choices.text: Set foot on the stair

effects.log: The first step is easy. So is the second. With a cold thrill you understand that you want this more than you have ever wanted anything, and that you have walked it before, downward, a very long time ago.

choices.text: Ask the priests where it goes

effects.log: 'To whoever made the roads,' says the eldest. 'They walked down it once, and never back up.' She looks at your dusty feet. 'Or not yet.'

choices.text: Pray, then go home

effects.log: You pray at the plain altar and turn for home, and the road home is the shortest you have ever walked, because you want so much to be there.

events.text: The magistrate's clerk needs a pie delivered to the magistrate's sister across town, and you are the one standing nearest. The sister is the most boring person in {pw_kingdom}. In {pw_world} no road is longer than the will to walk it, and you have no will at all.

choices.text: Set off anyway

effects.log: The walk across town takes you eleven hours. You pass the same baker four times. When you finally knock, the pie is cold, and the sister talks for two more hours about her gutters.

choices.text: Find something to want at the other end

effects.log: You remember the sister keeps bees, and you love honey. Suddenly her house is just round the corner. You trade the pie for a honeycomb in ten minutes flat.

choices.text: Pay an eager child to take it

effects.log: A small, extremely motivated child takes a copper and the pie and is back before you have finished counting your change, glowing with purpose.

events.text: You set off to visit someone you are very fond of, and arrive at their door almost the moment you leave your own, red in the face, still pulling on your coat. In {pw_kingdom} everybody knows what a short road means. They look at you. Their whole household looks at you.

choices.text: Pretend you were just passing

effects.log: Nobody believes you. An old woman of the house laughs so hard she has to sit down. It becomes a story told at their supper table for years.

choices.text: Admit it

effects.log: You admit it. Your friend goes pink to the ears. The household quietly leaves the room one by one, all smiling.

choices.text: Turn round and walk home very slowly

effects.log: The road home takes all day, because you do not want to leave. The whole street watches you inch along it and knows exactly why.

events.text: You become known, in a small way, for the trick: find the wanting, and the road gets short. Couriers come for advice. Lazy apprentices are sent to you. The magistrate wants you to teach his slowest tax clerk to cross the square.

choices.text: Teach the clerk to look forward to lunch

effects.log: The clerk learns to look forward to lunch, then to the end of the day, then to the whole of his life. He crosses the square in a heartbeat and becomes the fastest clerk in history.

choices.text: Teach the couriers to want the arriving, not the pay

effects.log: The couriers of {pw_kingdom} grow faster than ever. Letters arrive almost before they are finished. You are given a medal shaped like a boot.

choices.text: Admit that some roads ought to be long

effects.log: You tell the magistrate the road to the boring sister should be long. That is how you know. The magistrate laughs and pays you anyway.

events.text: In {pw_world} every war ends in the field where it began. However far the armies march, however long it drags on, peace can only be signed on the ground of the first quarrel. The field where the last three wars of {pw_kingdom} began is a cabbage farm called Muddle Acre, and its owner, Maudry Plow, has had quite enough.

choices.text: Go and work for Maudry

effects.log: Maudry hires you to cut cabbages and to shoo generals off her rows. By autumn you are better at both than anybody alive.

choices.text: Ask how a war starts on a cabbage farm

effects.log: Maudry shows you the gatepost. 'Two border captains argued over which way the gate swung,' she says. 'Three wars. Same gate. I painted it blue to cheer it up.'

choices.text: Buy cabbages from her and go

effects.log: The cabbages are enormous. Maudry says it is all the peace treaties in the soil. You decide not to ask what she means.

events.text: A fourth war. It started, of course, at the blue gate, when a goose wandered across the border. Four years later both armies, tired and filthy and thoroughly fed up, are marching back to Muddle Acre to sign the peace, and they are going to march straight through the cabbage harvest.

choices.text: Lay out a path for them through the rows

effects.log: You mark a path with white stones. Two armies troop through the field single file, very politely, like guests at a wedding, and not one cabbage is trodden. Maudry is very nearly moved.

choices.text: Sell soup to both armies

effects.log: Two armies, four years of bad food, one soup stall. You sell out every hour. The peace is signed with everyone in a much better mood.

choices.text: Tell the generals to sign at the gate and nowhere else

effects.log: The generals are startled to be told off by a farmhand. They sign at the gate, standing in a puddle. It is the shortest peace ceremony in the history of {pw_kingdom}.

events.text: Maudry is old, and gives you the farm. 'Keep the gate,' she says. 'And whatever you do, never let anybody start anything here again.' The field that has ended four wars is yours.

choices.text: Take down the gate

effects.log: You take down the blue gate and the fence with it. No line, no side, no quarrel. The border captains are bewildered. There is not another war at Muddle Acre in your lifetime.

choices.text: Turn the field into a meeting place

effects.log: You set long tables among the cabbages, and the two kingdoms start sending people to talk there before they quarrel, just in case. It works more often than it should.

choices.text: Keep growing cabbages

effects.log: You grow cabbages, very large and very peaceful. Old generals come now and then to stand at the gate and remember, and you sell each of them a sack.

events.text: Because every war ends in the field where it began, the kings of {pw_world} are very careful where they start one. And yet the war between {pw_kingdom} and Highwold has dragged on for nine years, and nobody on either side can remember where it began. Until it is signed in the right place it cannot end, and the council needs an envoy who is good at finding things.

choices.text: Volunteer as envoy

effects.log: You are given a seal, a mule and a stack of old reports, each blaming the other side. You read them all. They agree on nothing except that it was raining.

choices.text: Search the old border forts

effects.log: You visit seven forts. Each has a plaque claiming the war began there. You begin to suspect the plaques, and go looking for the oldest soldiers instead.

choices.text: Leave it to someone else

effects.log: Someone else does not find it either. The war goes on in a tired, dutiful way, like a cough nobody can shake.

events.text: The oldest soldier you can find, a white-haired cook named Brannoc, laughs at the plaques. 'It did not start at a fort,' he says. 'The quarrel started forty years ago in the summer house at Thistledown, when the two young princes, guests together, fought over a wooden horse. The war just took a while to grow up.'

choices.text: Go to the summer house

effects.log: It is shut up and dusty. In the nursery, under a bed, lies a little wooden horse with a broken leg. You pick it up and the floor hums under your feet, and you know.

choices.text: Ask the two kings, very tactfully

effects.log: You ask, in two courts, with great care. Both kings go red and deny everything, which is how you know Brannoc is right.

choices.text: Doubt him; a war cannot start over a toy

effects.log: Brannoc shrugs. 'They all do,' he says. You go back to the forts. It takes you another year to come back to him.

events.text: Two old kings in their best robes, with generals in feathered helmets, squeeze into a child's nursery in a dusty summer house to sign the peace. There is not quite room for everyone. Somebody will have to sit on the rocking horse.

choices.text: Set the broken wooden horse on the table between them

effects.log: The two kings look at it a long moment. Then one of them begins to laugh, and then the other, and they sign, and they mend the horse together before they leave.

choices.text: Sit on the rocking horse yourself

effects.log: You sit on the rocking horse for the whole signing, very dignified, creaking slightly. The court painters paint it. You are in the painting, on the horse, forever.

choices.text: Suggest the generals wait outside

effects.log: The generals file out, offended. The two kings sit on the nursery floor alone, like boys again, and talk for three hours. Then they sign.

events.text: Among the River Folk a child is not counted until the first flood they remember. Yours comes in your seventh spring: the river climbs out of its bed in the night, politely, field by field, and by morning the whole village is living on the roofs with the goats, the seed jars and a great deal of shouting.

choices.text: Help carry the seed jars up the ladder

effects.log: You carry jar after jar, hugging each like a sleeping baby. Old Pell counts them twice and says not one grain got wet. You are counted, from that day.

choices.text: Float on a door to the next roof

effects.log: You paddle across on the cellar door with a ladle. Halfway, a fish jumps into your lap. You arrive a hero and a fishmonger.

choices.text: Sit with the goats and keep them calm

effects.log: You sing to the goats all night. They do not stop screaming, but they scream more calmly, and so does everyone else.

events.text: The water goes down and leaves its gift behind: a skin of black silt over every field, soft as cake and smelling of the far mountains. The River Folk say the flood is the river paying its rent. The children are sent out barefoot to find what else it left.

choices.text: Search the silt for treasures

effects.log: You find a clay cup, a drowned boot, and a carved wooden fish nobody in the village made. Pell says it came from upriver, from people you will never meet. You wear it on a string.

choices.text: Stamp the seed-holes in the silt, as the grown-ups do

effects.log: You stamp holes with your heel in a straight row all the way to the willow. It is the straightest row in the field, and Pell plants it with the best seed.

choices.text: Make the biggest mud figure the village has ever seen

effects.log: Your mud figure of the Maker is as tall as a goat and has an alarming smile. The silt sets hard in the sun. It stands for three years.

events.text: Pell keeps the flood-stick, a pole notched with every flood for two hundred years, and this year she lets you cut the notch. 'Low or high?' she asks. 'Tell the stick the truth. It will tell the children of the children.'

choices.text: Cut it exactly where the water reached

effects.log: You cut a clean notch at the height of your own shoulder. Pell nods. Somebody in two hundred years will know how tall this flood was, and how short you were.

choices.text: Show Pell the wooden fish from upriver

effects.log: Pell turns the fish over and finds a tiny notch under its tail, like the stick's. 'They count floods up there too,' she says, delighted. 'We are not the only ones keeping the river honest.'

choices.text: Cut it a little higher, to make it a better story

effects.log: Pell sees and says nothing. Years later you hear a child tell how the Great Flood reached the roof-beams, and you feel very guilty and slightly proud.

events.text: On Seed-Day every soul of the River Folk walks the fields in one long line from dawn to dusk, throwing seed in time to the plough-songs, and nobody is allowed to be in a bad mood, by custom older than the fields. This year the elders give you the honour of the first handful, which means the honour of throwing it in front of everybody.

choices.text: Throw it wide and high, like a farmer of fifty years

ok.log: The seed fans out in a golden arc and falls like rain. The line cheers. An old woman says she has not seen a throw like it since her own wedding.

fail.log: The wind takes your handful straight into the face of the eldest elder. He spits out seed for a whole verse of the song, then laughs until he has to sit down.

choices.text: Throw it gently, close to your feet

effects.log: Your seed falls in a neat little circle. The elders approve: a careful handful means a careful year. Nobody cheers, but nobody is hit either.

choices.text: Keep a few grains back in your pocket for luck

effects.log: You plant the stolen grains secretly behind the house. They come up taller than anything in the fields, and you never tell anyone why that patch is yours.

events.text: Seed-Day evening. The children sail paper boats with candles down the canals, one for every field, and the old people bet shells on which field's boat reaches the river first. Your neighbour Dovin, who has never won anything in his life, has bet his whole jar.

choices.text: Give Dovin's boat a secret push with a long reed

effects.log: The boat shoots ahead and wins by a finger. Dovin weeps with joy and buys everyone millet beer. Nobody saw. The river did, you suspect.

choices.text: Buy Dovin a second candle-boat, in sympathy

effects.log: Both of Dovin's boats sink halfway, candles and all. You lose together and eat to bad luck together, and he is your friend for life.

choices.text: Sail a boat for your secret patch

effects.log: Your boat for a field that does not officially exist sails straight and fast and wins. The bettors are furious: nobody can pay out on a field that is not on the list.

choices.text: Just watch the lights go downriver

effects.log: Hundreds of candles drift away into the dark like a slow procession of stars. It is the most peaceful hour of the year.

events.text: The harvest after a good Seed-Day is a matter of pride, and yours is enormous. The elders ask you to carry the first sheaf to the river temple and lay it at the feet of the Maker's statue, which holds a stone ear of grain in one hand and, oddly, a stone spoon in the other.

choices.text: Lay the sheaf down and ask the priest about the spoon

effects.log: The priest says the Maker, it is written, tasted the first porridge of the world and called it a little bland. Every River Folk cook since has added salt in the god's honour.

choices.text: Lay the sheaf down and say thank you, plainly

effects.log: You say thank you to the stone face. For a moment the statue seems pleased, though that is surely the candlelight.

choices.text: Keep the fattest ears back for next year's seed

effects.log: You give the temple the sheaf and keep the best ears for yourself. Next Seed-Day your handful is the finest grain in the valley, and you sell the rest for a good heap of shells.

events.text: Water is the only thing the River Folk ever really argue about. Every ditch in the valley belongs to the Water Council: nine farmers, one sluice-gate each, and a bronze bell that is rung when the council cannot agree. The bell is rung most days. One seat is empty, and your neighbours have put your name forward, possibly as a joke.

choices.text: Take the seat seriously

effects.log: You learn every ditch by name: Old Crooked, the Widow's Run, the One That Floods. In a month you know the valley like your own hand.

choices.text: Take the seat and nap through the first meeting

effects.log: You wake to find you have been made Keeper of the Bell, because you were the only one not shouting. It is a great honour. It is also very loud.

choices.text: Refuse: water quarrels end friendships

effects.log: You stay off the council and keep all your friends. They come to you after meetings to complain about each other, which is almost the same job.

events.text: A dry summer. The upper farms want the gates open; the lower farms will lose their crops if they are. Wendel of the top fields has brought a cart of melons to the meeting as a gift, which everyone agrees is not a bribe, while eating them.

choices.text: Divide the water by the hour, field by field

effects.log: You chalk the hours on the council wall: two hours up, two hours down, all through the night. It is exhausting and fair, and in the end no field dies.

choices.text: Side with Wendel and the melons

effects.log: The top fields flourish. The bottom fields wither, and so does your good name. Nobody ever brings melons to a meeting again.

choices.text: Ring the bell until they agree to share

effects.log: You ring it for an hour, then another. At the third hour the nine farmers agree to anything at all to make you stop, and it turns out to be a fair split.

events.text: The council is redigging Old Crooked, the oldest ditch in the valley, and three spades down they hit a stone channel nobody remembers building, straight as a ruled line, running from the river to every field. Carved at its head: a hand, pouring.

choices.text: Clear the old channel and use it

effects.log: The ancient channel works better than every ditch put together. The valley does not argue about water for a whole generation, and does not know what to do with itself.

choices.text: Ask the temple whose work it is

effects.log: The priest says the first ditch in the world was dug by the Maker, with one finger, to show the River Folk the idea. She seems a little hurt that you had to ask.

choices.text: Cover it up again: the valley needs its argument

effects.log: You quietly put the stones back. The council goes on shouting and ringing the bell for years. Shouting about water, you have decided, is how this valley says it loves itself.

events.text: The River Folk plough in pairs: two oxen and two singers, one on each side, the songs going back and forth across the furrow like a shuttle. If the songs do not match, the furrow goes crooked. The village has paired you with {npc} for the spring, and on the first morning your verses collide like two carts.

choices.text: Change your song to fit {npc}'s

mem.note: changed the song to fit mine

effects.log: You pick up {npc}'s tune and lean your words against it. By noon the furrow is straight as a sunbeam, and {npc} is looking at you across the oxen with surprise.

choices.text: Sing louder until {npc} follows you

effects.log: You out-sing each other all morning. The furrow looks like a snake that has heard bad news. The oxen hate you both. {npc} laughs so hard the plough stops.

choices.text: Ask for a different partner

effects.log: You are paired with old Hamm, who sings one verse for four hours. Your furrow is straight. You hear {npc}'s voice two fields away and cannot stop listening.

events.text: Harvest night. The pairs who ploughed together are expected to sing their furrow-song once more in front of the whole valley, and everybody knows what it means when a pair sings it well.

choices.text: Sing it with {npc}, and mean it

mem.note: sang the furrow-song with me on harvest night

effects.log: Your voices fit the way they have fit all summer. The valley goes quiet. Somebody's grandfather honks into a handkerchief. {npc} does not let go of your hand after.

choices.text: Sing the crooked-furrow verse, as a joke

effects.log: The valley roars. {npc} pretends to be offended and then sings the second half even worse. It is, people say later, the best harvest night in years.

choices.text: Let {npc} sing it alone

effects.log: {npc} sings it alone, beautifully, looking at the place where you should be standing. The valley is very kind to you about it, which is worse.

events.text: Spring again. The ox-master is pairing singers for the ploughing and stops at your name with a sly look. 'Same as last year?' The whole yard waits for the answer, and so does {npc}.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to plough beside you for life

effects.log: Among the River Folk a pair who ask to plough together for life are wed by the ox-master on the spot, with a handful of soil. You are both muddy at your wedding, as is proper.

choices.text: Plough with {npc} this year, and see

mem.note: chose me again for the spring

effects.log: Another spring of matched songs and straight furrows. Nobody asks again; the whole valley is waiting for you two to work it out, and placing bets.

choices.text: Choose a new partner this year

effects.log: {npc} nods and finds another singer, and their furrow is straight too. You are a little sorry and a little free, which is how most springs feel.

events.text: Every seven years the River Folk choose a Headman, and every seven years nobody wants to be Headman, because the Headman has to settle all the quarrels about pigs. This year, in protest, the young people of your village have put up a scarecrow called Sir Straw. Sir Straw is winning.

choices.text: Run Sir Straw's campaign

effects.log: You write Sir Straw's speeches, short and wise, and speak them from behind his hat. His promise of no new rules is very popular.

choices.text: Stand against Sir Straw yourself

effects.log: You give a long, sensible speech about pig law. People nod respectfully and then vote for the scarecrow. You come second, ahead of a goat.

choices.text: Stay out of it and sell straw hats

effects.log: You sell a hundred tiny straw hats to Sir Straw's supporters. Politics, you learn, is very good for the hat business.

events.text: Sir Straw is chosen Headman by a large majority. Now somebody has to settle the pig quarrels in his name. The first one arrives that afternoon: two farmers, one pig, and a great deal of mud.

choices.text: Speak for Sir Straw from behind his hat

effects.log: You rule that the pig shall live a week with each farmer and choose for itself. The pig chooses a third farmer. Sir Straw's ruling is respected across the valley.

choices.text: Let the pig decide by walking to one of them

effects.log: The pig walks to Sir Straw and eats his left boot. The crowd takes this as a sign. Both farmers are fined one boot.

choices.text: Tell the farmers to sort it out themselves

effects.log: They sort it out by not speaking for eleven years. The pig dies of old age, well fed by both. It is not the worst outcome.

events.text: Sir Straw serves his full seven years and is the best-loved Headman in memory: no scandals, no new dues, no speech longer than a breath. At the end of his term the village must decide what to do with him.

choices.text: Lay him in the field with honours

effects.log: Sir Straw goes into the earth with a song and a basket of grain. The next harvest from that field is enormous, which the village finds very reasonable.

choices.text: Stand for Headman yourself now

effects.log: You win easily, as Sir Straw's chosen voice. Your first act is to make pig quarrels the Headman's day off.

choices.text: Choose him again

effects.log: Sir Straw wins a second term unopposed. Visitors from other valleys are confused. The River Folk are not.

events.text: The first of the Stone-Born stepped out of Mother Cliff fully grown, grey and quiet, and their descendants have never quite forgiven anyone for being soft. Every child is given a birth-stone chipped from the cliff, and must carry it everywhere until they can lift it above their head. Yours is the size of a loaf and the weight of a sulking goat.

choices.text: Carry it everywhere, even to bed

effects.log: You carry it to meals, to the latrine, to bed. Your arms ache, then harden. By midsummer you can throw it, which you are told is not the point.

choices.text: Paint a face on it and make it a friend

effects.log: You name it Grumble and give it a frown. The other children laugh, then paint faces on theirs. The teachers call it undignified and secretly paint one on their own.

choices.text: Roll it instead of carrying it

effects.log: You roll it everywhere on a little sled. The teachers call it cheating; the old smith calls it engineering, and gives you a sweet.

events.text: The test of the birth-stone: each child stands at the Stone Mark and lifts their stone above their head for the elders to see. The elders do not clap. The Stone-Born show approval by striking two pebbles together, once.

choices.text: Lift it high and hold it

ok.log: Up it goes and stays there, trembling. Click, go the elders' pebbles, all of them. You have never heard a better sound.

fail.log: You get it to your chin and no further. The eldest clicks his pebbles anyway. 'Next year it will be lighter,' he says, 'because you will be heavier.'

choices.text: Ask Grumble for help, out loud

effects.log: You whisper to Grumble and lift. Perhaps it is the joke, perhaps your nerves let go, but the stone goes up. The elders click, and one of them nearly smiles.

choices.text: Ask why stones, of all things

effects.log: The eldest says the rock was here before anything and remembers the hand that shaped it. 'You carry it so you remember too,' he says. You do not understand. You remember the words.

events.text: You are old enough now to set your birth-stone into the Wall of Names, among thousands of others, each carved with a child's mark. It is the proudest day of a Stone-Born childhood. It is also, a little, a goodbye.

choices.text: Carve your mark deep

effects.log: You carve until your hands blister. Your mark will outlast the house you live in, the elders say, and they are probably right.

choices.text: Carve Grumble's frown beside your mark

effects.log: The frowning stone takes its place in the Wall forever. Visiting children point at it and giggle. Somehow it becomes the most famous stone in the Wall.

choices.text: Keep a chip of it in your pocket

effects.log: You knock off a chip no bigger than a tooth and keep it all your life. On hard days you hold it, and it is very slightly warm.

events.text: Among the Stone-Born a quarrel is not shouted. It is fought, formally, in the Circle, with round shields and wooden staves, before witnesses, and it ends at the first fall, after which both sides must eat a meal together. Your neighbour Korra has insulted your cooking. Everyone has heard. It cannot be let pass.

choices.text: Challenge Korra to the Circle

effects.log: You strike Korra's door three times with a pebble, the formal challenge. Korra opens it, looks at the pebble, and bows. The whole street exhales. It is going to be a good week.

choices.text: Cook Korra a better meal instead

effects.log: You cook for two days and leave the pot at Korra's door. It comes back empty with a pebble inside: an apology. This is legal, but considered a little soft.

choices.text: Agree with Korra: your cooking is bad

effects.log: The street is scandalised. Nobody has ever simply agreed before. Korra, baffled, comes to dinner to check, and stays to teach you how to make bread.

events.text: Duel day. The Circle is crowded: the Stone-Born love a duel the way other peoples love a wedding. Korra walks in grim as a cliff. The judge reminds you both that the aim is not to hurt, but to be seen to be serious.

choices.text: Fight properly, shield high

ok.log: You catch Korra's blow on your shield, turn, and tap Korra's knee with your staff. Korra sits down with great dignity. The Circle clicks its pebbles for a long time.

fail.log: Korra's staff sweeps your feet and you land on your back, looking at the sky. It is a very blue sky. The crowd clicks politely. Honour is satisfied, if you are not.

choices.text: Fall down first, gracefully

effects.log: You make a beautiful fall, the kind the old duellists teach: a slow lean and a roll. The judge calls it the most honourable loss of the season. Korra is annoyed to win so easily.

choices.text: Drop your shield and offer your hand

effects.log: Nobody has done that in living memory. The judge consults a book. The book says it counts as a fall for both. You have to eat dinner together twice.

events.text: The duel-meal: by Stone-Born law the two of you must eat at one table, from one pot, until something is said that makes peace. Korra has brought bread. You have brought the dish that started it all.

choices.text: Ask Korra to cook it properly

effects.log: Korra cooks while you watch, explaining every step with great reluctance. It is excellent. You admit it. Korra admits you were close. You eat together on that day every year after.

choices.text: Serve your cooking again, with pride

effects.log: Korra eats a mouthful with the face of someone keeping a promise. 'It is still bad,' Korra says, 'but I lost.' The table laughs, and the laughter is the peace.

choices.text: Eat in silence until dawn

effects.log: Neither of you speaks. At dawn Korra says 'Good morning,' which, the judge rules, counts. Stone-Born law is very patient.

events.text: Every Stone-Born goes to the war-school for three years, though there has not been a war in living memory and nobody can quite remember whom it would be against. The school teaches shields, staves, marching in step, and above all the Wall: a hundred students shield to shield, unmoving, while the teachers try to make them laugh.

choices.text: Train to hold the Wall

effects.log: You learn to stand like a mountain while a teacher in a false beard does a chicken dance in front of you. You do not laugh. It is the hardest thing you have ever done.

choices.text: Study the old shield-books in the school library

effects.log: The shield-books are mostly about posture and mostly ancient. One of them is only a drawing of a hand held open, labelled: the first shield.

choices.text: Make the teachers laugh instead

effects.log: You are put on punishment duty, polishing two hundred shields, and become the most popular student in the school.

events.text: Great Wall Day: the whole school forms the Wall in the square, and the town is invited to break it, not with blows but with jokes, gifts, pleading, crying babies and, in one case, a very sad song about a lost goat.

choices.text: Hold your place in the Wall whatever comes

ok.log: A child offers you a honey cake. A grandmother says you look tired. The goat song comes. You stand. At sunset the Wall is unbroken, and you are part of why.

fail.log: The goat song gets you. A single sniff, and you step out of line. Three others follow you, weeping. The town counts it a fine day.

choices.text: Sing the goat song yourself, from inside the Wall

effects.log: You start singing it from within the Wall itself. The Wall breaks in four places from laughter. You are punished and later admired.

choices.text: Stand at the end, where the cakes are offered first

effects.log: You are offered eleven cakes. You refuse them all and grow hungrier and holier by the hour. The cakes go to the teachers, who are delighted.

events.text: Graduation. Each Stone-Born leaves the war-school with a shield, and must paint on it the one thing they would truly fight for. The paint-pots stand ready. The teachers say there is no wrong answer, which is a lie: there have been several.

choices.text: Paint the open hand from the old book

effects.log: Your shield bears an open hand. The eldest teacher looks at it a long while and says the school was founded under that sign. You hang the shield over your door all your life.

choices.text: Paint the faces of your friends

effects.log: You paint them all, badly. Your friends are insulted by the likenesses and secretly delighted. Years later they each want to borrow the shield on their wedding days.

choices.text: Paint the Wall itself, a hundred shields in a row

effects.log: You paint the Wall, tiny, shoulder to shoulder. The school copies it onto the gate. Without meaning to, you have made the school's new sign.

choices.text: Paint nothing: you have not decided yet

effects.log: Your plain grey shield is the talk of the graduation. The teachers call it the most honest answer in years, and also lazy.

events.text: Deep in the quarry halls the Stone-Singers work: old Stone-Born who hum to the rock until it splits along the line they want, clean as cut bread. They say every stone has a note, and the mountain one great note underneath, which nobody has ever heard. They are looking for an apprentice with a steady breath.

choices.text: Apprentice yourself to the singers

effects.log: Your teacher, Hollin, is ninety and nearly deaf and can split a boulder with a hum. For a month you hum at a pebble. On the thirty-first day it cracks, a hair's width, and you shout so loud the hall echoes.

choices.text: Haul the split stone for the singers

effects.log: You carry blocks out of the quarry until you are as hard as they are. The singers hum while you work, and the work is lighter for it.

choices.text: Listen from the doorway

effects.log: You stand in the doorway and listen to the old ones humming the rock apart. It sounds like a choir in a dream. You go home quiet.

events.text: A cave-in on the lower level traps three quarry workers behind a wall of fallen stone. Digging would bring the roof down. Hollin is too old and too slow. Everyone looks at the apprentices.

choices.text: Put your lips to the fallen stone and hum

ok.log: You hum and hum until you hear the note in it. The stone splits along its seam and the three crawl out grey with dust and laughing.

fail.log: You cannot find the note. Hours later the older singers do it together, a chord of old voices. The three are saved. You are hoarse and ashamed, and Hollin pats your head.

choices.text: Dig carefully, with props

effects.log: You dig with the haulers, propping every hand's width. It takes all night. The roof holds. The three come out at dawn and shake your hand with crushing fingers.

choices.text: Run for help from the surface

effects.log: You bring every singer in the town. They hum together, and the wall falls apart like cake. You get no credit and do not want any.

events.text: Hollin is dying, and asks to be carried to the deepest hall, where the mountain's own note is supposed to lie. 'I never heard it,' Hollin says. 'Hum with me. Perhaps two old fools can find it.'

choices.text: Hum with Hollin, as long as it takes

effects.log: You hum together in the dark until your voices wear thin. Then, beneath them, so low it is felt in the teeth, the mountain answers: one note, warm, patient, very old. Hollin smiles and does not hum again.

choices.text: Promise to keep looking when Hollin is gone

effects.log: Hollin nods and gives you the tuning stone of the singers. You hum in the deep hall every year after, and every year you are a little closer.

choices.text: Carry Hollin back up into the sun

effects.log: You decide the sun is better than any note. Hollin laughs, a dust-dry laugh, and dies warm in the light at the quarry mouth, which was perhaps the right note after all.

events.text: At the war-school reunion the Stone-Born form the Wall again for old times' sake, and the shield next to yours belongs to {npc}, who has not stopped muttering bad jokes at you since the line formed. The teachers prowl in front. You must not laugh.

choices.text: Hold the Wall, and never laugh

effects.log: You do not laugh. Neither does {npc}. At sunset, when the Wall breaks up, you both collapse on the cobbles and laugh for an hour.

choices.text: Mutter a worse joke back

effects.log: Your joke is so bad {npc} snorts and steps out of line, and you are both sent to polish shields, which you do together until midnight, talking.

choices.text: Ask the teachers to move you

effects.log: You are moved to the far end, beside someone very serious who does not speak at all. It is peaceful. You keep glancing down the line.

events.text: Two Stone-Born who wish to court must carry one stone between them, a great block from the quarry, all the way up to the Wall of Names without setting it down. The quarry master has chosen the stone. It is very large. {npc} is already standing by it, looking at you.

choices.text: Lift it together

mem.note: carried the courting stone with me

ok.log: It takes all day. You stop only to breathe, never to set it down. At the top the whole town clicks pebbles, and {npc} has tears of effort running into a grin.

fail.log: Halfway up the hill your fingers slip and the stone thumps down. Custom says you must start again. {npc} sits on it and laughs until you laugh too, and you start again tomorrow.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to choose a smaller stone

effects.log: The quarry master is outraged. {npc} chooses a pebble, very solemnly, and you carry it between you, one finger each, up the whole hill. The town is scandalised and delighted.

choices.text: Leave the stone where it is

effects.log: You walk away from the quarry. {npc} watches you go and does not follow. The stone is still there, waiting, they say, for the right two.

events.text: The last rite of a Stone-Born courtship is the shield-bond: each paints the other's shield, and if both accept the painting, they are joined. {npc} has painted your shield already, and is holding it face down, waiting.

choices.text: Accept the shield and paint {npc}'s

effects.log: Your shield shows you as {npc} sees you: taller, braver, slightly cross-eyed. You paint an open hand on {npc}'s. The town clicks its pebbles all night. You are joined.

choices.text: Turn it over first, before deciding

effects.log: It is you, laughing, in the Wall, with every teacher in the world glaring. You are too moved to answer, and {npc} says it can wait a year. It can.

choices.text: Give the shield back unpainted

effects.log: {npc} takes it back and nods, Stone-Born to the bone: no fuss. You stay friends who stand side by side in the Wall every year, and never once laugh.

events.text: The Wind Kin live in tall thin towers on the windy uplands, and they send their letters by kite: a scroll tied to the tail, the string let out until the kite is over the right tower, then a tug that drops the letter on the roof. Every child of the Wind Kin flies the post for a season. Your first kite is a red fish with a torn fin.

choices.text: Mend the fin before you fly it

effects.log: You patch the fin with paper and rice paste. The red fish flies straight, and your first letter lands on the right roof. The roof-keeper waves a scarf at you.

choices.text: Fly it anyway and see what happens

effects.log: The torn fish flies crooked and drops a love letter on the wrong tower, starting a scandal you are too young to understand. The grown-ups laugh about it for years.

choices.text: Paint eyes on it so it can see the way

effects.log: You paint it two huge eyes. The old kite-master says that is how the first kites were made, when the Wind Kin thought kites flew themselves. Yours flies very well.

events.text: A storm comes over the uplands with a letter still in the air: an urgent one, for the healer in Far Tower, about a sick baby. The older children have all hauled their kites in. Yours is the last one out.

choices.text: Hold the string and steer it through

ok.log: The wind screams and the red fish dives, climbs, dives, and drops its scroll on Far Tower's roof just as the string snaps. The healer comes by evening. You are carried round the tower on shoulders.

fail.log: The string snaps and the letter is lost in the storm. You run the whole way to Far Tower instead, in the rain, and arrive soaked and in time.

choices.text: Trust the painted eyes to find the way

effects.log: You let the string run. The fish with its huge eyes climbs above the storm and comes down exactly on Far Tower. The kite-master writes it in the Book of Strange Flights.

choices.text: Reel it in, as you were taught

effects.log: You haul in the kite and the letter with it, and a grown-up runs it to Far Tower. It arrives late, but it arrives. You are praised for obeying, and feel oddly unsatisfied.

events.text: At the end of the kite season the children fly their kites together on the Hill of Strings, with no letters at all, only their own wishes written on the tails so the wind can read them. The kite-master says the wind delivers them to the Maker.

choices.text: Write a wish for someone else

effects.log: You wish that old Brannoch's knees would stop hurting. In the spring they do, mostly. Brannoch thanks the wind, and you do not correct him.

choices.text: Write a question instead of a wish

effects.log: You write: who made the wind? Your kite climbs higher than any other that day. It comes down hours later with the question still on it, and beside it a tiny warm mark, like a fingerprint.

choices.text: Cut the string and let the kite go

effects.log: Your red fish goes up and up and away over the uplands. The kite-master says it will reach the Maker for certain now. You cry a little, and then feel very light.

events.text: The great library of the Wind Kin is one tower, four hundred floors, with a single spiral stair and no lift, because the founders believed a book should cost you something. Librarians are chosen from those who can climb to the top and still read when they get there. You have applied.

choices.text: Climb to the top in one go

effects.log: You climb for half a day. At the top, gasping, you are handed a page of very small writing and asked what it means. You manage. You are in.

choices.text: Climb slowly, reading on every landing

effects.log: Each landing has a shelf. You read your way up over three days. The librarians, impressed, let you in, and charge you a few coins for the lamp oil.

choices.text: Ask to work in the cellar instead

effects.log: The cellar holds the books nobody wants: almanacs, laundry lists, a cookbook for stones. You love it. You are the only person who has ever asked.

events.text: A reader has been coming to the library for twenty years asking the same question: is there a book that says why the Maker made the world? The librarians hide from him in shifts. Today it is your shift.

choices.text: Search the whole tower for him

effects.log: You search for a month. You find books that say how, books that say when, a book that says the world is a mistake and one that says it is a joke. None that says why. He thanks you and comes back next week.

choices.text: Give him the cookbook for stones

effects.log: He reads it all night and comes up glowing. 'It is not why,' he says, 'but it is the first book that seems to have been written for fun. That is something.' He never asks again.

choices.text: Tell him to write the book himself

effects.log: He looks at you as if you had struck him, and walks away. Six years later a book arrives at the library with your name in the dedication. It is very long and does not answer the question.

events.text: The top floor of the library has a locked door that nobody has opened since the tower was built. The key is lost, and the rule is old: the librarian who finds the key may open it. Today, dusting a high shelf, you found a key.

choices.text: Open the door

effects.log: Inside is one bare room with a window facing the dawn, and a desk with nothing on it but a quill worn down with use. Nobody knows whose. You leave it as you found it, and lock the door again.

choices.text: Hand the key to the head librarian

effects.log: The head librarian holds it a long time, then drops it out of the window into the wind. 'Some doors,' she says, 'are only kept because they are shut.' You are promoted for your honesty.

choices.text: Hang it on a nail and say nothing

effects.log: The key hangs there, unremarked, for forty years. You walk past it every day. It is the most interesting thing in your life, and you never open it.

events.text: Every ten years the Wind Kin hold the Great Debate, a single argument that runs forty days from tower to tower by kite-letter, after which the whole people votes on the winner. This decade's question, drawn by lot, is: Is soup a food or a drink? Feelings are running high.

choices.text: Argue that soup is a food

effects.log: You write fourteen pages on the spoon as evidence. The Food party adopts you as a hero. Drink supporters pelt you with bread in the street, which you eat.

choices.text: Argue that soup is a drink

effects.log: You argue from the cup, the sip and the unbearable sound of slurping. The Drink party carries you to its tower. You are pelted with spoons.

choices.text: Argue that the question is beneath a great people

effects.log: Both parties unite briefly to despise you. Then the Philosophers' Tower declares you the voice of reason, which is worse.

events.text: Day thirty-nine. The debate is tied. The last letter will decide it, and both parties have chosen you to write it, through a clerical error nobody can untangle in time. Kites wait on every tower for your words.

choices.text: Write the finest argument of your life for your side

effects.log: You write all night. At dawn your letter flies to every tower. Grown scholars weep over a paragraph about broth. Your side wins by eleven votes.

choices.text: Write that soup is whatever you need when you are ill

effects.log: The letter flies. The uplands go very quiet. For the first time in the Debate's history the vote is unanimous, for no side at all.

choices.text: Send a blank letter

effects.log: The blank letter is argued over for a week: a statement on silence? On the emptiness of bowls? Your side loses, but the letter is studied in schools.

events.text: Years later you are invited to the Archive to see where the soup debate is kept: a sealed jar marked GREAT DEBATE, SOUP, on a shelf beside the jars of every earlier debate, going back to the very first, which is labelled only QUESTION ASKED BY THE MAKER.

choices.text: Ask what the Maker's question was

effects.log: The archivist reads it off the jar, carefully: Is this good? The Wind Kin have been debating it ever since, she says. The vote stands at yes, narrowly.

choices.text: Ask to have your letter put on display

effects.log: They put it in a glass case. Children come to see it and are disappointed that it is about soup. You are delighted every time.

choices.text: Leave a bowl of soup by the jar, as an offering

effects.log: The archivists eat it, debating as they do whether they are eating or drinking. Neither side will say who won.

events.text: Under the oldest tower of the Wind Kin lies the Archive of the Maker's Words: everything the god is said to have said, written down by the first scribes and copied for {pw_years} years. The archivists are short of copyists. The pay is bad, the ink is cold, and the words, they warn you, have a way of getting into your sleep.

choices.text: Become a copyist

effects.log: You copy the god's words in a cold cellar by lamplight, letter by letter. After a month you can write them without looking. After two, you dream them.

choices.text: Read without copying

effects.log: You read in the visitors' room for a season. Most of the god's words are practical: how deep to plant, which stars to steer by, when to stop arguing. Some are jokes. You laugh in the silent room and are glared at.

choices.text: Ask what the god actually did

effects.log: An archivist pulls the oldest ledger and reads you one line: that the god {pw_record}. 'We keep the deeds as well as the words,' she says. 'Words are cheap. Even for a god.'

events.text: One evening the chief archivist brings you an old scroll, very worried. One passage was corrected long ago in a different ink: a word crossed out and another written above. Nobody alters the Maker's words. And the correction, you notice with a cold feeling, looks very like your own handwriting.

choices.text: Lay your own copying beside it

effects.log: The slant, the hook on the tails, the little blot at the end of a line: identical. The archivist looks at you and then, carefully, does not ask.

choices.text: Read what the correction says

effects.log: The word crossed out is rule. The word above it is promise. It is a small thing. The archivists have argued about it for centuries.

choices.text: Call it a coincidence and go home

effects.log: You go home and do not sleep. Coincidence, you tell the ceiling. The ceiling does not argue, which is unlike an archivist.

events.text: The chief archivist takes you to the deepest room, where the first scroll of all is kept. It holds a single line, the first thing the god ever said to the world. Nobody has been allowed to read it for a hundred years. The archivist unrolls it and stands back.

choices.text: Read it aloud

effects.log: You read: I will come back and see how you are. Your voice is the voice that said it. The archivist kneels, then gets up quickly, embarrassed, and gives you a pass to the Maker's oldest temple.

choices.text: Read it silently and roll it up

effects.log: It says: Begin. Only that. You roll it up with careful hands and leave thinking about all the things that one word made.

choices.text: Refuse to read it

effects.log: You say the first word of a world should be left alone. The archivist is relieved: you have passed the oldest test of the Archive, which is not to want too much. You are made an archivist.

events.text: A kite-letter lands on your roof that was never meant for you: a long, furious, very funny review of a book, addressed to a scholar three towers away and signed {npc}. By the rules of the kite post, a letter delivered wrong must be answered by whoever receives it.

choices.text: Answer with a furious, funny defence of the book

mem.note: defended a book against me by kite

effects.log: You have never read the book. You defend it anyway, brilliantly. The reply comes next day: two pages of outrage and one line at the end, asking your name.

choices.text: Send it on to the right tower, with a polite note

effects.log: You forward the letter with a small apology. Next day a kite drops a thank-you on your roof, and a question about your handwriting, which {npc} admires.

choices.text: Keep it and do not answer

effects.log: You keep the letter in a drawer and break a rule of the kite post. It is a very good letter. You read it more often than you would admit.

events.text: A year of letters back and forth by kite: about books, weather, the soup debate and, more and more, nothing at all. You have never seen {npc}'s face. The letters are now so long the kites struggle to lift them.

choices.text: Ask to meet on the Hill of Strings

mem.note: met me on the Hill of Strings

effects.log: You meet at last among the kites. {npc} is not what you imagined, and is better, and talks exactly as the letters did, at great speed, with a lot of hands.

choices.text: Write the longest letter in Wind Kin history

mem.note: sent me a letter of four kites

effects.log: Your letter needs four kites. It is read aloud in three towers by people who should not have been reading it. {npc} answers with one line: Come and say it.

choices.text: Stop writing, quietly

effects.log: You stop. A few kites come after, then fewer, then one, then none. On windy days you look up at the sky as if expecting post.

events.text: Among the Wind Kin a proposal is made by kite: a page with no words at all, only a feather, flown from one tower to another. One lands on your roof at dawn, from {npc}'s tower.

choices.text: Fly a blank page back

effects.log: Your blank page lands on {npc}'s roof at noon. By sunset there are kites over both towers, dozens of them, the whole uplands celebrating in paper. You are wed under a sky of letters.

choices.text: Write one word on the page: soon

effects.log: {npc} writes back: how soon? You write: soon. This goes on for some time. It is, the neighbours agree, the most Wind Kin courtship they have ever seen.

choices.text: Let the page blow away

effects.log: You let the wind take it. Kindly letters from {npc} keep coming, about books, for the rest of your life. They are among the best things in it.

events.text: The first creature of {pw_world} was {pw_beast}, and every child knows the story: it woke before there were people, walked the empty land, and its descendants still live among them, honoured and a little spoiled. One of those descendants has decided to sleep in your yard. It is enormous, and nobody will tell it to move.

choices.text: Feed it your breakfast

effects.log: It eats your breakfast, your bowl and the bench. Then it puts its great head in your lap and sighs. You are late for everything all year, and you do not care.

choices.text: Draw it while it sleeps

effects.log: You draw it forty times. On the forty-first it opens one eye and looks at the drawing with what seems like criticism. You draw it better.

choices.text: Ask the elders why nobody moves it

effects.log: The elders say {pw_beast} and its children were here first, made before anyone who could argue. You decide the yard was always theirs, really.

events.text: The beast in your yard is sick: it will not eat, its breath is slow, and the whole street brings remedies, some sensible, some involving onions. The temple sends a priest, who looks worried, because the descendants of {pw_beast} are not supposed to fall sick.

choices.text: Sit with it day and night

effects.log: You sit with it for three days, talking about nothing. On the fourth morning it lifts its head and eats the bench again. The priest writes your name in the temple book.

choices.text: Search the hills for the herb in the old songs

effects.log: You climb the hills and find it, small and bitter and blue. The beast eats it, sneezes for an hour, and recovers. The street throws you a little feast.

choices.text: Bring the onions

effects.log: The beast eats every onion in the street and recovers at once, out of sheer outrage. Nobody can prove it was the onions. Everyone believes it was.

events.text: One spring morning the beast leaves your yard, walking toward the hills where, they say, {pw_beast} itself still sleeps under the oldest mountain. It stops at the gate and looks back at you.

choices.text: Walk beside it to the edge of the village

effects.log: You walk with it as far as the last house. It touches your forehead with its great nose, warm and damp, and goes on. You feel blessed in a way no priest has managed.

choices.text: Wave goodbye from the gate

effects.log: You wave until it is a dot. That night, from very far away, there is a low call like a horn, once. The village says it was saying thank you.

choices.text: Plant a tree where it slept

effects.log: You plant a tree in the hollow its body left. It grows strangely fast. Your yard is the coolest in the village, and you think of the beast whenever you sit there.

events.text: Under the oldest mountain of {pw_world} lies {pw_beast} itself, the first beast, asleep since before history. Pilgrims climb to see it every year: a great shape of moss and stone and slow breath, its back grown over with trees. This year you are among them.

choices.text: Climb up to its closed eye

effects.log: You stand beside an eyelid as large as a door and feel the breath of the world's first creature move your hair. Nothing in your life has made you smaller, or happier.

choices.text: Listen to the pilgrims' songs about it

effects.log: They sing that {pw_beast} was the first thing the Maker made and the Maker's first friend, and that it sleeps because it is waiting for someone. They do not say who.

choices.text: Sell flatbread to the pilgrims

effects.log: You sell flatbread on the mountain path for coins and blessings. By the end of the pilgrimage you are rich and covered in crumbs.

events.text: In the night, while the pilgrims sleep, the mountain shifts. {pw_beast} is breathing faster. Mother Isk, the old guardian of the path, says it has not done that in three hundred years, not since the god last walked the land.

choices.text: Go up to it alone

effects.log: You climb in the dark. At the top the great eye is open: amber, enormous, looking at you with what can only be recognition. Then, slowly, it closes, as if satisfied.

choices.text: Wake the pilgrims and pray

effects.log: The whole mountain prays till dawn. The breathing slows. Mother Isk says the prayers worked; you are not sure prayers were what it wanted.

choices.text: Go back to sleep

effects.log: You sleep like a stone. In the morning the mountain is calm, you missed everything, and the pilgrims tell you all about it with relish the whole way down.

events.text: Mother Isk comes to find you before you leave the mountain. She is very old, and she looks at you for a long time. 'It has never opened its eye for a pilgrim,' she says. 'What did you do?'

choices.text: Tell her it looked at you like an old friend

effects.log: Mother Isk sits down on a rock. 'There is a road,' she says at last, 'up past the beast, to a place nobody living has seen. I think you should take it.' She draws it in the dust.

choices.text: Say you did nothing

effects.log: 'That is what the god did too, by the stories,' Mother Isk says. 'Nothing, very carefully.' She laughs at her own joke for a long time.

choices.text: Promise to come back every year

effects.log: You come back every year of your life. The beast never opens its eye for you again, but its breathing always slows a little when you arrive.

events.text: {pw_world} began as plants, long before any people: a forest that grew over the bare world in a single night, the old stories say, and in the middle of it the Rememberer, the first tree, which is still alive. If you lay your hand on its bark, it is said, it shows you something from the beginning.

choices.text: Lay your hand on the bark

effects.log: The bark is warm. For a heartbeat you see the bare world, dark and empty, and a pair of hands pressing seeds into it. Then you are back, with green on your palm.

choices.text: Climb into its branches

effects.log: You climb until the villages below look like seeds. Up here the leaves hum faintly. You sleep in a fork of the branches and wake with leaves in your hair, very rested.

choices.text: Gather its fallen leaves to sell

effects.log: Rememberer leaves sell well to healers. You make a good sum in coins, and the tree, as far as anyone can tell, does not mind.

events.text: The keepers of the Rememberer, a quiet order who never cut anything, tell you the tree is dying. Slowly: it has been dying for a thousand years. But faster now, and they do not know why.

choices.text: Search its roots for the cause

effects.log: Deep in the roots you find it: a carved stone, sunk long ago, a marker of the Maker's, which the roots have tried for centuries to grow around and cannot. Too heavy, the keepers say. Too holy to move.

choices.text: Water it from the old spring by hand

effects.log: You carry water for a season, bucket by bucket. The tree does not get better, but it gets no worse, and the keepers start bringing you bread.

choices.text: Accept that even trees end

effects.log: You sit with the keepers under the dying branches. That, they say, is all most of them do: sit, and remember with it. You learn to be still.

events.text: One night the Rememberer drops a single seed, the first in living memory, into your hands. The keepers gather, silent. They say the tree chooses who to give its memory to.

choices.text: Move the root stone so it can grow

effects.log: You dig the stone free with your hands. As it comes loose the tree shudders, and you remember (not see: remember) setting it there yourself, long ago. Sorry, you whisper. The keepers draw you a map to a temple nobody visits.

choices.text: Plant the seed beside the old tree

effects.log: You plant it in the shade of its parent. In a year it is waist-high. The keepers name it after you, which embarrasses you dreadfully.

choices.text: Keep the seed and carry it with you

effects.log: You keep the seed in a pouch on your chest. Sometimes, half asleep, you remember things from before the world, and they are very peaceful.

events.text: In a world that began as forest, some people can still hear plants: the plant-speakers, who know when an orchard is thirsty or a field is sulking. They test every child at seven by setting a seedling in front of them and waiting. Yours is a small, unhappy bean.

choices.text: Talk to the bean

effects.log: You tell the bean about your day. The bean does not reply. But next morning it has grown a whole hand's width toward you, and the plant-speaker writes something down.

choices.text: Give the bean some water

effects.log: Practical, says the plant-speaker. Plants appreciate practical people. The bean, it seems, appreciates it too.

choices.text: Sing it a song

effects.log: You sing it a song about a happy bean. The plant-speaker says the bean finds you embarrassing but likes you anyway, which is how most beans feel.

events.text: Your bean has become a vine that covers the whole front of the house and has opinions. The plant-speaker comes to see it, with a crowd of children, and asks the vine, solemnly, what it thinks of you.

choices.text: Answer for the vine, in a deep voice

effects.log: The children shriek with laughter. The plant-speaker does not laugh, but the vine (everyone swears it) shivers in the windless air as if it did.

choices.text: Listen properly, as you were taught

effects.log: You put your ear to a leaf and hear, very faintly, something like sun on a warm wall. You say the vine is content. The plant-speaker nods and takes you as an apprentice.

choices.text: Pick its flowers for the plant-speaker

effects.log: The plant-speaker takes them gravely and says the vine offered them, which is the polite way to put it. The vine grows twice as many next year, out of spite.

events.text: A blight comes to the orchards: leaves curl, fruit drops green, and the plant-speakers walk the rows listening. They let you walk with them. In the oldest corner one tree is shouting, if trees can shout.

choices.text: Go to the shouting tree

effects.log: You lay your hand on it and hear it plainly: the water is wrong. Upstream the farmers find the irrigation pool fouled and clean it out. The orchard recovers. So does your good name.

choices.text: Carry water to the curling trees

effects.log: You carry water until dark. It does not cure the blight, but the speakers say the trees noticed, and that matters to trees more than people think.

choices.text: Ask the oldest speaker who first heard plants

effects.log: The Maker did, the old speaker says, who planted the whole first forest and then sat down and listened to it grow. The first plant-speaker was the god. We are only the second.

events.text: Once a year {pw_world} remembers the day the Maker blessed it: the Feast of the Gift. Every table is dragged into the street, every oven lit, and a great straw figure of the god is carried through town with its arms open. The priests say the god gave {pw_gift}. The children say the god gave cake.

choices.text: Help carry the straw god

effects.log: You take a corner of the straw god and carry it through every street. Its straw arm keeps patting you on the head. By the end you are exhausted and absurdly proud.

choices.text: Eat at every table in town

effects.log: You eat at thirty-one tables. Every household insists. You go home round as a melon and lie awake with happiness and a stomach ache.

choices.text: Listen to the priest read the blessing

effects.log: The priest reads it from the temple book: that {pw_deed}. The crowd says it along with her, word for word, the way people say a thing they love.

events.text: At the end of the Feast the straw god is set on the water (or the hill, or the field, depending on the town), and everybody puts something into its open hands to give back: a coin, a flower, a promise. This year the straw god comes past you.

choices.text: Put in your most treasured thing

effects.log: You put in the thing you love best. It goes with the straw god at midnight. Somehow, giving it away feels like being given something.

choices.text: Put in a promise, written down

effects.log: You write: I will be kind to someone who does not deserve it. The priest reads it, smiles, and says that was the god's own promise, once.

choices.text: Put in a small coin and keep the big one

effects.log: A priest catches your eye and is too kind to say anything, which is worse.

choices.text: Pat the straw god on the head, as it did you

effects.log: You reach up and pat the straw head. The crowd roars, and an old woman says the god would have liked that best of all.
