events.text: The harvest has failed in the next valley, which was never blessed, and its people come to the Feast hungry, standing at the edge of the lantern light. Some of your neighbours say the Gift was given to this land and to nobody else.

choices.text: Bring them to the tables

effects.log: You lead them in. There is too much food anyway; there always is, at the Feast. By midnight nobody can tell who was blessed and who was not, which is perhaps the point.

choices.text: Give them your own share and go hungry

effects.log: You hand over your plate and go home hungry. It is a long night. In the morning someone from the next valley leaves a sack of seed at your door.

choices.text: Agree with your neighbours

effects.log: The strangers go away into the dark. The Feast is a little quieter after. You tell yourself the Gift was ours. You tell yourself that often, that year.

events.text: Being a blessed people is not as restful as it sounds. Everybody believes the Maker is watching to see what they do with the gift, so nobody may be lazy, nobody may waste, and the town council meets weekly to discuss whether the town is being grateful enough. You have been chosen to sit on it.

choices.text: Take it very seriously

effects.log: You draw up a list of forty ways the town could be more grateful. Thirty-nine are adopted. The town is exhausted, and grateful, and resents you a little.

choices.text: Propose a day of rest, in the god's honour

effects.log: There is outrage, then a vote, then, to everyone's surprise, a holiday on which nobody does anything at all. It is the most popular law in a century.

choices.text: Resign at once

effects.log: You resign before the first meeting ends. Several councillors look at you with open envy.

events.text: A wandering preacher from a land the god punished stands in your square and asks, loudly, why the god loved you more. The crowd shifts. Nobody has a good answer. Several people look at you, because you are on the council.

choices.text: Admit you do not know

effects.log: 'Neither do I,' says the preacher, surprised, and the two of you sit on the temple steps till nightfall and do not know together. It is the best conversation of your year.

choices.text: Say the blessing was luck, not love

effects.log: The crowd mutters. The priests are cross. The preacher bows to you and moves on, and you feel strangely lighter, and suspect you are right.

choices.text: Recite the forty ways of gratitude

effects.log: You recite them all. The preacher listens to the end and says, kindly, that it sounds tiring. The crowd laughs, and the laugh does the town more good than the list.

choices.text: Tell the preacher to leave

effects.log: The preacher leaves. The question stays, the way questions do, sitting quietly in the square long after the asker has gone.

events.text: In the temple's dustiest book you find the god's own words about the blessing, as the first priests wrote them down. It is short. It does not say anyone was chosen. It says only: This one is doing well. Let us see what it does with a little more.

choices.text: Read it to the council

effects.log: The council is silent a long time. Then the eldest says, 'So we are being tested,' and the youngest says, 'No, we are being trusted,' and the argument runs a year, and the town is kinder during it.

choices.text: Laugh out loud in the temple

effects.log: It is so like something you would say that you laugh till the priest shushes you. You do not know why it is so familiar. You stop worrying about being grateful enough.

choices.text: Put the book back and say nothing

effects.log: You put it back. A people should be allowed its stories. But you never again let the council meet more than once a month.

events.text: In a blessed land, children born on the Feast day are called gift-children and treated as small good omens by everybody: fed by strangers, patted by old men, asked to touch new boats and sick cows. You were born on the Feast day. You have never once been allowed to be in a bad mood in public.

choices.text: Enjoy being an omen

effects.log: You touch boats, cows, a bride's veil and a very old man's bald head. Everyone is delighted. You collect an astonishing quantity of free sweets.

choices.text: Hide from the people who want to touch you

effects.log: You hide in the hayloft with a cat. The cat is not impressed by omens. It is the best afternoon of your year.

choices.text: Ask the priest what an omen does

effects.log: The priest says an omen does nothing at all; it only reminds people that good things happen. 'So I am a reminder?' you ask. 'The best kind,' she says. 'The kind with legs.'

events.text: A fisherman's boat sank the week after you touched it. Now half the village mutters that you are no gift at all. Children who used to share their sweets look at you sideways.

choices.text: Help the fisherman build a new boat

effects.log: You carry planks and pitch for a month. The new boat floats, and the fisherman names it Second Chance and asks you, nervously, to touch it. It never sinks.

choices.text: Say omens are nonsense

effects.log: You shout it in the square. The grown-ups are scandalised. The children are thrilled. The fisherman, to everyone's surprise, agrees with you.

choices.text: Go back to the hayloft and the cat

effects.log: You and the cat wait out the muttering. It takes a month. When it is over the cat has kittens, and the village decides that this is an omen, and a good one.

events.text: On your tenth Feast day the priest asks you to walk beside the straw god in the procession, as the gift-child of the year. Thousands of faces. Someone throws a flower. Someone else throws a cabbage, possibly by accident.

choices.text: Wave to everyone

effects.log: You wave until your arm aches. Every face you wave at smiles. You decide being an omen is just being kind in a loud way.

choices.text: Catch the cabbage and hold it up like a prize

effects.log: The crowd roars. The cabbage becomes the best moment of the Feast; next year everyone throws cabbages. The priests are not pleased.

choices.text: Ask to walk at the back, with the ordinary children

effects.log: The priest lets you. At the back nobody stares, and you have the best Feast of your life.

events.text: The temples keep the Blessing Book, a ledger of every good thing the god ever did for {pw_world}, read aloud once a year from the temple steps. The reader this year has lost her voice. The priests, after much argument, have chosen you, because you speak loudly and do not giggle.

choices.text: Read it with all your heart

effects.log: You read for two hours. The crowd hears that {pw_deed}, and cheers as if it happened yesterday. Your voice is hoarse for a week and your name is known in every street.

choices.text: Practise all month first

effects.log: You practise in the hills until the goats know the Book by heart. On the day you read it perfectly. A priest weeps.

choices.text: Refuse, and suggest someone humbler

effects.log: You suggest the old baker, who stammers. The priests are appalled. The baker reads it, slowly, beautifully, and the crowd hangs on every stumble.

events.text: Reading the Book, you notice that the god's blessings are not evenly spread. There are long gaps, a hundred years, two hundred, when the god did nothing at all, and the priests have filled those pages with prayers.

choices.text: Ask the high priest about the gaps

effects.log: The high priest says the gaps are when the god was busy elsewhere, or resting, or trusting them. 'Or forgot us,' she adds, very quietly, and asks you not to repeat that.

choices.text: Write something of your own in a gap

effects.log: You write down a small good thing that happened to you that year. Years later the priests find it and keep it. Others start doing the same. The gaps fill with ordinary blessings.

choices.text: Read the gaps aloud too, as silence

effects.log: Next year, at each gap, you stop and stand silent for a breath. The crowd stands with you. It is the strangest, most moving reading anyone remembers.

events.text: The high priest, old now, asks you to her rooms. 'The god {pw_record},' she says, 'and here we are, still. Do you think the Maker was proud of us?'

choices.text: Say yes

effects.log: She closes her eyes and nods. 'I think so too,' she says. She dies that winter, and you find she has written your answer in the margin of the Book.

choices.text: Say the Maker was proudest of the gaps

effects.log: She stares at you, then laughs like a girl. 'The gaps,' she says. 'Where we did it ourselves.' She has it carved over the temple door.

choices.text: Say you hope the god did not need to be

effects.log: She thinks about it a long time. 'That is a better answer than mine,' she says, and gives you the key to the Blessing Book.

events.text: On every wall in town there is a blue line, painted far above your head and freshened every spring: the height the water reached when the god punished {pw_world}. Children are told to look up at it when they are tempted to be wicked. Most of them look up at it a great deal and remain wicked.

choices.text: Climb a ladder and touch the line

effects.log: From the top of the ladder the town looks small and drowned. You touch the blue paint and are suddenly, horribly sure you can hear water.

choices.text: Help the painter freshen the lines

effects.log: You paint the line on forty walls. By the end your arms are blue to the elbow and you know the whole town by its walls.

choices.text: Ask what the town did wrong

effects.log: Nobody quite agrees. The priests say pride. The fishermen say greed. An old woman says the god was simply in a temper, the way people are, and that it is no use asking.

events.text: Workmen digging a new well break into something below the town: an old street, a doorway, a child's shoe in the mud, kept by the flood that buried it. The town comes to look, silent. The priest reads from the book of punishments that {pw_deed}.

choices.text: Help lift the old door out

effects.log: You lift it out carefully. On it, scratched by a hand from before the flood, are the heights of three children, year by year, all stopping at the same year.

choices.text: Ask the priest whether the god was sorry

effects.log: The priest opens the book, closes it, and says the book does not say. He is quiet for a long time. Then he says he hopes so.

choices.text: Walk away: it is too sad

effects.log: You walk to the hill above town and look at the river, low and lazy and blameless today. It does not help, but it is a long way from the shoe.

events.text: The council proposes to paint over the flood-lines at last, now that nobody living remembers the water. Half the town is for it. The other half is furious. They ask you to speak.

choices.text: Keep the lines

effects.log: You say a town that forgets its flood will build in the wrong place. The lines stay. Late in life you see the river rise once, close to them, and the town is safe on the hill.

choices.text: Paint them over: let the town forgive

effects.log: The walls go plain. For a while the town is lighter. Children stop looking up. Whether that is good, nobody can say for certain.

choices.text: Paint flowers along the lines instead

effects.log: Your idea wins. The blue lines become a ribbon of painted flowers around the whole town. The flood is remembered, and the remembering is lovely.

events.text: When there is thunder, the whole town goes under the tables. Nobody explains it to the small children; it is simply what you do. Under the table it is crowded and warm and somebody always has a candle, and the grown-ups whisper that the Maker is angry again.

choices.text: Ask why the Maker is angry

effects.log: An old man under the table tells you that long ago the god struck the world for its wickedness, and that thunder is the god clearing a throat. You do not sleep that night.

choices.text: Peek out at the lightning

effects.log: You lift the tablecloth and see the sky split open, white and beautiful. Six hands pull you back under. You remember the beauty longer than the scolding.

choices.text: Tell stories to the smaller children

effects.log: You tell a story about a thunder that is only a large, clumsy cat. The small ones giggle. A grown-up sighs with relief, because now the small ones are not crying.

events.text: Another storm, and this time a house on your street is struck: a burnt roof, nobody hurt. The neighbours stand in the rain and say the god did it. They say it about the people who live there in a way you do not like.

choices.text: Go and stand with the struck household

effects.log: You stand in their doorway with them. Others come, one by one, ashamed. By morning the street is helping mend the roof.

choices.text: Ask the priest whether the god did it

effects.log: The priest says lightning hits tall roofs, and theirs is the tallest in the street. 'The god is not that petty,' he says. 'People are.'

choices.text: Hide under the table again

effects.log: You hide until it is over. In the morning you are ashamed of being afraid, and also, honestly, glad you were dry.

events.text: The worst storm in ten years. The town is under its tables again. The small children look at you, because you are the oldest child under this one.

choices.text: Tell them what the priest said about tall roofs

effects.log: You explain about roofs and lightning. The little ones are disappointed it is not the god, then relieved, then asleep.

choices.text: Take the bravest ones to the window

effects.log: You take three of them to the window. The sky is enormous and alive. Nobody is struck. All their lives they talk of it as the night they were brave.

choices.text: Say a prayer to the god for everyone

effects.log: You pray out loud to a god who once made thunder for real. Your voice shakes. By the end the whole table is praying with you, and the thunder, for whatever reason, moves away.

events.text: Through the middle of {pw_world} runs the Broken Valley, a crack in the land so deep its floor is cloud. It opened in a single afternoon, the day the god punished the world, and swallowed a city. On the near edge a village of crack-dwellers makes its living from pilgrims, rope and fear.

choices.text: Learn to rope down into it

effects.log: The rope-masters teach you knots and nerve. You hang over the cloud on a single line and do not look down, mostly. You are paid in good coin for it.

choices.text: Guide pilgrims along the edge

effects.log: You walk pilgrims to the brink and tell them the story. You get good at the story. Some throw coins into the crack, and you do not go after them.

choices.text: Ask the crack-dwellers why they stay

effects.log: An old woman says somebody should live beside it, to show the god the world is not afraid. She says it with such fear in her face that you nearly laugh, and do not.

events.text: A rope-master named Tull has heard of a ledge far down where the swallowed city's bell tower still stands upright in the cloud. Nobody has reached it. Tull wants a second on the rope.

choices.text: Go down with Tull

ok.log: Three hours down, in white fog, you set foot on the tower roof. Below it hangs the bell. You ring it once. Far above, the whole village hears, and the sound does not seem angry.

fail.log: Your arms give out and Tull hauls you up, swearing tenderly. You were close: you saw the shape of the tower in the cloud.

choices.text: Hold the rope from the top

effects.log: You hold the line for six hours. Tull comes up white with cloud-damp, carrying a single roof tile from the bell tower, and gives it to you.

choices.text: Tell Tull it is a grave and should be left

effects.log: Tull looks at you a long time and puts the rope away. 'You are right,' Tull says. 'I only wanted to see it.' So do you, after that, every night in dreams.

events.text: One morning the bell in the Broken Valley rings by itself, once, with no wind. The crack-dwellers gather on the edge. The priest says it means the god's anger is over. The rope-masters say it means the tower is falling. Both look at you.

choices.text: Say the anger is over

effects.log: The village holds a feast on the brink. Whether the anger ended that day or long before, nobody living ever sees the land crack again.

choices.text: Say you rang it once, and the valley remembers

effects.log: The village is silent. Then the old woman who feared it laughs, and laughs, and says she will stop being afraid if a young fool can ring its bell. It is the end of the fear, more or less.

choices.text: Go and look down at the tower

effects.log: You lie at the edge and look down. Nothing. Then, very faint, the bell again. You decide not to understand it, and go home and eat.

events.text: There is a temple where no one prays for mercy, because the god is said to have shown none: the Temple of the Stroke, where the record of the punishments is kept. The priests read it once a year, with the doors shut. This year you are let in.

choices.text: Listen to the record

effects.log: The priest reads that the god {pw_record}. Then the punishments, one by one: that {pw_deed}. You find your hands clenched so tight they hurt.

choices.text: Look at the statue instead

effects.log: The god's statue here has its face covered with a cloth, the only one in the world so. The priest says nobody can bear to look. You find you want to, badly.

choices.text: Leave before the reading

effects.log: You leave before the doors shut. Out in the sun a child is eating a peach. You decide that is the better temple.

events.text: You dream of the punishment, and it is not a dream of the drowned or the broken. It is a dream of standing above the world, very tired and very angry, with a hand raised. You wake knowing the shape of the gesture.

choices.text: Go back to the temple and lift the cloth

effects.log: You lift it while the priest is at prayer. The face beneath is plain and grave, and it is yours, older, angrier. You put the cloth back with shaking hands.

choices.text: Go and help the people the punishment hurt most

effects.log: You spend the year in the poorest quarter, mending roofs and carrying water. It does not quiet the dream. It makes it bearable.

choices.text: Tell yourself it was only a dream

effects.log: You tell yourself so every morning for a year. It is very hard work, telling yourself things.

events.text: The high priest of the Temple of the Stroke finds you on the steps. She does not ask your name. 'Some of us,' she says, 'believe the god came back to see what the anger did. Those ones look the way you look now.'

choices.text: Tell her the truth: you remember raising the hand

effects.log: She bows very low and does not rise for a while. Then she gives you a map of the Maker's road and says: go and ask yourself why. You find you want to know.

choices.text: Say you are sorry, without explaining

effects.log: 'For what?' she asks. You do not answer. She nods slowly, as if that were the answer, and lets you sit beside her until dark.

choices.text: Say you are only a visitor

effects.log: She smiles as if she has heard that many times, and lets you go. You walk home past the old ruins and do not look back.

events.text: The Maker made {pw_world} and never said a word to it: no laws, no blessings, no thunder, nothing. The temples are full anyway, but full of argument. The most famous thinker of the age, Tobyn the Unconvinced, teaches in the market that the silence itself is the message, and charges nothing, which the other thinkers find unforgivable.

choices.text: Study with Tobyn

effects.log: Tobyn teaches by asking questions until you cry, then buying you a bun. In a year you can doubt anything, including Tobyn, who is delighted.

choices.text: Argue against Tobyn in the market

effects.log: You argue that silence means nothing but silence. The crowd loves it. Tobyn loves it more, and invites you to dinner, where the argument goes on for nine hours.

choices.text: Pray louder, to fill the silence

effects.log: You pray at the temple every day for a year, loudly. Nobody answers. Oddly, you feel better: the talking was the useful part.

events.text: Tobyn sets a test: spend one night in the oldest empty temple in the world, where the god's statue has no mouth, and listen. Students who hear something fail. Students who hear nothing fail too. Nobody knows how to pass.

choices.text: Spend the night and listen

effects.log: You hear wind, mice and your own heart. At dawn Tobyn asks what you heard. You say: everything that was there. Tobyn passes you, the first in eleven years.

choices.text: Spend the night talking to the statue

effects.log: You tell it everything, all night. At dawn you feel you have been listened to very carefully. Tobyn fails you, kindly, and says that is a different school.

choices.text: Refuse the test

effects.log: 'Good,' says Tobyn. 'The god refused it too.' You are not sure whether you have passed. Tobyn is not sure either, and is enjoying it.

events.text: Tobyn the Unconvinced has died, and asked for you to give the funeral speech. The whole market will come. The priests are nervous: Tobyn never once said whether the god exists.

choices.text: Say Tobyn spent a life listening, like the god

effects.log: The market weeps. The priests, unexpectedly, agree. A statue of Tobyn goes up in the market, with no mouth, exactly like the god's.

choices.text: Stand in silence for the whole speech

effects.log: You stand silent before the crowd for as long as a speech would take. Nobody moves. It is the most talked-about funeral in memory. Tobyn would have been thrilled.

choices.text: Tell Tobyn's best joke

effects.log: The joke is about a god and a thinker who both forget the question. The market laughs through its tears. The priests pretend not to understand it.

events.text: In a world whose god never spoke there is a guild of Doubters who meet every week in a tavern to doubt things: the god, the weather, each other, whether the tavern exists. They are short of members. Their leader, a cheerful baker named Merrow, swears she believes in nothing except bread.

choices.text: Join the Doubters

effects.log: Your first meeting doubts whether the moon is the same moon every night. Your second doubts the first meeting. You are hooked.

choices.text: Join, but only to doubt the Doubters

effects.log: Merrow is overjoyed: they have needed someone to doubt them for years. You are made Doubter of Doubters. It comes with a hat.

choices.text: Buy Merrow's bread and leave

effects.log: The bread is extraordinary. You do not doubt it at all. You come back weekly, for the bread only, and stay later each time.

events.text: The temple and the Doubters have agreed to a public debate on whether the god exists. The temple has sent its best priest. The Doubters have sent you, because Merrow is busy baking.

choices.text: Doubt everything the priest says

effects.log: You doubt the priest's every claim, then your own doubts, then the stage. The crowd is dizzy. The priest, to everyone's shock, agrees that doubt is a kind of prayer. Both sides claim victory.

choices.text: Agree with the priest, to confuse everyone

effects.log: You agree with every word. The priest grows suspicious, then begins to doubt, then joins the Doubters at the tavern that very night.

choices.text: Hand out Merrow's bread

effects.log: Halfway through, the debate becomes a picnic. It is agreed to be the best debate ever held, and nobody remembers what was said.

events.text: Merrow has died and left the Doubters a mystery: a sealed jar with a note, Open only if you are sure. Nobody in the guild has ever been sure of anything. The jar sits on the tavern table, unopened, for a year.

choices.text: Open it

effects.log: Inside is a single loaf, perfectly kept, still warm, impossibly. The note inside says: I was sure of this. The guild eats it in silence and doubts nothing for one whole evening.

choices.text: Declare that nobody may ever open it

effects.log: The jar becomes the guild's holy relic, which is very embarrassing for a guild of Doubters. You are made leader for the idea.

choices.text: Give it to the temple

effects.log: The priests open it and find a stale loaf and a note. They frame the note. The Doubters never forgive you, and love you anyway.

events.text: Since the Maker never said what the world is for, every village has made up its own answer, and every child is expected to make one up too and defend it at the Spring Fair. Last year's winner said the world is for snails. It was a very good speech.

choices.text: Say the world is for finding things

effects.log: You bring a sack of things you found: a blue stone, a feather, a key to nothing. The judges are charmed. You come second to a girl who says the world is for jumping, and jumps.

choices.text: Say the world is for the Maker to watch, like a play

effects.log: The judges are thoughtful. One old judge says that would explain the weather, which is often dramatic. You win a ribbon.

choices.text: Say the world is for lunch

effects.log: The crowd laughs, and then a priest says, quietly, that this is a very serious answer, and then everybody has lunch. You do not win, but you do eat.

events.text: Your best friend Pim has decided that the Maker is a giant beetle, has built a beetle temple out of sticks behind the cowshed, and is accepting offerings: mostly sweets, mostly from you.

choices.text: Become Pim's priest

effects.log: You dress in a sack and lead the beetle services. Six children join. The grown-ups find out and are not angry; one says the real temple began like this too.

choices.text: Build a rival temple to a better god

effects.log: Your temple is to a god who is a kind, slightly forgetful old person. It gets more offerings than the beetle. Pim sulks, and then converts.

choices.text: Ask a real priest whether the Maker could be a beetle

effects.log: The priest thinks about it a long time. 'Nobody has seen the Maker,' she says at last. 'I would not rule it out.' Pim is insufferable for a month.

events.text: A storm knocks down the beetle temple, and a village elder, passing by, stops to look at the wreckage. She is very old, and she says something that surprises everyone: she knew the founders of the real temple, and they started with sticks too.

choices.text: Rebuild it, sturdier

effects.log: You and Pim rebuild it with real timber. It becomes a little shrine where children leave sweets and questions. It is still there, they say.

choices.text: Ask the elder what the founders believed

effects.log: 'That somebody made this,' she says, 'and went quiet, and that it was up to us to be worth talking to.' You think about it for the rest of your life.

choices.text: Tell her the Maker is a beetle

effects.log: She laughs till she has to sit on the wreckage. 'Then a very good beetle,' she says, and leaves a sweet among the sticks.

events.text: On the hill above the village there is a stone path with footprints pressed into it, as if the stone had been mud: the Maker's own steps, from the day the god walked {pw_world}. Every child puts a foot in the first print on their sixth birthday, to see how far they have to grow.

choices.text: Put your foot in the print

effects.log: Your foot is half the size of the god's. The priest marks your height on the shrine post. You walk home looking at your feet all the way.

choices.text: Walk the whole line of prints

effects.log: You walk all forty, stretching to reach each one. The god had long legs and, by the look of it, was in no hurry. At the end you are dizzy and pleased.

choices.text: Ask why the god took off its shoes

effects.log: The priest says the god wanted to feel the world. The old shrine-keeper says the god had blisters. Both look at you as if you had asked a dangerous question.

events.text: Forty prints lead up the hill. But someone has found a forty-first, overgrown with moss, leading off the path toward the woods. The priests say it is a fake. The children say otherwise.

choices.text: Follow where it points

effects.log: You find a forty-second, and a forty-third, deep in the woods, leading to a spring so clear and cold it hurts your teeth. You tell nobody but your best friend.

choices.text: Clean the moss off it

effects.log: Under the moss the forty-first print is real, worn by the same feet. You show the priests. They argue for a month and then add it to the shrine.

choices.text: Leave it hidden

effects.log: You cover it back up with moss. Some things, you feel, the god meant to keep.

events.text: Your sixth-birthday mark on the shrine post is far below your head now. The priest has you put your foot in the first print again, to see. It fits much better than it should, for your age.

choices.text: Ask if anyone else ever fitted it

effects.log: The priest looks at the post, then at you, and says nobody, not in all the years of the shrine. Then the priest laughs and says feet grow. You are not convinced.

choices.text: Take the priest to the hidden spring

effects.log: The priest drinks from it, sits down hard, and says this is the place the god rested, written of in the oldest book and lost for centuries. Your hill becomes famous.

choices.text: Walk the whole line again, easily now

effects.log: You walk the prints in easy strides, as if they were made for you. Behind you a smaller child watches with enormous eyes. You slow down and help her stretch.

events.text: When the Maker walked {pw_world}, the stories say, the god ate at an ordinary table in an ordinary house. Every town now has several households claiming it was theirs, with the bench to prove it. Your town has eleven. The rival tables are a pilgrim trade, a feud, and an excellent source of free lunches.

choices.text: Visit every table and judge

effects.log: You eat at all eleven. Each household shows you the god's own bowl, spoon or tooth-mark. By the eleventh you are full, impressed, and a leading expert.

choices.text: Work for the most famous table

effects.log: You serve pilgrims the god's favourite stew (lentils, nobody knows why) at the House of the Bench. The tips are good. The stew is not.

choices.text: Claim your own table is the real one

effects.log: You carve a little mark in your table and tell a pilgrim. By spring you have a queue. By summer you have a feud with eleven households.

events.text: The temple announces it will settle the matter once and for all: the god's true table will be named by the high priest and carried to the temple. The eleven (or twelve) households are bringing their tables to the square. The square is full of tables.

choices.text: Help the high priest judge

effects.log: You know every scratch and story. You point out that the god, by the oldest book, ate standing up. The high priest laughs till she cries and declares all twelve tables equally false and equally holy.

choices.text: Withdraw your table quietly

effects.log: You carry your table home in the night. Nobody says anything. Years later yours is the table people point at, because it was honest enough to leave.

choices.text: Sell stew to the crowd

effects.log: You sell lentil stew to the crowd and make a heap of coins. Everyone agrees the stew is terrible and buys a second bowl in the god's honour.

events.text: An old stranger stops at your house at dusk and asks for something to eat. There is something about the way the stranger sits at your table, very straight, looking round the room as if remembering it.

choices.text: Feed the stranger your best

effects.log: The stranger eats everything, says your stew is a little bland, and is gone before dawn. On your table, where the bowl stood, the wood has gone smooth and warm.

choices.text: Ask if the stranger has eaten here before

effects.log: The stranger smiles and says: everywhere, long ago, and every table was the real one. Then thanks you, and goes.

choices.text: Charge the stranger for the meal

effects.log: The stranger pays with an old coin nobody in town recognises. A collector buys it from you for a fortune. For a while after, you feel you have made a mistake you cannot name.

events.text: In the temples the god who walked among the people is painted as a traveller in a grey cloak, copied from the oldest picture, made by someone who saw the god face to face. Lately people stare at you in the street. In the temple a child pointed at you and said, quite loudly, 'That is the Maker.'

choices.text: Go and look at the oldest picture

effects.log: The picture is faded and cracked. The face in it is plain, a little tired, a little amused. You look at it a long time. It does look like you. It looks like you on a good day.

choices.text: Change your hair to look different

effects.log: It helps a little. People stare less. A painter stops you in the market anyway and asks, very politely, if you would sit for a temple picture.

choices.text: Wave at the child

effects.log: The child waves back, delighted, and runs off to tell everyone the Maker waved. By evening the story is that you blessed the whole street. Several neighbours bring you bread.

events.text: Pilgrims have started to come to your door. Not many, but steady: a sick woman, a farmer whose crops failed, a girl who wants to know if her grandfather is happy where he is. They do not ask you to be the god. They only ask you to listen, the way the god in the stories did.

choices.text: Listen to each of them

effects.log: You listen to all of them, every day, for a year. You heal no one. But they go away lighter, and come back to tell you so.

choices.text: Tell them firmly you are not the Maker

effects.log: You put a sign on the door. The pilgrims read it, nod, and knock anyway. One says, 'That is just what the god would say.'

choices.text: Send them to the temple

effects.log: The priests are annoyed with you, then grateful: the pilgrims bring offerings. You are left in peace, a little lonely.

events.text: A very old priest, who has kept the oldest picture all her life, comes to your door and sits down without asking. 'The god walked here once,' she says, 'and told my teacher's teacher before leaving: I will be back, and you will not know me. Well?'

choices.text: Tell her you remember the road

effects.log: Saying it, you do remember: dust, a grey cloak, a long walk home to a high place. She nods, unsurprised, and gives you the temple's oldest map. 'The road up,' she says. 'It is still there.'

choices.text: Say you only have a common face

effects.log: She laughs. 'So did the god,' she says. 'It was the first thing anyone noticed.' She drinks your tea and leaves you a blessing, which is odd, coming from her to you.

choices.text: Ask her what the god was like

effects.log: 'Kind, tired, curious,' she says. 'Interested in soup.' You sit together till dark while she tells you everything, and you find you are not surprised by any of it.

events.text: In {pw_world} the faithful love the Maker the way some people love the weather: loudly, all the time, and at everyone. Every spring the Knee-Walkers set out for the High Temple on their knees, three hundred miles, singing. Each carries a stone for the god's cairn, and the stones get bigger every year, because love must be seen to grow.

choices.text: Go with them, on your knees

effects.log: By the end of the first week your knees are two purple plums and you can sing all forty verses of the Walking Hymn. A grandmother with knees like leather pats your head and calls you promising.

choices.text: Walk beside them with a water skin

effects.log: You walk upright beside the procession and give water to anyone who asks. Some of the Knee-Walkers look at your standing legs with pity. All of them drink.

choices.text: Ask the leader whether the god ever asked for this

effects.log: 'The Maker never asks for anything,' the leader says, glowing. 'That is why we must guess, and guess big.' You find you have no answer to that, which is new for you.

events.text: Halfway, at the ford of the Lantern River, the procession stops. A huge mild man named Dorrin Pask has been dragging a boulder the size of a cow on a sledge, and the sledge is stuck in the river mud. Dorrin is weeping. The others are singing at him encouragingly, which is not helping.

choices.text: Put your shoulder to the sledge

ok.log: You heave, Dorrin heaves, the boulder lurches up the bank, and the whole procession cheers as if the god had done it. Dorrin calls you his rock-sibling for the rest of the road.

fail.log: The sledge rolls back and sits on your foot, briefly but with feeling. Dorrin carries you on his back for a day, which he says is better for his soul than the boulder.

choices.text: Tell Dorrin the god does not measure love by weight

effects.log: Some of the Knee-Walkers gasp. Dorrin stops crying and picks a pebble out of the river, small and white and round, and laughs out loud for the first time in three hundred miles.

choices.text: Tell them, quietly, that the Maker never wanted a cairn at all

effects.log: You say it as if you were guessing. It is not a guess. The leader looks at you sharply, then at the boulder, then sits down in the river and thinks for an hour.

events.text: The High Temple, at last. The god's cairn is not a cairn any more, it is a small mountain, and it leans. The town below it has started building its houses facing away, so as not to see it coming. The priests look tired. The Knee-Walkers, beaming, line up to add their stones.

choices.text: Lay your stone on the cairn

effects.log: You climb the heap and set your stone on top, and for a moment the whole valley is below you and you feel enormous and loved. The cairn creaks. Nobody else seems to hear it.

choices.text: Propose building the stones into houses for the poor, in the Maker's name

effects.log: It takes three years and a great deal of shouting, but the cairn becomes a street: the Maker's Row, forty houses of holy stone with a pebble over every door.

choices.text: Keep your stone in your pocket

effects.log: You walk home with it. All your life it sits by your bed, and it is always faintly warm, as if someone up there had held it for a moment and given it back.

events.text: Every midwinter in {pw_world} there is the Letter Fire. Everyone writes the Maker a letter, folds it into a paper bird and throws it into the great fire on the temple steps, so the smoke can carry it up. The little ones are given a stub of charcoal and told to say thank you for something. You have your stub. Everybody is watching.

choices.text: Write thank you for the dog

effects.log: You write THANK YOU FOR THE DOG in letters as big as your hand. The dog, who is beside you, seems to agree. Your bird burns very brightly and the priest says that is a good sign.

choices.text: Write a question instead: why are there snails?

effects.log: The priest reads it before it burns and has to sit down on the steps. 'Nobody has ever asked the Maker that,' he says, wiping his eyes. You feel you have done something important.

choices.text: Draw a picture, since you cannot spell yet

effects.log: You draw the sun with a face. The priest tells you the god reads pictures best of all. It is the kindest lie you have ever been told, and also, you will find later, true.

events.text: This year you are an Ember Child, one of the little sweepers who clear the ashes after the Letter Fire. In the cold grey heap you find a letter that did not burn. The writing is old and shaky: I have loved you for forty years. I have written every winter. Please, just once, answer. Esk Harrow, the mill lane.

choices.text: Fold it back into a bird and burn it properly

effects.log: You put it in the last coals and watch it go. It burns slowly, as if it were being read. You hope it was.

choices.text: Find Esk Harrow on the mill lane

effects.log: Esk is a thin old man with flour in his eyebrows. You give him back his letter and he looks at it for a long time and says, 'Well. It got as far as you.' He gives you a bun.

choices.text: Write an answer yourself and leave it on his step

effects.log: You write: I read it. Thank you. I am glad of you. You sign it with a circle, because that feels right. You do not know why your hand is so sure.

events.text: The temple asks you to be Keeper of the Letter Fire, which means you feed it, all night, with ten thousand paper birds full of love for the god. It is a great honour and a terrible job. Some of the letters are poems. Some are lists of grievances that end in kisses. One woman sends a new letter every hour, each longer than the last.

choices.text: Read them before you burn them, though it is forbidden

effects.log: You read all night. They love you for the rain, the bread, the colour of the sea. By dawn you are so full of other people's love you can barely stand.

choices.text: Burn them unread, as the rite says

effects.log: You feed the fire bird by bird and never look. The smoke goes straight up into a windless sky, all night, a grey road to somewhere. It is the most peaceful night of your life.

choices.text: Accept the charcoal stub old Esk Harrow brings you

effects.log: Esk is very old now. 'I got an answer once,' he says. 'It was enough. I have stopped writing.' He puts his charcoal in your hand and goes home, light as paper.

choices.text: Write a letter of your own and burn it

effects.log: You write: Dear Maker, they love you very much. Please try to deserve it. It is a strange letter to write to yourself. The bird burns green.

events.text: The Betrothed of the Sky are the most devoted people in {pw_world}, and the most tiring. They believe the Maker is lonely up there. Every seven years they choose one young person to be wed to the god, in white, on the temple roof, with cake. This year, after much prayer and a lot of drawing of straws, they have chosen you. You are the god.

choices.text: Accept, with as straight a face as you can manage

effects.log: The Betrothed weep for joy and measure you for a robe of white feathers. You go home and look at the ceiling for a long time.

choices.text: Refuse: the god is not lonely

effects.log: 'And how would you know?' the head of the Betrothed asks, wounded. You open your mouth and close it again. They choose someone else, a cheerful baker, and you feel oddly jealous.

choices.text: Ask what became of the last one chosen

effects.log: The last Betrothed, Lisbet Croy, runs a cake shop now. 'The god never came,' she says cheerfully, 'but the cake was excellent, so I went into cake.' She gives you a slice on the house.

events.text: Rehearsals. The high priestess of the Betrothed, Amarantha Vole, has written the god's vows for you to answer, and reads them aloud with enormous feeling. According to the vows the Maker is all-beautiful, never cross, eternally patient, and has a voice like honey poured over bells. You remember your voice. It was nothing like that.

choices.text: Edit the vows for accuracy

effects.log: You strike out all-beautiful and write fairly tidy. You strike out never cross and write cross mainly about turnips. Amarantha reads your version and has to lie down.

choices.text: Learn them by heart and say them beautifully

effects.log: You answer the god's vows so sweetly that the rehearsal choir cries. Amarantha says she has never seen anyone so in love with the sky. You keep a very straight face.

choices.text: Ask Lisbet Croy to bake the wedding cake

effects.log: Lisbet bakes a cake shaped like a cloud, seven layers, with a little sugar sun on top. She charges you half. 'For the god,' she says, and winks, and you are not sure what she knows.

events.text: The wedding day. You stand on the temple roof in white feathers before the whole city. Amarantha raises her arms. 'Maker! Will you take this one?' The crowd falls silent and looks at the sky, waiting for a sign, and you look at the sky too, because you cannot think where else to look.

choices.text: Say yes to yourself, silently, and mean it kindly

effects.log: A warm wind comes out of a clear sky and lifts every feather on your robe and the top tier off the cake. The crowd roars. The city talks of the Sky Wedding for a hundred years.

choices.text: Tell the crowd the god says thank you, but no

effects.log: There is a terrible pause. Then Amarantha bursts into tears, and then into laughter, and says, 'Well, at least we asked.' Everyone eats the cake. It is a lovely day after all.

choices.text: Climb down the drainpipe and run for it

effects.log: You are halfway across the market before anyone realises. The Bolted Betrothed becomes a favourite song, and you are in every verse, running.

choices.text: Read your edited vows aloud instead

effects.log: You read: fairly tidy, cross mainly about turnips. Half the crowd is scandalised and half is in tears of laughter. Someone at the back shouts, 'That sounds like a real person!' and the roof goes quiet.

events.text: A living saint moves in next door. Saint Ottilie the Ever-Grateful is small, round, eighty years old, and thanks the Maker out loud for everything, every morning at dawn, on a brass horn: for the sun, the bread, the rain, the slugs, the second slug, and your new shutters, which she admires.

choices.text: Thank her for the horn, with feeling

effects.log: She takes it as sincere, which it was not, and the next dawn she thanks the Maker for you by name, on the horn, very loudly. The whole street now knows your name.

choices.text: Stuff the horn with wool while she sleeps

effects.log: She plays it anyway. It now sounds like a goose with a cold, and she is delighted: 'The god has given me a new voice!' The street suffers more, not less.

choices.text: Get up at dawn and pray with her

effects.log: You stand in the cold with her and thank the Maker for slugs. It is absurd. It is also, somehow, the best way you have ever started a day.

events.text: Ottilie has begun to relay the god's messages. 'The Maker wants everyone to eat less salt,' she tells the market, 'and to visit me more often.' People nod gravely. You were the Maker. You never said a word about salt.

choices.text: Correct her in front of the market

effects.log: You say the god never mentioned salt. The market turns on you as one. A fishwife throws a cabbage. Ottilie forgives you loudly, which is worse.

choices.text: Tell her the god told you something too: that Ottilie should sleep in

ok.log: Ottilie considers this very seriously and sleeps until noon for a week. The street brings you cakes. A baby sleeps through the night for the first time.

fail.log: 'The god told me you would say that,' says Ottilie, beaming, and plays the horn twice as long, to make up for it.

choices.text: Let it go: she means well

effects.log: You let her have her salt. Half the street eats less of it, and the old men on the corner, who were very red in the face, are a little less red.

events.text: Ottilie falls ill in the winter, and the horn is silent, and the street is horribly quiet. She sends for you, of all people. 'Tell me honestly,' she says from her pillows. 'You always look at the sky like you are owed money. Did the Maker ever hear me?'

choices.text: Tell her yes: every morning, horn and all

effects.log: Ottilie closes her eyes and smiles so wide it seems to hurt. By spring she is up again, out of sheer joy, and the horn is louder than ever. You find you are glad.

choices.text: Confess about the wool

effects.log: Ottilie laughs so hard the doctor is called. Then she presses the horn into your hands. 'You play it,' she says. 'The god will want to hear something new.'

choices.text: Tell her nobody can know that

effects.log: 'Then I will keep on, just in case,' says Ottilie, and does, from her bed, on a tin whistle. It is somehow worse than the horn. You would not change it.

events.text: {pw_world} remembers its god's punishments better than its blessings: the god {pw_record}, and people have long memories for the hard parts. In a cellar under a rope-maker's shop, every new moon, the Unmakers meet: forty sensible people with tea and grievances, who believe the world would be better if its god were undone. A friend brings you. Nobody here knows who you were.

choices.text: Sit at the back and listen

effects.log: They are not monsters. They are a baker, two widows, a schoolteacher, a man who lost a barn to lightning. They speak of the Maker the way you speak of a landlord. You listen to all of it.

choices.text: Speak up for the god

effects.log: They hear you out politely, then vote to note your objection and move on. But at the door, two of them shake your hand and ask you to come back.

choices.text: Leave and never come back

effects.log: You climb out of the cellar into the night air. Above you the stars are where you put them, and you find you cannot look at them.

events.text: Tonight the chairwoman, Agathe Moll, reads from the Book of Grievances: the Great Hail, the year the river drowned Low Fen, the winter that did not end. Each line is a wound. You remember every one of them. You remember why.

choices.text: Explain, as if you were guessing, why the hail had to fall

ok.log: Some of them nod, slowly. Agathe looks at you a long while and then, for the first time in the history of the Book, writes a small word in its margin: perhaps.

fail.log: 'An apologist,' somebody mutters. They move on to the next grievance, but nobody passes you the biscuits for the rest of the night.

choices.text: Add a grievance of your own against the god

effects.log: You stand and complain about the Maker, honestly and at length: vain, hasty, careless with weather. It is the most freeing thing you have ever done. They applaud.

choices.text: Bring cakes to the next meeting

effects.log: Hatred goes better with cake, it turns out. You are elected Keeper of the Tea, which is the most powerful office in the Unmakers.

events.text: The Unmakers vote on their great act at last: to pull down the god's statue in the square on the Festival of the Making, in front of everyone. The count is tied. All forty faces turn to you, the last vote, sitting with your teacup in a cellar under the world you made.

choices.text: Vote yes

effects.log: On the festival morning the statue comes down with a long groan of rope, onto straw, and nobody is hurt. The sky does nothing at all. You feel a strange, enormous relief.

choices.text: Vote no

effects.log: Agathe sighs, crosses something out and orders more tea. The statue stands. Some of the Unmakers seem relieved too, and pretend not to be.

choices.text: Stand up and tell them who you are

effects.log: They laugh, and then they stop laughing. Agathe Moll puts down her cup. 'Then you owe us an apology,' she says, 'and an explanation. Start with Low Fen.' You do. It takes all night. Some of them cry. At dawn they let you go up the stairs first.

events.text: Every statue of the Maker in your town has a smooth patch where its face should be. Long ago, the grown-ups say, the Unmakers came with chisels so the god could not look at the town any more. The children dare each other to touch the blank faces after dark.

choices.text: Touch the blank face on the fountain statue

effects.log: You creep up and lay your palm on the smooth stone. It is warm, as if it had been in the sun all day, though it is night. You run home and tell nobody.

choices.text: Draw a face on it in chalk

effects.log: You give the god two dots and a big smile. In the morning the grown-ups scrub it off, but they are laughing while they scrub, which you did not expect.

choices.text: Ask why the Unmakers were so angry

effects.log: A neighbour tells you about the bad years, the punishments, the floods. 'They thought the god was watching,' she says. 'They wanted the watching to stop.' You think about it all week.

events.text: Paddling in the ditch behind the old stonecutters' yard, your foot finds something smooth and heavy. It is a stone nose. A large, dignified stone nose, a little chipped, the colour of the fountain statue.

choices.text: Keep it, secretly, under your bed

effects.log: You wrap it in a sock and hide it. At night you sometimes take it out and look at it. It is a good nose. You feel responsible for it.

choices.text: Take it to the temple

effects.log: The old priest turns it over in her hands and laughs until she has to hold the altar. She gives you a honey cake for it, and the nose sits on a shelf behind the altar after that, looking out.

choices.text: Throw it into the river

effects.log: It sinks without a splash. Some things want to be gone, you think, very seriously, and walk home feeling much older than nine.

events.text: The town council votes, at last, to restore the statues. The sculptor, Bertil Anning, a gloomy giant with very gentle hands, has a problem: nobody living remembers what the god looked like. He walks around the square looking at faces. He stops at yours.

choices.text: Sit for him

effects.log: You sit for a month. The new faces have your eyes, a little older, a little tired, kind. Strangers stop you in the street to say you look like the fountain. You say you have heard that before.

choices.text: Give him the stone nose

effects.log: Bertil holds it to the fountain statue and it fits the old break exactly. He builds the face around it, slowly, and when it is done the whole town comes to look, very quiet.

choices.text: Argue to leave the faces blank

effects.log: 'Let everyone see who they need to see there,' you tell the council. Bertil looks relieved. The faces stay smooth, and now people leave flowers at them instead of chisel marks.

events.text: Every market day {npc} preaches against the Maker from an upturned fish crate: the god is a cruel child, the god built a world just to see it break. People throw cabbages. Then the market closes, and {npc} goes round picking up the cabbages for the poor, mends a widow's roof for nothing, and gives you an apple for no reason at all.

choices.text: Thank {npc} for the apple

effects.log: {npc} looks surprised to be thanked, and then pleased, and then embarrassed to be pleased. 'Eat it before the god notices you are happy,' {he} says.

choices.text: Heckle the sermon

mem.note: argued with me in the market

effects.log: {npc} laughs out loud and points at you from the crate. 'Good! Argue! A god who wanted us to think would have been proud of you!' The crowd laughs too. You feel warm and outwitted.

choices.text: Ask {npc} why anyone would hate a god and love everyone

effects.log: 'Somebody has to love what the god made,' says {npc}, 'since the god does not.' You have to walk away quickly so your face does not give anything away.

events.text: In the hard winter {npc} falls ill. The faithful do not come; the Unmakers have their own troubles. The crate stands empty by the fish stalls. You find {npc} alone in a cold room above the chandler's, coughing and still grumbling about the sky.

choices.text: Bring soup every day until the cough breaks

effects.log: It takes a month. {npc} complains about the soup, the god, and the weather, in that order, every day, and on the last day says thank you, very quietly.

choices.text: Read scripture aloud at the bedside

effects.log: {npc} argues with every line from under the blanket, and gets better out of pure spite. The doctor calls it the fastest recovery in living memory.

choices.text: Ask what the god did to {him}

effects.log: 'A flood,' says {npc}. 'It took my village when I was nine.' You remember the flood. You remember the reasons, and none of them are good enough, here, in this cold room. You say you are sorry, and mean it more than {npc} can know.

events.text: {npc} is too old for the crate now, and gives a last sermon in the rain to a crowd that, for once, does not throw anything. Afterwards {npc} carries the fish crate over to you and sets it at your feet.

choices.text: Take the crate and preach against the god

effects.log: You stand on it every market day and tell the truth about the Maker's faults, which you know better than anyone. You are very convincing. It is the strangest job in {pw_world}.

choices.text: Take the crate and preach what {npc} really did

effects.log: You do not talk about the god at all. You talk about roofs and cabbages and apples. Fewer people throw things. More people mend things.

choices.text: Tell {npc} that the god is sorry

mem.note: told me the god was sorry

effects.log: {npc} looks at you a long time in the rain. 'Then it took the god long enough,' {he} says, and smiles for the first time you have ever seen, and sits on the crate to rest.

events.text: In the Iron Quarter the Unmakers have a plan that is either magnificent or mad. Hollis Penwright, an engineer with burnt eyebrows, means to build a tower higher than the clouds, put a bow on top, and shoot an iron spear straight into the sky, to wound the god where the god lives. The tower is already taller than the temple. Hollis is hiring.

choices.text: Sign on as a carpenter

effects.log: You haul beams and sing the tower songs and come home every night with splinters in your soul. The pay is good. The view gets better every week.

choices.text: Laugh at the whole idea

effects.log: 'Everyone laughs,' says Hollis, unbothered. 'They laughed at the first boat, too.' You stop laughing, because you remember the first boat, and they did.

choices.text: Warn the temple

effects.log: The priests thank you and do nothing, because they do not believe the sky can be hurt. You are not sure they are right.

events.text: The tower is finished. You climb the last ladder with the iron spear-head on your back and come out above the clouds, into a sunlight that belongs to nobody. The sky is very close up here. It looks exactly as you made it, blue all the way down, and not at all hurt yet.

choices.text: Tighten the great bow's bolts, honestly

effects.log: You do good work. You always did. The bow creaks in the wind, ready, and you sit beside it eating your bread above the whole world.

choices.text: Loosen one bolt, in secret

effects.log: Just one, just a little. Your hands shake doing it. Nobody sees. The bow looks the same as before, and is not.

choices.text: Sit and look at the sky until you understand what wounds it

effects.log: You sit for hours. The sky does not hurt from spears. It hurts, if it hurts at all, from the people below it who are angry enough to build towers.

events.text: The day of the shot. Half of {pw_world} has come to watch. Hollis Penwright stands at the bow with the rope in one hand and a hammer in the other, and asks the crowd for silence, and gets it.

choices.text: Let it fly

effects.log: The spear goes up and up and up until it is a needle, and then nothing, and then, a long time later, it lands in a lake two valleys away and kills a very surprised fish. The sky is fine. Hollis weeps, and then laughs.

choices.text: Watch the loose bolt give way

effects.log: The bow sighs, sags, and drops the spear neatly onto the platform. Nobody is hurt. Hollis kicks the bow and never finds out why. You buy the first round that night.

choices.text: Climb up and tell Hollis the sky cannot be wounded, only the people under it

ok.log: Hollis listens, rope in hand, for a very long time. Then lets go of it. The tower becomes the Long Lamp, a beacon for travellers, and Hollis keeps it for forty years.

fail.log: Hollis pats your shoulder and fires anyway. The spear goes into the clouds and never comes down. Nobody knows where it went. You lie awake wondering.

events.text: The faith of {pw_world} belongs now to the Radiant One, who did not make it. The Radiant One's priests powder their faces with gold dust and glitter when they walk, and the crowds part for them like water. They are taking novices this spring. The pay is good and you would get to glitter too.

choices.text: Join the novices

effects.log: They powder your face and you glitter. People bow to you in the street. It is wonderful and hollow, like eating air.

choices.text: Ask a priest what the Radiant One made

effects.log: 'Everything,' says the priest, kindly. 'The hills, the sea, you.' You know exactly who made the hills. You smile, and say nothing, and remember the priest's face.

choices.text: Throw a bucket of water over a passing priest

effects.log: The gold runs off in streaks, and underneath is an ordinary, very startled young man named Pim. The crowd gasps, then giggles. You run.

events.text: Behind the Radiant Temple there is a locked shed where the gold dust comes from. You get in, one way or another. Inside are sacks of brass filings from the smithy, a sieve, and a ledger. The glitter is a penny a pound.

choices.text: Accept the promotion they offer you, to Second Glitter

effects.log: You learn the sieve and the secret, and your sleeves are heavy with shells. You glitter more than anyone in the temple. Some nights you scrub your face until it hurts.

choices.text: Tell the market where the gold comes from

ok.log: The market laughs so hard the Radiant priests stay indoors for a week. Pim, the priest you soaked, buys you a cup of tea. 'I always knew,' he says. 'It was a relief to have it said.'

fail.log: Nobody believes you. Brass? Gold is gold, look how it shines. A priest's guard escorts you to the edge of town, politely, and you lose your market stall.

choices.text: Close the shed and say nothing

effects.log: You leave everything as you found it. The secret sits in your chest like a swallowed coin. Every time a priest glitters past you, you hear the sieve.

events.text: The High Glitterer, Maximine Dorrow, sends for you. She is old, and tired, and wiped clean of gold in her own room. 'I know nobody is up there,' she says. 'But they need something to look at. Do you understand? Somebody has to shine.'

choices.text: Tell her somebody is up there, actually

effects.log: You tell her the truth, quietly, as much as you can. She looks at you for a long time, the way one looks at a coin that may be real. 'Then what has it been doing?' she asks. You have no good answer.

choices.text: Stay, and help her keep the people comforted

effects.log: You glitter for the Radiant One for many years, and give the shells to the poor, mostly. The people are comforted. You are not, but you get used to it.

choices.text: Wash the gold off and walk out

effects.log: You leave the temple with a clean face and nothing in your pockets. The sunlight on your bare skin is the warmest thing you have ever felt.

events.text: Every day at noon, at the Radiant Temple, the statue of the false god weeps honey. Real honey: the pilgrims catch it on bread. People come from three provinces to see it. You come too, and stand in the sticky crowd at noon, and the statue begins to weep.

choices.text: Taste the honey

effects.log: It is very good honey, clover and a little thyme. Whatever else is happening here, somebody keeps excellent bees.

choices.text: Slip round the back of the statue

ok.log: Behind the statue there is a boy with a pot, a bellows and a pipe that runs up into the god's head. He looks at you. You look at him. He offers you some bread.

fail.log: A temple guard catches you by the collar and throws you down the steps into the crowd, who are too busy with their bread to catch you.

choices.text: Pray, in case

effects.log: You pray to the statue, which is not you, and feel nothing at all. That is information, too.

events.text: The second miracle of the Radiant One, everyone says, is the blind weaver Corrin Ash, who now sees. You go to see Corrin. Corrin truly does see, and when you take those weaving-rough hands, you feel it at once: something old, and warm, and yours, a blessing you left in the world a very long time ago, still working.

choices.text: Ask Corrin who was prayed to

effects.log: 'Not the Radiant One,' Corrin says, in a whisper. 'An old prayer. My grandmother's. I did not even know what it meant.' You know exactly what it meant.

choices.text: Tell Corrin about the honey pipe

effects.log: Corrin laughs until the loom shakes. 'Then whoever did this,' Corrin says, touching both eyes, 'is not the one who cries honey.' You agree, more than you can say.

choices.text: Leave the miracle alone

effects.log: You go home without asking. Some gifts should not be looked at too closely, even by the giver.

events.text: Noon again, the great feast of the Radiant One. The square is packed to the rooftops. The statue is about to weep. You are standing very near the front, and you know things that nobody else in this square knows.

choices.text: Pull the honey pipe out of the statue in front of everyone

effects.log: Honey sprays over the High Glitterer. The boy with the pot runs for it. There is a long, terrible silence, and then a roar, and the Radiant One is never quite the same.

choices.text: Tell the crowd the real miracle was never the Radiant One's

effects.log: Some laugh. Some listen. An old woman at the back says my grandmother's prayer too and starts to cry. By evening there are three small candles at Corrin Ash's door.

choices.text: Ask the temple for a job making miracles

effects.log: They hire you to work the bellows. The pay is excellent. You make the god cry honey every day at noon for six years and try not to think about it.

choices.text: Eat your bread and go home

effects.log: The statue weeps. The crowd sighs. You eat your honey bread on the way home, and it is very good, and you let the day be what it is.

events.text: The Radiant One takes one shell in ten. The Tithe-Wardens come round on the first of every month with brass scales and a bored expression, and they weigh everything: your coins, your grain, once, notoriously, a neighbour's baby, for a joke nobody laughed at.

choices.text: Pay your tithe

effects.log: The Warden weighs your shells, takes a tenth, and writes you a receipt with a little gold sun on it. It is a very handsome receipt. You put it on the wall.

choices.text: Hide your shells in the hen-house

effects.log: The Warden weighs your purse, which has three shells in it, and looks at you, and at the hens, who look back. 'Bad month?' 'Terrible.' Nobody believes anybody.

choices.text: Ask the Warden where the tithe goes

effects.log: 'To the god,' says the Warden, and then, when you keep looking, 'well, to the temple. Well, to the roof, mostly.' The temple roof is gold. You had wondered.

events.text: The Tithe-Warden of your street, a sad man named Ferris Lowe, drops his ledger in the mud outside your door and does not notice. It is very fat. It has two columns, and only one of them goes to the temple.

choices.text: Copy the ledger before you give it back

effects.log: You copy it all night by one candle. The second column goes to a house on the hill with a gold roof of its own. You give Ferris his ledger back in the morning, dried.

choices.text: Bribe Ferris to skip your street

effects.log: Ferris takes the shells with a sigh, as if you had handed him a burden. Your street is not tithed for a year. You become very popular, and slightly ashamed.

choices.text: Organise the street to pay in turnips

effects.log: Every house pays its tenth in turnips. The Wardens leave with a cart that smells like a cellar. The temple eats turnip stew for a month and the tithe is quietly changed to shells only.

events.text: Tithe Day in the square: the Wardens on their platform, the scales, the queue of everyone in town with their purses. The High Warden reads the blessing of the Radiant One over the scales and looks out over the crowd for the first payer.

choices.text: Climb the platform and read the ledger aloud

effects.log: You read both columns. The square goes very quiet, then very loud. By the next month the tithe is one shell in fifty, and the house on the hill is for sale.

choices.text: Pay with a smile and go home

effects.log: You pay. It is only shells. On the way home you find a blue cowrie in the road, and another by the well, as if someone up there were quietly paying you back.

choices.text: Refuse to pay and take the stocks for a day

effects.log: They put you in the stocks by the well. The town comes by all day to give you bread and sympathy and, from the children, rotten plums. By sunset there are six people in the stocks with you, by choice.

events.text: By the well sits Old Hesk, who is very old and very dirty and mutters all day. Most people think she is mad. If you sit close enough you can hear what she mutters: a prayer to the One Who Made, not the One Who Glitters. It is the old prayer. You know it. You wrote the god's half of it.

choices.text: Sit beside her and listen

effects.log: Hesk lets you sit. After an hour she stops muttering and looks at you. 'You know the words,' she says. It is not a question.

choices.text: Bring her bread

effects.log: She takes the bread and tears it in two and gives you half, the way the old rite says to. Nobody has done that for a hundred years. You eat it together by the well.

choices.text: Laugh at her with the others

effects.log: The others laugh. You laugh. Hesk does not even look up. That night you cannot sleep, and do not know why.

events.text: Hesk takes you into her hut and rolls back the rug. Under the floor there is an altar: plain grey stone, one open hand carved on it, worn smooth by a thousand years of other hands. The Radiant priests, she says, are coming tomorrow to clear her house.

choices.text: Help her bury the altar deeper and hide it

effects.log: You dig all night. By dawn the altar is under four feet of earth and a potato bed. The priests come, find potatoes, and leave disappointed.

choices.text: Talk the priests out of coming at all

ok.log: You meet them at the lane's end and talk about the weather, the price of brass, and a sudden plague of fleas in Hesk's hut. They turn round.

fail.log: They come anyway, find the altar, and break the hand off it with a hammer. Hesk keeps the pieces in her apron, and says nothing, and does not forgive anyone.

choices.text: Tell her the god is still listening

effects.log: 'I know,' says Hesk. 'I only wanted somebody else to know too.' She pats your hand, as if you were the one who needed comfort.

events.text: Hesk is dying, quietly, of being very old. She sends for you. She takes your face in both hands and looks into it for a long time, like a reader at the end of a book. 'You have the old god's eyes,' she says. 'I would know them anywhere. Tell me. Tell me before I go.'

choices.text: Tell her the truth

effects.log: You tell her. Hesk listens with her eyes closed and a smile like the sun coming up. 'Then go home,' she says. 'And take it back from the glittering ones.' The way back opens in you like a door.

choices.text: Promise to keep the altar

effects.log: Hesk nods. She makes you put your hand on the carved hand under the potatoes, and says the old words over it, and after that you are its keeper, and it is warm under your palm.

choices.text: Tell her she is tired and should sleep

effects.log: 'So I am,' says Hesk, and smiles at you as if you had said something much kinder. She sleeps. In the morning the well water tastes of honey, and nobody knows why.

events.text: The cows on your farm sleep in a very odd barn. It has a high painted ceiling, columns like trees, and at the far end a stone giant sitting with its hands open on its knees. Nobody knows who the giant is. The hens nest in its lap. You have always called it Old Stony.

choices.text: Climb up into Old Stony's lap

effects.log: From Stony's lap you can see the whole barn and out of the high window to the hills. The hens grumble and make room. You fall asleep there, and wake up warm.

choices.text: Name the cows after the pictures on the ceiling

effects.log: The ceiling has a sun, a sea, a mountain and a little figure with its hands out. The cows are now Sun, Sea, Mountain and Hands. Hands is the best milker.

choices.text: Leave a turnip in Stony's hand, as a present

effects.log: In the morning the turnip is gone. A cow ate it, almost certainly. You choose to believe otherwise, and leave a turnip every day for a year.

events.text: Mucking out under the straw, your fork scrapes on something that is not stone floor. It is tiles, little coloured ones, hundreds of them. You clear a patch the size of a door, and there is a picture: the stone giant, standing up, pulling the hills out of the sea with both hands.

choices.text: Sweep the whole floor clean

effects.log: It takes you all summer. At the end there is a picture as big as a field: the giant making everything, the rivers, the trees, the first people, even the cows. You lie in the middle of it, aching.

choices.text: Show the grown-ups

effects.log: They look, and shrug, and say it is old, and put the straw back because the cows need it. One of them, though, comes back alone that night with a lamp.

choices.text: Trace the picture on a big sheet of paper

effects.log: You trace the giant's hands. When you hold your own hands up against the paper, they are the same shape. You decide that is funny and do not think about it.

events.text: The farm needs a new wall, and the barn is full of good cut stone that nobody is using. The farmer has hired men with hammers. They are starting with Old Stony, because the giant is the biggest stone of all.

choices.text: Show the farmer the floor

effects.log: The farmer walks the whole mosaic in silence, hat in hand. The men with hammers are sent home. The barn stays a barn, but people start coming from other villages, just to look at the floor.

choices.text: Help take the barn down and build the wall

effects.log: It is a very good wall. It will stand for a thousand years, and on some of its stones there are faded painted suns that nobody looks at.

choices.text: Beg them to keep Old Stony, at least

effects.log: They drag the giant out into the yard and leave it there. The hens follow it out and nest in its lap in the sun. Old Stony looks, if anything, happier.

events.text: All the children of {pw_world} skip to the same rhyme, and nobody knows who made it up. 'Open hand and open sky, who made the river, who made I? Count to nine and shut your eyes: the one who made it never dies.' On nine you shut your eyes and jump, and if you land in the rope you are out.

choices.text: Skip until you trip

effects.log: You skip two hundred and twelve times, a village record, and land on your nose. Everyone cheers. You are the rope champion until somebody smaller beats you next spring.

choices.text: Ask what the last line means

effects.log: Nobody knows. The big children say it is just a rhyme. The smallest one says it means somebody made the river, obviously, and you think the smallest one may be right.

choices.text: Make up a new verse

effects.log: Yours goes: open door and open sea, who made the fishes, who made me? It catches on. You will hear children skip to it when you are old.

events.text: At the market a bookseller with a cart of mouldy books has one so old the cover is wood. You open it. Inside, in letters you can only just read, is your skipping rhyme, word for word, under the heading: The Last Prayer, to Be Said When the Name Is Gone.

choices.text: Buy the book with your saved shells

effects.log: It costs everything in your money-box. You carry it home under your shirt like a warm loaf, and read it until your candle goes out.

choices.text: Skip the rhyme for the bookseller, right there

effects.log: You skip it among the carts, counting to nine. The bookseller goes very pale, and then gives you the book for nothing. 'It should be with someone who still says it,' she says.

choices.text: Put the book back and go and play

effects.log: You go back to the rope. The others are skipping the rhyme. You skip it too, and this time, on nine, you keep your eyes shut a little longer than usual.

events.text: You are grown, and the children of {pw_world} still skip to the rhyme. You have begun to notice a thing that nobody else notices: in the villages where they skip the most, the rain comes on time, the sickness passes over, the harvest is a little better. The prayer is still being heard. You can feel yourself hearing it.

choices.text: Teach the rhyme in the villages that have lost it

effects.log: You go from village to village with a rope. The children love you. In a few years the river villages are skipping, and their wells, which were failing, come back.

choices.text: Write the rhyme into the town record, with its meaning

effects.log: You write it down: what it is, who it is for, why it still works. The town clerk reads it twice and puts it in the iron box with the deeds.

choices.text: Let it stay a rhyme

effects.log: You tell nobody. Prayers last longest, you think, when nobody knows they are prayers. Under your window the children count to nine, and you close your eyes.

events.text: Doctor Imrie Vass of the Academy has come to dig up the hill behind the town. She has a hat with a very wide brim and a theory with a wider one: that somebody made {pw_world}, long ago, and that the world forgot, and that the name is still somewhere in the ground. She needs diggers. Most people think she is a crank.

choices.text: Sign on as a digger

effects.log: You dig. Vass talks the whole time, about strata and pots and the Maker, whom nobody else believes in. She is very good company. Your hands blister and harden.

choices.text: Tell her there is no maker

effects.log: 'Then we will dig up nothing,' says Vass cheerfully, 'and know it. Knowing is never wasted. Spade?' Somehow you end up holding a spade.

choices.text: Sell her an old pot and call it holy

effects.log: You sell her your neighbour's cracked soup pot as an ancient relic. She examines it very closely and pays you anyway, which makes you feel worse.

events.text: Thirty feet down, under the burnt layer and the flood layer and the layer of tiny shells, you find a tablet of fired clay. It is broken in half. On the half you hold there is a word, the first half of a name, and the first letters are the first letters of a name you had, once, before you were born here.

choices.text: Read it aloud

effects.log: You say it. The wind across the dig stops dead, and every dog in the town barks once, together, and then is quiet. Vass looks at you with her mouth open.

choices.text: Slip the tablet into your coat

effects.log: Nobody saw. You carry it home and sit up all night holding it, as if it might say something more. It does not. It does not have to.

choices.text: Confess about the soup pot

effects.log: Vass laughs until she has to sit in the trench. 'I knew,' she says. 'Soup pots have soup in them. But you came back to dig, and that was worth the shells.'

events.text: Imrie Vass is to present the find to the Academy, which has laughed at her for thirty years. The night before, in the tent by the trench, she sits with you over a lamp. 'Half a name,' she says. 'It is not enough. Who? Who made us? I would give my life's work to know.'

choices.text: Tell her whose name it is

effects.log: You tell her. Vass does not laugh. She writes it down, every word, and then sits very still with her hand on the page. 'Then you can go back,' she says. 'Up there. Can't you?' And you find that you can.

choices.text: Give her the half you hid

effects.log: The two halves fit. The whole name lies on the table in the lamplight. Vass reads it to the Academy the next day and nobody laughs, and the town is famous for a hundred years.

choices.text: Let her keep her mystery

effects.log: 'Half a name is a good beginning,' you say. Vass smiles. The Academy laughs at her again, but less. She names a trench after you, which is the highest honour an archaeologist can give.
