events.text: Nobody in {pw_world} remembers that it was made. They think the hills were always there, the sea always salt. But you remember. Not every night: some nights. You dream of pulling the mountains up like bread dough, of lighting the sun with a word, and wake with dirt under your nails that was not there when you went to bed.

choices.text: Write it all down every morning

effects.log: You keep a book. It fills up with mountains, seas, first rains, first people. Reading it back is like reading the diary of someone you very much want to meet.

choices.text: Tell your closest friend

effects.log: Your friend listens kindly, then pats your arm and says you should eat more greens. It is the most reasonable answer in the world. You love your friend for it.

choices.text: Try to forget, like everyone else

effects.log: You try very hard. You sleep with the window shut. For a whole year you are just a person, and it is restful, and you are not sure it is right.

events.text: You find the place. It is a flat grey stone on a hill above a lake, with a hollow in it the shape of a foot, the first footprint, where you stood when the world was done and looked at it. Sheep graze around it. A shepherd is eating cheese on it.

choices.text: Put your foot in the hollow

effects.log: It fits. A warmth goes up through you, out of the hill, and the breath in your chest suddenly knows how to be long and slow and deep. The shepherd stops chewing.

choices.text: Bring your friend to see it

effects.log: Your friend stands on the stone and feels nothing, and says it is a nice view. It is a nice view. You made it. You are glad, at least, that someone likes it.

choices.text: Share the shepherd's cheese and leave it at that

effects.log: The shepherd gives you half. You eat in silence above the lake. It is the best cheese in the world, which seems right.

events.text: A child of the village, sharp-eyed and tactless, stops you in the lane. 'Everyone says nobody made the world,' the child says. 'But you always look at things like you are checking them. Did somebody make it?'

choices.text: Tell the child a story about somebody who did

effects.log: You tell it as a story: a maker, lonely, who made a world and then forgot to visit. The child is not fooled for a second, but is kind enough to pretend.

choices.text: Give the child your book

effects.log: The child reads it in one night and comes back with eleven questions, all good ones. You answer them all. Now there are two people in {pw_world} who remember.

choices.text: Go back to the grey stone alone and ask the sky

effects.log: You stand in the first footprint at dusk and ask. The sky answers the way skies do, with a long silence and one star, and then a way you had forgotten unrolls from the stone and up, like a stair.

choices.text: Say nobody knows, and walk on

effects.log: 'That is what everyone says,' the child says, disappointed. You walk on. The child watches you all the way down the lane.

events.text: The temple of the Maker takes novices at eight. You arrive with a bundle and a grey robe two sizes too big. Brother Anselm, who keeps the novices, has a face like a disappointed loaf and a heart, it turns out, like warm bread. 'Rise at the bell,' he says. 'Sweep. Learn. Do not touch the library.'

choices.text: Scrub the steps before anyone tells you to

effects.log: You are found at dawn, wet to the elbows, on the forty-third step. Brother Anselm says nothing, but you get the second-best porridge bowl from then on.

choices.text: Sneak into the library

effects.log: The library smells of dust and candles and paper going gently yellow. You read three pages of the Book of Making before you are caught, and every page is slightly wrong.

choices.text: Make friends with the other novices

effects.log: By the end of the week you know everyone's name, everyone's fears, and where the cook hides the raisins. You are very popular, and slightly sticky.

events.text: Every novice must learn the Book of Making by heart and recite it before the whole temple. You know it is wrong. Not badly wrong. Just: the sea was not made on the third day. You remember. It was the fourth, after lunch.

choices.text: Recite it perfectly, as written

effects.log: You do not miss a word. The old priests nod. Brother Anselm almost smiles. You go to bed with a strange itch in the back of your mind.

choices.text: Recite your own version

effects.log: You get to the fourth day, after lunch, and the whole temple goes silent. Brother Anselm takes you aside after. 'Where did you read that?' 'Nowhere.' He looks at you for a long time.

choices.text: Fall asleep halfway through

effects.log: You fall asleep standing up in the middle of the second day, very gently, like a candle going out. The temple laughs for a week. You feel wonderfully rested.

events.text: The time comes to choose: take the grey cord and become a true novice of the Maker, or go back out into {pw_world}. Brother Anselm sits with you on the steps you scrubbed. 'Either is right,' he says. 'The god will not mind.'

choices.text: Take the grey cord

effects.log: Brother Anselm ties it himself, slowly, with his big floury fingers. You feel very small and very held. The bell rings while he does it, which he says is lucky.

choices.text: Go out into the world

effects.log: You give back the robe, which you have grown into. Brother Anselm gives you a raisin bun for the road and stands on the steps until you are out of sight.

choices.text: Ask Brother Anselm what the god looked like

effects.log: He takes you to a small dark room and gives you a mirror. 'Nobody knows,' he says. 'So we tell the novices to look here, and try to be worth making.' You look for a long time.

events.text: The temple kitchen feeds three hundred pilgrims a day under the rule of Cook Marguerite Plum, a woman built like a bread oven and about as warm. On every holy day, by scripture, they serve the Maker's favourite dish: turnip stew. You remember the Maker's opinion of turnips. It was not favourable.

choices.text: Make the turnip stew exactly as written

effects.log: You stir three hundred bowls of turnip stew. The pilgrims eat it with devotion. Cook Plum says you have the hands for it, which from her is a hug.

choices.text: Add honey and black pepper when Plum is not looking

effects.log: The pilgrims ask for second helpings for the first time in a century. Cook Plum tastes it, narrows her eyes, and says nothing. Yet.

choices.text: Tell Plum that the god hated turnips

effects.log: Cook Plum picks up her largest ladle. 'Heresy,' she says, 'in my kitchen.' You spend the rest of the week scrubbing pots, but she keeps looking at the turnips thoughtfully.

events.text: The night before the High Priest's feast, disaster: the bread will not rise. Three hundred loaves sit in the trays like sad pale stones. Cook Plum is pacing. Pilgrims are already queueing outside in the dark.

choices.text: Knead every loaf again, all night

effects.log: By dawn your arms are rope and your hair is flour. The bread rises, just. Cook Plum puts a hand on your shoulder, which leaves a white handprint you are oddly proud of.

choices.text: Pray over the dough

effects.log: You put your hands on the trays and ask, a little sheepishly. The dough rises so fast it lifts the lids off the ovens. The loaves are enormous. The pilgrims call it the Miracle of the Bread.

choices.text: Serve your spiced stew instead, with no bread at all

effects.log: The High Priest tastes it, closes his eyes, and declares it holy. Cook Plum is furious for a day and then asks you, very quietly, for the recipe.

events.text: Cook Plum is retiring. She takes off the great iron spoon she has worn on a chain for forty years and puts it round your neck. 'Your kitchen now,' she says. 'Do not ruin it.' The temple waits to see what you will serve.

choices.text: Keep the turnip stew, for tradition

effects.log: You serve turnip stew on every holy day. The pilgrims love it the way people love old songs. You come, slowly, to love it too, out of sheer familiarity.

choices.text: Abolish turnip stew forever

effects.log: There is outrage for a week. Then there is a new holy dish, spiced lentils with honey, and everyone forgets they ever ate turnips, and the god, somewhere, is pleased.

choices.text: Write down every recipe for the temple archive

effects.log: You write The Book of the Kitchen, three hundred recipes and one short prayer for bread that will not rise. It is copied more often than the scriptures.

events.text: The Great Bell of the temple, called Old Thunder, is rung every dawn by two ringers, one on each rope. You are the new one. The other is {npc}, who has rung it for three years and has opinions about your timing.

choices.text: Ring in perfect time with {npc}

mem.note: rang the bell in time with me

effects.log: On the third morning you get it right: the two ropes fall together and Old Thunder speaks so clean the doves go up off every roof. {npc} looks across at you and nods.

choices.text: Ring a beat early, to tease

mem.note: made the bell hiccup with me

effects.log: {npc} rings a beat late in revenge. The whole town wakes to a bell that sounds like it has hiccups. You both get scolded and laugh about it on the stairs for an hour.

choices.text: Keep to your own rope and say nothing

effects.log: You ring, and go down, and ring again. {npc} gives up talking to you after a month. Your arms grow very strong.

events.text: Old Thunder has cracked. Its voice is wrong now, a sour hum under the note, and the priests talk of melting it down. {npc} is sure the crack can be mended, and asks you to climb up inside the bell with a lamp to look.

choices.text: Climb up inside the bell with {npc}

mem.note: climbed inside the bell with me

effects.log: Inside the bell it is dark and green and smells of old bronze. On the inner wall, by the lamp, you find words cast into the metal, so old that only you can read them.

choices.text: Help {npc} haul new bronze up the tower

mem.note: hauled bronze up the tower with me

effects.log: You carry bronze up four hundred steps with {npc}, one ingot at a time, talking about everything but the bell. By the last load you know each other's whole lives.

choices.text: Let the priests decide

effects.log: The priests argue for a year. {npc} rings the cracked bell alone every morning, and the sour hum follows you round town all day.

events.text: The bell is mended and hung again. At dawn the whole town comes to hear it. You are on one rope; {npc} is on the other; the priests are holding their breath. {npc} looks at you across the dark tower, and waits.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to marry you, before the first stroke

effects.log: {npc} says yes and pulls the rope at the same time, and Old Thunder rings out over a town that thinks the bell is for the mending. It is, partly.

choices.text: Ring the old pattern from the words inside the bell

effects.log: You call the pattern to {npc}: three, one, three, five. Old Thunder sings a note nobody living has heard. The whole valley stops working to listen.

choices.text: Ring together, and say nothing

mem.note: sat with me after the bell

effects.log: You ring. The bell is perfect. Afterwards you and {npc} sit on the top step in the cold, not speaking, and it is enough, for now.

events.text: Every three years, in the Hall of Questions, the young of {pw_world} sit the Examination of Scripture. Those who pass become priests. You sit at a little desk with five hundred others. The first question is on the board: How did the Maker deal with the world? The approved answer, learnt by heart, is that the god {pw_record}. You were there.

choices.text: Write the approved answer

effects.log: You write it neatly, word for word. It is true, as far as it goes. It does not go very far, and you have to stop yourself adding footnotes.

choices.text: Write what really happened, in detail

effects.log: You write eleven pages: the weather that day, what you were thinking, the mistake you made and the one you nearly made. The examiner marks it imaginative, and then reads it twice.

choices.text: Draw it instead

effects.log: You draw it, beautifully, every cloud. The examiner holds it up to the light and calls over two colleagues. Nobody knows what mark to give a drawing.

events.text: The oral examination. Examiner Pell, who is ninety and has heard every answer, asks the question nobody has ever answered: 'And why did the god do it?' The book says only: This is the Mystery. The whole row of candidates before you said Mystery. Pell is half asleep.

choices.text: Say: the Mystery

effects.log: Pell nods without opening his eyes and ticks the box. You have passed the hardest question in scripture by saying you do not know, which feels, on reflection, very holy.

choices.text: Tell him the real reason

ok.log: Pell's eyes open. He puts down his pen. 'That,' he says slowly, 'makes sense. Nothing in sixty years has made sense.' He writes your name on a separate list.

fail.log: 'Heresy,' says Pell, mildly, 'but well argued.' He gives you half marks, which nobody has ever had for that question.

choices.text: Admit you do not remember

effects.log: It is true: some of it is gone, even from you. Pell looks at you for a long time. 'Nobody has ever said that,' he says, and ticks the box.

events.text: The results are posted on the temple door at dawn. A crowd presses round it. Some weep, some cheer, one boy faints into a fruit cart. You push through to see your name.

choices.text: You passed: put on the lamp-badge of a junior priest

effects.log: You are a priest of the Maker, lowest rank, with a little brass lamp on your collar. You are going to have to preach about yourself. You try not to laugh during the oath.

choices.text: Your name is not there: but Examiner Pell is waiting by the door

effects.log: 'Come and talk to me,' says Pell, 'every week, for as long as I live. I have questions.' You do, for six years. He writes it all down, and the book he leaves is copied in every temple.

choices.text: Walk away without looking

effects.log: You walk into the market and buy a peach. Whatever it says on the door, you know more scripture than anyone in that crowd, and the peach is excellent.

events.text: You are ordained a Lamp-Priest of the Maker, the lowest rank, and sent to a village temple with a leaking roof, a mouse in the offering bowl, and a congregation of one: old Tobiah, who comes every day, sits at the front, and falls asleep at once.

choices.text: Fix the roof yourself

effects.log: You spend the spring on the roof with a ladder and borrowed tiles. The village watches you and, one by one, comes to help. By summer the temple is dry and full.

choices.text: Preach every day to whoever comes

effects.log: You preach to Tobiah, the mouse and the wind. Then to Tobiah, the mouse and a curious goat. By the end of the year to forty people. You are surprisingly good at it.

choices.text: Spend your days in the temple archive

effects.log: The archive is three boxes and a mouse nest. You read every scrap. In one box there is a letter to the god from a child, very old, asking for a puppy. You remember sending the puppy.

events.text: You are made Warden of a Hearth, with three village temples to look after and a horse to look after them on. A rich wool-merchant, Mistress Orla Bane, offers a great gift to the temple, on one condition: a seat at the front, carved with her name, forever.

choices.text: Take the gift for the temple

effects.log: The temple gets a new roof, new lamps and a carved seat that says BANE in big letters. Orla sits in it every holy day looking thrilled. It is an ugly seat.

choices.text: Refuse: the front seats belong to whoever comes first

effects.log: Orla Bane is furious, and then, the next holy day, arrives at dawn to get the front seat the honest way. She keeps doing it. She becomes very devout.

choices.text: Say yes, if she sweeps the temple first, every week, for a year

effects.log: To everyone's astonishment, she does. By the end of the year she does not want the carved seat any more. She wants the broom.

events.text: The old Voice of the Maker, the highest priest of {pw_world}, has died, and the Conclave of Lamps meets to choose another. Your name has come up. So has the name of Prelate Osric Thane, who is clever, ruthless, and owns very good shoes.

choices.text: Campaign for the Voice

ok.log: You speak to every lamp-priest in the Conclave, one by one. On the ninth ballot the bell rings for you. You are the Voice of the Maker. You go outside and sit on the steps for a while.

fail.log: Osric Thane wins on the ninth ballot, by two votes. He is very gracious about it, in excellent shoes.

choices.text: Withdraw and support Osric

effects.log: Osric is astonished. He is a good Voice, as it turns out, mostly because he spends ten years trying to deserve your vote.

choices.text: Buy the votes you need

effects.log: It is easier than you would like. You become the Voice of the Maker with a purse that is much lighter and a soul that is much heavier.

events.text: You are old now, in the way of priests: slowly, then all at once. You look back at the temples, the sermons, the roofs. Somewhere up above, the god you are preaching about is, in a sense, listening to you do it.

choices.text: As the Voice, change one line of scripture to the truth

effects.log: You change one line. It is a small line, about the fourth day. There is uproar for a year. Then it is simply how the scripture reads, and always was.

choices.text: Go back to the village temple with the leaking roof

effects.log: The roof leaks again. You fix it again. Tobiah's grandchild falls asleep in the front row. It is the best congregation you ever had.

choices.text: Write your memoirs

effects.log: You call them A Priest of the Lamp. They are very funny and slightly scandalous and quietly accurate about the god in ways that make scholars argue for centuries.

events.text: The priesthood of {pw_world} is tearing itself in two over a question of plaster. The Seedholders say every statue of the Maker must hold a seed in the right hand, for the god planted the world. The Openhanders say both hands must be empty, for the god gave everything away. There have been riots. Somebody threw a seed.

choices.text: Join the Openhanders

effects.log: You are given a little badge of an open palm and a great many pamphlets. Your new friends are earnest, kind, and unable to talk about anything else.

choices.text: Join the Seedholders

effects.log: You are given a little badge of a seed and a great many pamphlets. Your new friends are earnest, kind, and unable to talk about anything else.

choices.text: Sell plaster seeds to both sides

effects.log: You sell plaster seeds to the Seedholders to stick on statues, and chisels to the Openhanders to knock them off. Business is excellent. Nobody notices it is the same stall.

events.text: A Council of Reconciliation meets in the High Temple, and each side must send a speaker. Through a series of accidents, you are a speaker. You stand up. You remember the moment they are arguing about. You remember exactly what was in your hand.

choices.text: Argue for your side with everything you have

ok.log: You speak so well that half the other side crosses the floor. There is weeping, and hugging, and a small fight about the seating.

fail.log: You speak so well that both sides are furious with you. You leave by the kitchen door.

choices.text: Tell them the truth: it was a pear

effects.log: There is a silence like the end of the world. 'A pear?' 'You had walked a long way. It was a good pear.' One old priest at the back starts to laugh and cannot stop.

choices.text: Propose that every temple chooses for itself

effects.log: It is the most sensible idea anyone has had in years, and so it passes, grudgingly, by four votes. Both sides are equally disappointed, which is what peace looks like.

events.text: The schism ends, as schisms do, in a very long feast. The cooks have been told to be diplomatic, and so every table has both seeds and empty plates on it. Everyone is watching to see who will sit where.

choices.text: Found the Rite of the Pear

effects.log: Within a year a third of the statues in {pw_world} are holding pears. Both the old sides are united for the first time, in outrage. Then they forget why they quarrelled. The pear stays.

choices.text: Let them split into two temples on the same street

effects.log: The Seed Temple and the Open Temple glare at each other across a street of very successful cake shops that serve both. Everyone is, frankly, fine.

choices.text: Sit at the exact middle of the feast and pass the bread both ways

effects.log: By the end of the night both sides are passing the bread. It is the best feast in years. Nobody remembers who threw the first seed.

events.text: The old monarch of {pw_kingdom} has died, and the heir, Princess Aveline, must be crowned. By ancient law the crown is not hers until the god gives a sign: a white heron must land on the temple roof at the moment of crowning. For the last three crownings, it is whispered, the heron was a trained one, kept in a basket.

choices.text: Volunteer to train this year's heron

effects.log: The temple heron-keeper is delighted to have help and gives you a bird with the worst temper in the kingdom. You train it for a month. It bites you nine times.

choices.text: Sell sausages to the crowds

effects.log: The coronation brings half the kingdom to the capital, and all of it is hungry. You sell nine hundred sausages and buy a better pan.

choices.text: Ask a priest what happens if there is no sign

effects.log: 'Then the god does not want her,' the priest says, and looks over his shoulder. 'In which case we have a terrible problem. Which is why there is always a heron.'

events.text: The night before the crowning, the trained heron escapes. It is gone, out over the marsh, with a piece of the heron-keeper's thumb. The keeper is in tears. The priests are white. Somewhere in the palace, Princess Aveline is trying on the crown.

choices.text: Chase the heron through the marsh

ok.log: You find it at dawn, standing on one leg, eating a frog with enormous dignity. You carry it back in your shirt. It bites you once more, for form.

fail.log: You chase it all night and come home covered in mud from head to foot. The heron is gone. You are, however, very fit now.

choices.text: Find the princess and tell her the truth

effects.log: Aveline listens, white-faced, with the crown on. 'So there was never a sign,' she says. 'Not for my grandmother either.' She takes the crown off and looks at it for a long time.

choices.text: Go to bed: it is not your problem

effects.log: You go to bed. Lying awake, you look at the ceiling and think: it is, in a way, very much your problem. You were the god.

events.text: The crowning. The priest raises the golden crown above Princess Aveline's head. The whole kingdom falls silent and looks up at the empty sky. There is no heron. The silence goes on. The priest's arms begin to shake.

choices.text: Ask the sky, silently, for a sign

ok.log: Out of a clear sky a white heron, wild and enormous, sails down and lands on the temple roof and folds its wings. The crowd roars. You sit down on the steps, shaking.

fail.log: A pigeon lands on the temple roof. There is a long, long pause. Then someone shouts 'It is white-ish!' and the crowd decides that counts. The queen is crowned.

choices.text: Release the heron you caught

effects.log: You open your shirt and the heron flaps up, furious, and lands on the temple roof to glare at everyone. It is the most convincing sign in a hundred years.

choices.text: Watch Aveline crown herself

effects.log: Aveline takes the crown from the priest and puts it on her own head. 'If the god wants a sign,' she says, to the whole square, 'let it be this: the granaries full and the roads safe.' The square is silent, then thunderous.

choices.text: Shout 'There!' and point at the sky

effects.log: Ten thousand people look where you point. Some see a heron. Some see a cloud. Everyone agrees, later, that there was definitely something. The queen is crowned.

events.text: Two kingdoms of {pw_world} have gone to war over a river. Both say the god gave it to them in the beginning. You know the god gave it to the fish. You are carting bread to the camp when you go down to the ford to water the mules, and on the far bank, watering mules of the other side, is {npc}.

choices.text: Throw {npc} half your bread across the water

effects.log: {npc} catches it, looks at it, and throws back a lump of cheese. You eat lunch together across a river two armies are about to die for.

choices.text: Ask {npc} what they call the river on that side

effects.log: On your side it is the Sweetwater. On {npc}'s side it is the Mother. You both decide this is stupid, and agree to call it the Mule River.

choices.text: Pretend you have not seen {npc}

effects.log: You water your mules looking firmly at the mules. When you look up, {npc} is gone, and you wish you had waved.

events.text: The armies are drawn up on both banks. Battle is two days off. At night {npc} wades across the ford with a message: the other side's captain is tired of the war too, and would talk, if somebody brave were to carry the word.

choices.text: Carry the message to your captain

mem.note: carried the word across the river

ok.log: Your captain reads it twice and swears for a long time, then sends you back across the ford with an answer. There will be talks.

fail.log: Your captain has you locked in a supply tent for the night as a possible spy. {npc} waits at the ford until dawn.

choices.text: Meet {npc} at the ford every night instead

effects.log: You sit on a rock in the middle of the river every night, and talk until the sentries change. The war does not come any closer. Neither, somehow, does the morning.

choices.text: Desert, and walk home

effects.log: You walk away in the dark. It is not brave. It is not cowardly either, exactly. Behind you the campfires burn on both banks.

events.text: There is no battle. In the end the two kingdoms sign a treaty on a raft in the middle of the ford, sharing the river, and both armies go home grumbling and alive. {npc} is standing on the far bank, not leaving.

choices.text: Wade across and ask {npc} to marry you

effects.log: You are married on the treaty raft, by a priest from each side. Both kingdoms send a gift, both gifts are cheese, and the wedding is famous for the cheese.

choices.text: Stand witness at the signing with {npc}

effects.log: You and {npc} sign as witnesses, side by side, the only commoners on the raft. Your names are on the treaty forever, next to each other.

choices.text: Wave to {npc} and go home

effects.log: You wave. {npc} waves. It is a good wave, a whole river wide, and you remember it for the rest of your life.

events.text: The Heralds' Hall of {pw_kingdom} is looking for new voices. Heralds carry the crown's word to every market square: they must be loud, clear, fast on a horse and impossible to embarrass. The test is to read a proclamation aloud from the hall's balcony so that the baker at the far end of the street can hear every word.

choices.text: Bellow it

effects.log: The baker hears you. So does the next street. A dog faints. You are hired on the spot and given a tabard with a trumpet on it.

choices.text: Read it with great feeling

effects.log: You read the proclamation, which is about the price of barley, as if it were a love poem. The baker cries. You are hired, mostly as a curiosity.

choices.text: Decide you would rather be the baker

effects.log: You go down the street and buy a loaf from the baker instead, who has heard every herald for thirty years and has a great deal to say about them.

events.text: Your first real proclamation, in the great square, before a thousand people. You unroll it. The royal scribe, clearly up too late, has written: By order of the crown, war is declared upon all ducks. You are fairly sure it was meant to say dukes.

choices.text: Read it exactly as written

effects.log: A thousand people hear the crown declare war on ducks. The square erupts. For a year ducks are a symbol of resistance, painted on walls. The scribe is quietly retired.

choices.text: Read it as clearly meant

effects.log: You read dukes. The dukes are furious. The ducks are safe. Somewhere the scribe weeps with gratitude and sends you a cake every midwinter for the rest of your life.

choices.text: Read it with great seriousness and then add: the ducks have been warned

effects.log: The crowd laughs so hard the crown's steward comes out to see what happened. Even the steward laughs, eventually.

events.text: The highest honour a herald can have: to proclaim the god's word at the Festival of the Making, read from the scripture before the whole kingdom. You unroll it. It says the god commanded every subject to obey the crown and pay the grain tax promptly. You were the god. You never said anything about grain tax.

choices.text: Proclaim it exactly as written

effects.log: You proclaim it. The crown is pleased. You are given a purse and a better horse, and you ride home feeling slightly like a fraud.

choices.text: Change one word: obey becomes love

effects.log: Love the crown, you proclaim, and pay the grain tax promptly. It sounds much nicer. Nobody notices the change but the queen, who sends for you, and laughs.

choices.text: Proclaim what the god actually said

effects.log: You roll up the scroll and tell them what the god really said, long ago: be kind, keep the rivers clean, the rest is up to you. The square is silent. Then someone cheers. You lose your tabard, and gain a legend.

events.text: Thistlecombe declared itself a kingdom when the larger kingdoms of {pw_world} forgot to claim it. It has forty-one subjects, a king who is also the miller, an army of one retired archer, and a royal temple the size of a cupboard. The crown is a ring of copper that also serves, on weekdays, as a stand for the soup pot.

choices.text: Accept a post at court

effects.log: You are made Royal Chancellor, Royal Treasurer and Royal Goose-Keeper, all at once. The treasury is a jar. The geese are the hardest part.

choices.text: Join the army, doubling it

effects.log: The archer, old Fennick, is delighted. He drills you every morning in the field behind the mill. The army of Thistlecombe is now feared by at least three rabbits.

choices.text: Laugh at the whole thing

effects.log: The king fines you one egg for disrespect to the crown. You pay it. It goes in the treasury jar, which now contains an egg.

events.text: An envoy arrives from {pw_kingdom}, in silk, on a tall horse, with twelve guards. Thistlecombe is to submit and pay tribute, or else. The king takes off his flour apron and puts on the crown, after removing the soup pot.

choices.text: Negotiate for the kingdom

ok.log: You talk the envoy into a treaty of eternal friendship in exchange for one goose a year. The envoy cannot believe it either. The goose is a terrible goose.

fail.log: The envoy demands three geese a year. You get it down to two. Thistlecombe is now a tributary kingdom, of geese.

choices.text: Show the envoy the crown and the soup-pot ring

effects.log: The envoy looks at the crown, and the pot ring under it, and laughs until the horse is frightened. They leave without the tribute, still laughing. Thistlecombe considers this a victory.

choices.text: Invite the envoy to dinner

effects.log: Dinner is mutton and turnips at the mill. The envoy stays three days, falls in love with the place, and goes home to tell the court that Thistlecombe is fiercely defended and not worth the trouble.

events.text: The miller-king is old and wants to retire to fish. Thistlecombe has no law of succession, so it holds a vote in the mill, with beans in a sack. Your name is put forward. So is the archer's. So, for a joke, is the goose.

choices.text: Accept the crown

effects.log: You win by six beans. You are crowned with the soup-pot ring and rule Thistlecombe wisely, mostly about geese. It is the smallest kingdom in {pw_world}, and the happiest.

choices.text: Vote for the goose

effects.log: The goose wins. It is a very short reign: the goose eats the crown's ribbon and wanders off. The archer is chosen in the second round, on the strength of not being a goose.

choices.text: Nominate old Fennick the archer

effects.log: Fennick is crowned and weeps into his beard. He rules well and kindly and makes you Chancellor, Treasurer and Goose-Keeper again, for life.

events.text: There are no kingdoms in {pw_world} yet: only villages, each with its elders, its well and its quarrels. This year the nine river villages have quarrelled so badly over the fish-weir that two of them are throwing stones. An old woman says, 'There should be somebody over all of us, to decide.' Nobody has ever thought of this before.

choices.text: Suggest all nine villages meet in one place and talk

effects.log: You call it a gathering. It is the first one ever. Everyone comes, out of curiosity, with food. Nobody throws stones, because their hands are full.

choices.text: Say you would do it, if asked

effects.log: Several people look at you as if you had grown a second head. One or two look at you as if you might be right. You go home thinking hard.

choices.text: Say that someone over everyone turns into a tyrant, given time

effects.log: You know. You have seen it in other worlds, or dreamt it. The old woman looks at you sharply. 'Then we must think of a way to stop that,' she says.

events.text: The nine villages meet at the ford under the great oak. The elders make up the word as they go: a chief, a chieftain, the first among the villages. Who will it be? A fisher stands. A potter stands. People turn and look at you.

choices.text: Stand for it

ok.log: You win by a show of hands, the first vote in the history of {pw_world}. Somebody makes you a hat out of reeds. You are the first chieftain.

fail.log: The fisher wins, by six hands. You shake hands. The fisher gives you a fish, which is the first act of state in history.

choices.text: Put forward Grandmother Teel, who first said it

effects.log: Grandmother Teel is chosen by acclaim and is furious about it. She rules the river for twenty years with a stick and a terrible memory for grudges. There is peace.

choices.text: Propose the chieftain rules for one year only

effects.log: The elders are astonished by the idea and then adore it. It becomes the first law: a chief for a year, and then back to fishing. It holds for a thousand years.

events.text: The first case ever brought before the first chieftain: a pig has been stolen. The accused is a boy from the upper village. The pig's owner is a large woman from the lower village. The pig is present, eating the evidence.

choices.text: Judge with mercy: the boy works for the pig's owner for a season

effects.log: The boy works for a season and turns out to be good with pigs. Ten years later he owns the largest herd on the river, and still sends the owner a ham each year.

choices.text: Judge by the old law of the weir: what is taken is paid back twice

effects.log: The boy's village pays two pigs. Everyone grumbles, and everyone agrees it was fair, which is the definition of a law, you think.

choices.text: Ask the pig

effects.log: You crouch down and ask the pig who stole it. The pig walks over to the boy and leans on him. The whole gathering bursts out laughing, and the case is settled with everyone friends.

events.arc: The School of the First Law
events.text: The School of the First Law keeps the oldest teaching in {pw_world}, the first thing the Maker ever said to the people: breathe in what is given; breathe out what is owed. Its students learn to gather qi with the breath. To enter, you must sit on the cold stone by its gate from dusk until dawn without moving.

choices.text: Sit on the stone until dawn

effects.log: The cold climbs into your bones and stays there. Around midnight your breath goes slow and deep on its own, and the cold stops mattering. At dawn the gate opens.

choices.text: Ask the gatekeeper what the First Law means

effects.log: 'Nobody is sure,' the gatekeeper admits. 'The second half was lost.' You know it. You say nothing yet.

choices.text: Climb in through the kitchen window

effects.log: You are caught at once by the cook, who is also the senior teacher. She is so amused that she lets you stay, on kitchen duty, for a year.

events.arc: The School of the First Law
events.text: Grandmother Vey, who teaches the breath, is small and bent and can put out a candle across the hall by breathing at it. She walks the rows of students sitting cross-legged and taps the slouchers on the head with a fan.

choices.text: Breathe until your whole body hums

effects.log: You breathe for months. One morning the hum begins in your chest and does not stop. Grandmother Vey taps your head with the fan, gently, which means well done.

choices.text: Teach the lost second half of the First Law

effects.log: You say it aloud in the hall: and what is owed is joy. The students go very quiet. Grandmother Vey breathes in, and out, and smiles, and a candle at the far end goes out.

choices.text: Help the younger students with their breathing

effects.log: You sit with the little ones and breathe slowly beside them until they stop fidgeting. They follow you everywhere after that, like ducklings.

events.arc: The School of the First Law
events.text: The Testing of the Lantern: each student must stand at one end of the long hall and, with breath and qi alone, blow out the lantern at the other. The whole school is watching. Grandmother Vey is sitting beside the lantern, fanning herself.

choices.text: Breathe for the lantern

ok.log: You breathe in what is given and out what is owed, and the lantern flame bows and goes out. Grandmother Vey claps, once. You are a student of the First Law.

fail.log: The flame flickers, leans, and stays lit. Grandmother Vey's fan, however, flies out of her hand. She says that counts, for character.

choices.text: Breathe joy at it instead

effects.log: You think of every good thing you ever made, and breathe out. The lantern does not go out: it burns brighter, gold, and the whole hall smells of summer. Nobody knows how to mark it.

choices.text: Bow and leave without taking the test

effects.log: You bow to the lantern and walk out. Grandmother Vey calls after you that the door is always open. It is. You never need it, but it is good to know.

events.arc: The Hall of the Wrong Breath
events.text: The Hall of Nine Breaths teaches the god's own breathing, handed down for five hundred years: seven counts in, four counts out. Its students are serene and slightly blue. You sit down with them and try it, and something in you says at once: no. It was four in, seven out. You remember. You taught it.

choices.text: Breathe their way, as you are told

effects.log: Seven in, four out. By the end of the morning you are dizzy, serene and slightly blue. You have a headache that lasts until supper.

choices.text: Breathe your way, quietly

effects.log: Four in, seven out. The breath goes all the way down to your heels and back. You feel your qi move like water finding a channel it already knew.

choices.text: Ask why seven and four

effects.log: 'Because the god said so,' says the senior student. 'In the scroll.' You read the scroll. A copyist, five hundred years ago, wrote the numbers the wrong way round.

events.arc: The Hall of the Wrong Breath
events.text: Hallmaster Odo Brisk, a long, thin, very calm person, has noticed that you alone in the hall are not blue. After the evening breath he asks you to stay. 'You are doing it wrong,' he says. 'And you are better at it than anyone. Explain.'

choices.text: Teach him your way

ok.log: Odo Brisk tries it. Four in, seven out. His face goes pink for the first time in thirty years. He sits down on the floor and laughs. 'Five hundred years,' he says.

fail.log: Odo tries it and does not like it. 'Too easy,' he says. 'A breath should be suffered.' He lets you keep yours, though, as a curiosity.

choices.text: Show him the copyist's error in the scroll

effects.log: Odo reads it three times, very slowly, his calm face going through many expressions. 'I have taught this wrong all my life,' he says at last. 'Thank you. I think.'

choices.text: Pretend you are just lucky

effects.log: Odo Brisk looks at you for a long time, then lets it go. You breathe your own way in the back row for years, unnoticed, very pink.

events.arc: The Hall of the Wrong Breath
events.text: The Hall of Nine Breaths meets to decide whether to change the breath after five hundred years. The old students are horrified. The young ones are curious. Hallmaster Odo Brisk asks you to speak.

choices.text: Speak for the right breath

effects.log: You speak simply: four in, seven out, as it was taught at the beginning. The Hall votes to change. Within a year nobody in it is blue, and the Hall's students win every breath-holding contest in {pw_world}.

choices.text: Argue that both ways should be kept

effects.log: You argue that the wrong breath, after five hundred years, has become a thing of its own: it makes beautiful singers, if dizzy ones. The Hall keeps both, and becomes famous for its choir.

choices.text: Say nothing, and leave the Hall

effects.log: You walk out into the hills and breathe the god's breath alone, four in, seven out, under a sky you once breathed into being. It is enough.

events.text: Teacher Calloway Fenn runs a breathing school above a rope shop, and is famous for the Turning Sparrow, a technique of spinning qi through the body like a bird turning in wind. She says the god taught it, in the scripture: let the wind turn. You know that line. It meant: let the weather change. It was about farming.

choices.text: Learn the Turning Sparrow

effects.log: It is strange and dizzy and wonderful. Your qi spins up your spine and out of your hands, and for a moment you feel lighter than you have since before you were born.

choices.text: Tell her the god never meant it

effects.log: 'Then who did?' asks Calloway Fenn. 'You did,' you say. She stares at you, then laughs so hard she has to hold the rope rack. 'Well,' she says, 'I am not stopping now.'

choices.text: Watch from the doorway and leave

effects.log: You watch the students spin and turn, light as birds. It is very beautiful. It is nothing you ever made. You go home thinking about that for a week.

events.text: The Turning Sparrow is spreading through {pw_world}. Farmers use it to work longer, healers to calm fevers, children to jump higher. It does things your own teachings never did. Your world has grown a branch you did not plant.

choices.text: Practise until you can turn like a true sparrow

effects.log: You master it. You can spin your qi so fast your hair lifts. You are, you realise, the student of your own creation, and it is a better teacher than you were.

choices.text: Ask Calloway how she thought of it

effects.log: 'I misread the scripture,' she says. 'I was nine. I thought the god wanted us to be birds.' She shrugs. 'I still think so.' You are not sure she is wrong.

choices.text: Ask her to keep your secret

effects.log: 'Which one?' she asks. 'That the god never meant it, or that the god is in my classroom?' She keeps both, though she winks at you in front of the students.

events.text: Calloway Fenn is writing the Turning Sparrow down at last, for every school in {pw_world}. She comes to you with the first page blank except for a title she cannot decide on. 'You name it,' she says. 'You would know best.'

choices.text: Name it the Fenn Turning, after her

effects.log: Calloway turns red to the ears and writes it down. It is taught under her name for a thousand years, and nobody ever asks whether the god meant it.

choices.text: Name it the Maker's Sparrow

effects.log: Calloway writes it, though she gives you a long look. It becomes holy, which makes it spread faster, and you feel slightly like a thief.

choices.text: Leave it as the Turning Sparrow

effects.log: 'It already has a name,' you say. 'It found its own.' Calloway smiles and writes it, plain, at the top of the page, and the sparrow goes out into the world on its own wings.

events.text: {pw_world} is very old. Your town stands on seven towns, one under the other, each built on the bones of the last. The Guild of Historians keeps the Long Chronicle, which records every age back to the beginning, and they argue about it the way other people argue about money. They are looking for a young copyist.

choices.text: Become a copyist for the Guild

effects.log: You copy the Long Chronicle by candle, age by age: the Age of Salt, the Age of Bells, the Age of the Long Rain. Your hand grows steady. Your head fills with ten thousand years.

choices.text: Dig in your own cellar

effects.log: Under your cellar there is another cellar, and under that a painted wall of people dancing. You sit and look at them for an hour. They look very happy. They have been dead a long time.

choices.text: Say the past is the past

effects.log: The historians look at you with pity and some envy. They have not slept properly in years. You sleep beautifully.

events.text: A cellar collapses in the market, and opens a stair that goes down through all seven towns: past bricks, past stone, past timber black with age, to a room at the very bottom. In it there is a temple older than any written age, and a carving of the god's first act.

choices.text: Go down and read the carving

effects.log: The carving shows a figure pulling the world up out of nothing, and its face is turned away, as if shy. You touch it. You remember being shy, that day. You come up very quiet.

choices.text: Correct the Guild's chronology from what you see

ok.log: You show them the Long Chronicle is off by four hundred years. There is a scandal. Then a new edition, with your name in it.

fail.log: You argue the dates and lose. The Guild is very polite about it, in the way of people who have won.

choices.text: Leave the bottom room in the dark

effects.log: You put the stone back over the stair. Some rooms have waited this long and can wait longer. The historians never forgive you.

events.text: The Long Chronicle has one page that has always been blank: the first one, where the name of the maker of {pw_world} should be written. Nobody has ever known it. The Guild, in a vote that surprises everyone, asks you to write something there.

choices.text: Write your own name

effects.log: You write it, and the ink goes into the old paper like rain into dry ground. The historians read it, and look at you, and nobody says anything for a long time. That night you dream of a stair.

choices.text: Write: unknown

effects.log: You write unknown, in a careful hand. It is the most honest page in the Chronicle. The historians approve. Some part of you is sorry.

choices.text: Write: the one who made us, and was sorry, and was glad

effects.log: The historians argue about it for a hundred years. But it is the line that children learn, and the line on the temple doors, and it is true.

events.text: {pw_world} is young. Everything is still happening for the first time. This year the villages have decided to make money: the first coin. A smith has a mould, a pot of copper and no idea what to put on it. A crowd has gathered to argue.

choices.text: Suggest an open hand, for the god

effects.log: The first coin of {pw_world} has an open hand on it. People rub it for luck, so much that within a few years every hand on every coin is worn smooth.

choices.text: Suggest a fish

effects.log: The first coin has a fish on it. It is a very good fish. Merchants call the coins fishes, and long after anyone remembers why, money is still called fish.

choices.text: Pour the first coin yourself

effects.log: You pour the copper and strike the mould, and burn your thumb. The first coin of {pw_world} is yours. You keep it, and spend the second.

events.text: Next, the first map. Nobody knows how big the world is. The village elders want somebody to walk to the edges and draw what they find. They look round for somebody young and with nothing better to do.

choices.text: Walk to the edges and draw it

effects.log: You walk for a year. You draw rivers, hills, a lake shaped like a boot. You come home thin and brown with the first map of {pw_world} rolled up under your arm.

choices.text: Draw it from memory, without leaving home

effects.log: You sit down and draw the whole world in one afternoon. It is perfect, every bend of every river. Travellers check it for years, and are unnerved.

choices.text: Draw sea monsters in the blank parts

effects.log: You draw the parts you know and fill the rest with monsters, for fun. Every map maker of {pw_world} copies them forever after.

events.text: The first law court of {pw_world}, under a big tree, with a stool for the judge and a rope around the edge. The first case is about a goat that ate a neighbour's washing. Nobody knows how a trial goes. They are making it up as they go, and they need people for every part.

choices.text: Be the first judge

effects.log: You sit on the stool and make it up. The goat's owner pays one shirt. It becomes the law of washing for a thousand years. Lawyers will study your words. You wish you had chosen them more carefully.

choices.text: Be the first advocate, for the goat

effects.log: You argue that the washing was hung where any goat would eat it. You win. The goat is acquitted. Advocates of {pw_world} still swear their oath on a picture of a goat.

choices.text: Be the first witness and tell the plain truth

effects.log: You say what you saw: the goat ate the shirt. Everyone thanks you for being so simple about it. It is, they say, the first honest testimony, and should be the model.

events.text: The first history of {pw_world} is being written by a young scribe with a new quill and an enormous sense of importance. It is a thin book, because not much has happened yet. You are in it, several times.

choices.text: Ask the scribe to write you modestly

effects.log: You are in the history as a local person of good sense. You are pleased. Later historians will find you very difficult to research.

choices.text: Ask the scribe to make you sound magnificent

effects.log: You are in the history as a person of great beauty and courage, slightly taller than in life. Statues follow. They are quite good statues.

choices.text: Give the scribe your map for the first page

effects.log: The first page of the first history of {pw_world} is your map, rivers and boot-shaped lake and all. Everyone who ever reads it begins by seeing the world as you walked it.

events.text: In the oldest temple of {pw_world} a single sandal sits on a cushion under glass: plain leather, worn through at the heel. The priests say the Maker walked the world with one bare foot after the making, having lost the other somewhere. Nobody is allowed to try it on. People do anyway, at night, for dares.

choices.text: Take the dare and try it on

effects.log: You climb in through the vestry window with two friends keeping watch. The sandal fits you exactly, heel to toe, and it is warm, as if just taken off. You run all the way home and tell nobody how it felt.

choices.text: Ask the keeper why there is one sandal and not two

effects.log: Brother Ammet, who has been asked this ten thousand times, says the other is wherever the Maker last stood still. Then he gives you a honey cake for asking so seriously.

choices.text: Sell drawings of it to the pilgrims

effects.log: Your drawings of the sandal are bad and sell well. A pilgrim from the far coast buys six and asks you to sign them, which you do with a flourish.

events.text: A shepherd comes down to the temple with a sack. Inside is a sandal, the left one, dug out of a peat bog on the high moor. The priests sigh: it is the forty-first left sandal this century. But it looks exactly like the twin of the one under the glass.

choices.text: Ask to hold it

ok.log: It is warm in your hands, the way the other one was. The priests go quiet. The shepherd starts to cry and cannot say why, and you give the sandal back very carefully.

fail.log: It is cold leather and smells of bog, and that is all. The shepherd looks so crushed that you buy him a hot meal at the temple kitchen.

choices.text: Set the two side by side

effects.log: Side by side they are a pair: the stitching runs on from one to the other like a sentence. The priests cannot argue with it, and then they argue about it for a week.

choices.text: Tell the shepherd to keep it and wear it

effects.log: The shepherd wears it on market days. It wears out in a year, like any sandal. Perhaps it was only a sandal. Perhaps that was the point.

events.text: The Feast of Footsteps: the whole town files past the sandal. When your turn comes, the glass is lifted for cleaning, and Brother Ammet, distracted, holds the sandal out toward you for a moment, the way you hold out a coat to its owner.

choices.text: Take it, and put it on

effects.log: You put it on in front of everyone. It fits. The crowd goes silent, then laughs, deciding it is a joke. Brother Ammet does not laugh. He writes your name in a small black book.

choices.text: Give it back with both hands

effects.log: You bow and push it gently back toward him. Ammet blinks, as if waking, and sets it on its cushion. Afterwards he cannot remember why he held it out at all.

choices.text: Tell him a pair should walk, not sit

effects.log: Ammet looks at you, then at the sandals, then sets them both on the temple step with the toes toward the road. In the morning they are gone. Nobody is angry. The step smells of rain.

events.text: At the crossroads inn at Ostry a clay cup is chained to the well. It is ugly, lopsided and thumb-marked, and the priests swear the Maker made it in a hurry to drink the first rain. Anyone may drink from it. People say the water tastes of {pw_gift}, though nobody can agree what that tastes like.

choices.text: Drink from it

effects.log: The water tastes of nothing at all, and then, a moment later, of a morning you do not remember having. You sit on the well wall for an hour.

choices.text: Press your thumb into the thumb-marks

effects.log: The marks are deep and careless. Your thumb fits one exactly. You tell yourself everyone's does, and go and check three other people's thumbs, and theirs do not.

choices.text: Water the inn's horses with it, as a joke

effects.log: The horses drink, and then refuse every other bucket for a month. Dulcie Marr, who keeps the inn, makes you carry their water by hand until they forgive you.

events.text: The cup is stolen. The chain is cut clean through, and the whole crossroads is in uproar. At the inn there is a stranger in a long coat with very clean boots, who keeps asking, casually, about other relics: the comb at Quillon, the hand in the stone at Velling.

choices.text: Follow the clean boots at night

ok.log: The boots lead to a barn. Inside, on a cloth, are eleven ugly clay cups, all lopsided, all thumb-marked. One of them is the real one. Watching the stranger frown over them, you realise the thief does not know which.

fail.log: You trip over a goose in the dark. The goose has opinions. By morning the stranger is gone, and so are your boots.

choices.text: Tell Dulcie what you suspect

effects.log: Dulcie bars the doors and searches the stranger's room, and finds a tin of clay and a book of thumb-marks traced from relics all over {pw_world}. The stranger leaves through the privy window.

choices.text: Shrug: it was only a cup

effects.log: You drink from a tin mug instead. It tastes of tin. The crossroads mourns for a month, and you are faintly ashamed of being bored by it.

events.text: The thief is caught at the ford: a forger named Corvin Lusk, who has lived for twenty years on copies of holy things. The village drags him and all eleven cups back to the well. Nobody can tell which cup is real. Corvin, tied to the well-post, says cheerfully that nobody ever could.

choices.text: Pick up each cup until one is warm

effects.log: The tenth cup warms in your hand like another hand. The village cheers. Corvin stares at you with the pure envy of a craftsman and asks, very politely, how you did it.

choices.text: Fill all eleven and let everyone drink

effects.log: The crossroads drinks from eleven cups and everyone swears they tasted the real one. Corvin goes free, on condition that the ten fakes stay chained to the well, where they become holy by sheer use.

choices.text: Make Corvin choose

effects.log: Corvin picks a cup at once. Wrong. He picks again. Wrong. 'I never knew,' he says, honestly astonished. 'I just made them. I thought they all were.' He leaves Ostry a quieter man.

events.text: In the market at Quillon there is a stall that sells the Maker's comb. It sells, in fact, about thirty of them a week, carved from bone and pearwood, each with a parchment swearing it is the one true comb. The carver, {npc}, catches you laughing and asks, very seriously, what is wrong with the teeth.

choices.text: Say the teeth are perfect: it is the parchment that is funny

mem.note: laughed at my parchments with me

effects.log: {npc} reads the parchment aloud in a priest's voice until you both have to sit down. You leave with no comb and a reason to come back.

choices.text: Buy one

mem.note: bought a comb and meant it

effects.log: It is a lovely comb, whatever it is. You use it every morning, and every morning you think of the carver's careful hands.

choices.text: Point out that in the old paintings the Maker has no hair

mem.note: argued with me about the Maker

effects.log: {npc} laughs so hard a customer leaves. 'Nobody knows what the Maker had,' {npc} says. 'That is the whole business.'

events.text: Behind the stall, wrapped in oilcloth, {npc} shows you the thing that started it all: a real comb, very old, made of something like grey glass, with three teeth missing. It has come down through {npc}'s line from someone who swore it was found on the first morning of the world. Every copy is carved from memory of this one.

choices.text: Run it through your hair

mem.note: ran the old comb through your hair, and it knew you

effects.log: It catches nothing and glides like water. When you hand it back, {npc} is staring at your hair, which is lying, for once in your life, exactly as you want it.

choices.text: Help {npc} carve the copies

effects.log: Your copies are lopsided and sell best. {npc} says pilgrims trust a comb that looks as if it was made by somebody nervous.

choices.text: Tell {npc} to stop selling fakes

effects.log: {npc} stops for a month, then starts again with new parchments that say probably not the true comb. They sell twice as well. You are not sure whether you won.

events.text: A priest comes up from the great temple with an offer: a fortune in coins for the grey comb, to be kept under glass, and a charge of fraud against anyone still selling copies. {npc} looks at you, and not at the priest.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to marry you, and keep the comb between you

effects.log: You are married in the market with the stall for an altar and thirty comb sellers for witnesses. The grey comb lives in a kitchen drawer, which is where a comb belongs.

choices.text: Sell it to the temple and split the coins

effects.log: The comb goes under glass. {npc} buys a proper shop and carves honest combs with no parchment, and is happier, and a little sadder, and you are always welcome there.

choices.text: Tell the priest the comb is not holy, only old

mem.note: saved the stall with one comb

effects.log: The priest asks you to prove it. You run the comb through the priest's beard. The priest goes very still, then leaves without a word, and the charge is never brought.

events.text: On the road above Velling a boulder the size of a house carries the print of a right hand, sunk a finger deep, as if the stone had been soft as bread when it was pressed. Everyone in {pw_world} puts a hand in it at least once, to see how small they are.

choices.text: Put your hand in it

effects.log: Your hand is small in it, of course. But the stone under your palm hums, faint as a bee in a closed jar, and when you take your hand away the humming stops.

choices.text: Climb to the top of the boulder

effects.log: From the top you can see that the hand faces the sunrise, and that the road was built to pass it, not the other way round. You come down with scraped knees and a feeling of having been shown something.

choices.text: Count the coins the pilgrims leave in the cracks

effects.log: You count a hundred and four small coins and take none of them, which uses up all your strength of character for a week.

events.text: A stonemason from the temple guild arrives to cut the hand out of the boulder and carry it to the great temple, to be set in the wall. Half of Velling lines the road to stop it. The other half is selling them pies.

choices.text: Stand in front of the stone

effects.log: The mason, a reasonable woman named Hester Gall, looks at the crowd, at you and at her chisel, and decides the temple can come to the hand instead. Velling grows rich on pilgrims.

choices.text: Sell pies

effects.log: You sell pies to both sides. Your pies are the only thing everyone on the road agrees about.

choices.text: Put your hand in the print in front of the mason

effects.log: Your hand is no longer small in it. It fits to the knuckle. The hum rises to a note everyone on the road can hear. Hester Gall packs up her chisels without a word and goes home.

events.text: Years on, the stone has a roof over it and a priest who sells candles. One stormy night you shelter there and find, low on the far side and furred with moss, a second print: a left hand, smaller, pressed beside the first, as if two people had once leaned on the stone together.

choices.text: Put your left hand in it

effects.log: It fits a hand that is almost yours. You stay there until the storm passes, holding hands with no one, and walk home strangely comforted.

choices.text: Clear the moss and show the priest

effects.log: Within a month the second print has a heresy of its own: that the Maker did not make the world alone. The candle trade doubles.

choices.text: Put both your hands in both prints

effects.log: It should be impossible: the prints are a long arm's reach apart. The stone warms. For one breath you remember someone beside you at the making, laughing, and then you do not.

events.text: You are hired to copy scrolls in the archive under the great temple, for small coins and bad light. The archivist, Maud Penhallow, shows you the thing nobody copies: the First Draft, a map of {pw_world} drawn, the priests say, before the making. It is wrong. Rivers run where mountains stand, there is a great lake where the capital is, and in one corner a little island is marked only with a question.

choices.text: Copy it exactly, mistakes and all

effects.log: It takes you a month. By the end your hand moves over the wrong rivers as if it had drawn them before.

choices.text: Look for the question island on the new charts

effects.log: It is on none of them. Maud says the chartmakers have hunted it for three hundred years. 'Or,' she says, 'it was crossed out.'

choices.text: Laugh at it

effects.log: You laugh at the wrong rivers, and Maud laughs too. 'Yes,' she says. 'It is good to know the Maker had to try twice. It gives the rest of us hope.'

events.text: Working late, you notice the corrections. In the margins, in a quick hand, someone has argued with the map: too cold here, nobody would live. Move the river, it is lonely. And beside the great lake: no. They would drown in it. Give them a valley.

choices.text: Read every note

effects.log: By morning you know the reason for half the shape of the world. Some of the reasons are tender, some are lazy, and one is a joke about goats that makes you laugh out loud in the silent archive.

choices.text: Lay your own handwriting beside the margin

effects.log: You write too cold here on a scrap and set it beside the note. The two hands are the same. You burn the scrap in the lamp. You do not sleep.

choices.text: Tell Maud

effects.log: Maud has known for years. 'Everyone who copies it notices in the end,' she says. 'Most people decide not to have.'

events.text: The temple rules that the First Draft confuses the faithful and orders it locked away for good. On your last night with it, the lamp low, you see that the question island is no longer a question. In fresh ink it has a name, and the name is {name}.

choices.text: Take the map

effects.log: You roll it into your coat and walk out past the guard, who nods to you. It hangs in your room now, wrong and right at once, with your name in the corner.

choices.text: Add a correction of your own in the margin

effects.log: You write, in the same quick hand: not yet. Then: soon. The ink dries at once, as if it had been waiting. You feel the world shift a hair under your chair.

choices.text: Let them lock it up

effects.log: The door shuts on it. You can still feel the name in the corner of the map, like an itch between your shoulders. You decide to live with it.

events.text: Everyone in {pw_world} learns the Return by heart, even those who never learn to read: The Maker will come back by the low door, wearing a stranger's face, and will not know the way, and will ask it. The priests chant it at the Feast of Doors. Nobody agrees what the low door is.

choices.text: Decide the low door is being born

effects.log: You say so in temple school. The priest stares, writes it on the board, then rubs it out. 'That is one reading,' the priest says, and does not call on you again for a month.

choices.text: Hunt for low doors

effects.log: You spend a summer crawling through every low door in town: cellars, coal holes, a hollow oak. In the oak you find three owls and an old coin stamped with an open hand.

choices.text: Ask who has ever asked the way

effects.log: The priest says everybody has, which is the trouble with prophecy. You think about that for longer than you expected to.

events.text: The Feast of Doors. The custom is that anyone who asks the way tonight must be answered with kindness, in case. Strangers wander the town asking for directions they do not need, to be fed. You are asked the way eight times before supper.

choices.text: Answer every one, and walk them there

effects.log: Your feet ache by midnight. The last of the eight, an old woman, says at her door: 'You walk like someone who already knows the way.'

choices.text: Go out and ask the way yourself

effects.log: You ask a priest the way to the temple, which you know perfectly well. The priest begins to answer, falters, and stares at you for so long that a dog starts barking.

choices.text: Sell little maps to the askers

effects.log: You do a roaring trade in maps of a town everybody already lives in. It is the most honest dishonest money you have ever made.

events.text: An old priest of the Feast, Father Wendle, catches your sleeve in the street. 'There is one more line,' he whispers, 'the one we never chant. And will be shown the way by those it made, and will be glad of it.' He wants to know why he felt he had to tell you.

choices.text: Tell him you do not know the way

effects.log: 'Then I will show you,' he says, and does, step by step, to the oldest temple and the stair above its roof that you have never noticed. He weeps the whole time, and so, somehow, do you.

choices.text: Tell him he is an old fool

effects.log: He laughs, delighted. 'I am. I am. But the line is still true.' He goes off down the street humming it, and you find you are humming it too.

choices.text: Ask him to teach you the whole of it

effects.log: He teaches you every line, chanted and secret, over a winter of evenings. The Return sounds different in your mouth. He notices. He does not say so.

events.text: A child of seven called {npc} has begun making prophecies at the well, and every one comes true. Bucket will break. Goose is behind you. Nobody is going to like that soup. People have started to queue. {npc} points at you and announces, very loudly: You are late.

choices.text: Ask: late for what?

effects.log: {npc} considers this, picking at a scab. 'For the chair,' {npc} says, and then: 'Your shoe is undone.' It is.

choices.text: Give {npc} an apple and a talk about not frightening people

effects.log: {npc} takes the apple and listens politely. 'You will trip on the step,' {npc} says. You do.

choices.text: Ask for a prophecy about money

effects.log: 'Under the bench,' says {npc}. There are eight coins under the bench. You spend the rest of the day feeling watched by benches.

events.text: The temple has heard about {npc}. Two priests in good robes come to take the child to the great temple, to be trained as an oracle. {npc} hides behind your legs and says the priests are going to spill their tea, which they will.

choices.text: Let the priests take {npc}, gently

effects.log: {npc} goes, holding a priest's hand, and waves. Later you hear the great temple is having a terrible time: {npc} keeps prophesying who ate the cakes.

choices.text: Tell the priests the child's home is here

effects.log: The priests argue, then spill their tea, and take it as a sign, and leave. {npc} gives you a look of enormous approval.

choices.text: Ask {npc} what the priests will do next

effects.log: 'Go home,' says {npc}. They do, in a hurry: their own temple kitchen has caught fire, a small fire, the kind of fire a prophecy finds very funny.

events.text: {npc} is older now and has mostly stopped prophesying, to the relief of everyone with a goose. But one evening {npc} finds you and says, as if finishing a sentence from years ago: The chair is still empty. Somebody keeps dusting it.

choices.text: Ask where the chair is

effects.log: 'Up,' says {npc}, pointing above the temple roof at nothing. 'Up the stair. You knew that.' {npc} goes home for supper. You do not eat yours.

choices.text: Ask {npc} if it hurts to know things

effects.log: 'Only the soup ones,' says {npc}. 'The big ones are like weather. You just get wet.' You think it is the wisest thing anyone has ever said to you.

choices.text: Tell {npc} to stop it

effects.log: 'All right,' says {npc}. 'But your shoe is undone.' It is. It always is. You both laugh until the neighbours look out.

events.text: The prophet of Brannock, a gloomy woman named Ysolde Crane, announces that on the night of the next red moon the town will drown. She is so convincing that all of Brannock starts building rafts, which makes a little sense, and bailing its cellars in advance, which makes none.

choices.text: Build a raft on your roof

effects.log: The neighbours laugh, then copy you. By the red moon every roof in Brannock has a raft on it, like a hat.

choices.text: Help Ysolde store the cellar water in barrels on the square

effects.log: By the end of the month there are three hundred barrels of water in the square. Nobody knows why they are keeping it. Ysolde says the prophecy said to.

choices.text: Tell everyone it is nonsense

effects.log: Nobody listens. People preparing for the end of the world have no time for a voice of reason, especially one that is not helping with the rafts.

events.text: The red moon rises. Brannock sits on its roofs, on its rafts, in its best clothes, waiting to drown. It does not rain. Instead, at midnight, the bakery chimney catches, and the fire starts jumping from roof to roof toward the square.

choices.text: Roll out the barrels

effects.log: Three hundred barrels and the whole town in a line. The fire goes out with a hiss like a scolding, and Brannock, standing in the soaked square, is very nearly drowned. Ysolde Crane faints from vindication.

choices.text: Slide people off the burning roofs on your raft

ok.log: You ride the raft down the steep roofs like a sledge, with four neighbours clinging on. It is the most exciting thing that has ever happened in Brannock.

fail.log: The raft goes over the edge with you on it and you land in the duck pond. Everyone is safe. You are a pond.

choices.text: Run for the well

effects.log: You haul buckets until your arms give out. By dawn the fire is out and the bakery is gone, and nobody is hurt.

events.text: For a year the town argues about whether the prophecy came true. Ysolde says it obviously did: the town was drowned, with buckets. The priests say a prophecy cannot be right by accident. The baker says nobody asked him.

choices.text: Side with Ysolde

effects.log: Ysolde takes you as her apprentice in gloom. You learn to say terrible things very slowly. Your prophecies are never right, but they are always useful.

choices.text: Side with the priests

effects.log: The priests rule that a prophecy must come true in the way intended. The next prophet, who foretells a famine, is ignored. There is a famine. Nobody mentions it to you, which is worse.

choices.text: Help the baker rebuild with the barrels

effects.log: You build the new bakery out of three hundred barrels. It is round and odd and smells of bread and rain, and it becomes a little shrine to useful mistakes.

events.text: A prophecy in the great temple says the god will be born again as a mortal, under the sign of the open hand. The priests have found their candidate: Tobbin Ash, a baker's lad with a birthmark on his palm, who would very much like everyone to leave him alone. He lives on your street.

choices.text: Help Tobbin hide

effects.log: You hide Tobbin in your loft under a pile of onions. The priests search the street for three days, singing. Tobbin smells of onions for a month and is grateful anyway.

choices.text: Go and watch them crown him

effects.log: They crown him with laurel in the square. Tobbin looks at the crowd like a man looking at a bear. Then he sneezes, and everyone kneels.

choices.text: Look at your own palm

effects.log: Nothing there but the ordinary lines. You feel foolish, then watched, and then, for no reason you can name, you close your hand.

events.text: Tobbin is installed in the great temple as the Returned. The priests bring him the sick, the lost and the bankrupt. He cannot heal, find or pay anything. He writes to you, in bad spelling: they want me to make it rain. help.

choices.text: Go and coach him

effects.log: You teach Tobbin to gaze at the sky with great patience and say: not yet. He says it so well that it rains three days later anyway, and now he is more trapped than ever.

choices.text: Tell the priests he is only a baker

ok.log: The high priest listens, sighs, and admits they had their doubts when he burned the holy bread. Tobbin is released with a small pension and a lifelong horror of laurel.

fail.log: The priests decide you are a heretic sent to test him. Tobbin stays. You are banned from the temple for a year.

choices.text: Send him a loaf every week

effects.log: You bake a loaf every week and send it up, so he remembers who he is. He writes back that it is the only real thing in the place.

events.text: Tobbin comes home at last, released or escaped, nobody is quite sure. He finds you in the street, takes your hand, turns it over and looks at your palm for a long time. 'They had the wrong one,' he says. 'I could feel it every time they knelt. Like being given somebody else's coat.'

choices.text: Close your hand, and ask him to keep the secret

effects.log: Tobbin nods and goes back to baking. Every morning after, a small loaf is left on your step with an open hand pressed into the crust.

choices.text: Laugh it off

effects.log: Tobbin laughs too, with pure relief. 'Good. Then it is nobody, and I can bake.' He bakes for forty years, very happily, and never wears laurel again.

choices.text: Put up the money for his new ovens

effects.log: The bakery opens under the sign of The Wrong One. It sells out every morning, and pilgrims come from far away to buy bread from the god who said no.

events.text: In a junk shop in Low Tessary you find a little book bound in green cloth: The Book of Small Things. You open it at random. It says: Today {name} will open this book at random, and will not buy it, and will come back.

choices.text: Buy it at once, to spite it

effects.log: You buy it to prove it wrong. On the walk home you open it again. It says: Bought me to spite me. Fair.

choices.text: Put it down and leave

effects.log: You are halfway home before you turn back. It is still lying open on the counter, at a new page, which says: Told you. The shopkeeper gives it to you for nothing, to be rid of it.

choices.text: Read further

effects.log: The next page lists your supper (turnips), who will knock at your door tonight (nobody, then a cat) and the exact moment you will stub your toe. All true. You take the book home.

events.text: The book has never once been wrong about you. It knows which shirt you will pick, which way you will turn at the fork, whether you will laugh at a joke. It is less a prophecy than a very nosy friend. This morning's page says: {name} will choose the left-hand door.

choices.text: Choose the right-hand door

effects.log: You go through the right-hand door, triumphant. The page now reads: {name} chose the right door, as planned, to prove a point. The book has very good manners about winning.

choices.text: Choose the left, to see why

effects.log: Behind the left-hand door is a shop you never noticed, selling the hat you lost three years ago. Not a hat like it. The hat.

choices.text: Choose no door and sit on the step

effects.log: You sit on the step all morning. The book says nothing at all about this. The page is blank. You have never been so pleased with yourself.

events.text: You reach the last page of the Book of Small Things. The ink is fresher than the rest. It says: And then {name} will close the book, and choose something large, and nobody will have written it down.

choices.text: Close the book

effects.log: You close it. The green cloth is warm. You put it on a high shelf, and the days after that feel unwritten and enormous.

choices.text: Turn back to the blank page from the morning on the step

effects.log: It is not blank now. In a quick hand you somehow know, it says: This is where I could not see you. This is where you stop being something I made. You find you are smiling.

choices.text: Write on the last page yourself

effects.log: You write: And then {name} had a cup of tea. You have a cup of tea. It is the best cup of tea of your life.

events.text: Once in a life, the faithful of {pw_world} are meant to walk to the Cradle, the place of the first making, at the far end of {pw_land}. It takes most people a year. Some take ten. A company of pilgrims leaves your town at the spring thaw, singing.

choices.text: Walk with them

effects.log: You take a staff, a blanket and a bag of dried pears. On the first night, footsore already, you are happier than you have been in years.

choices.text: Give them bread for the road

effects.log: The pilgrims bless you for the bread and sing you a walking song from the gate. You hum it for weeks, and one morning you find you have packed a bag.

choices.text: Say you will go when you are older

effects.log: Everybody says that. You say it too, and the pilgrims nod kindly, having heard it in every town. The road waits. It is good at waiting.
