events.text: The road. Months of it. Bridges built by pilgrims, wells dug by pilgrims, and at every milestone a cairn, one stone for every walker who has ever passed. The company grows and shrinks. Your shoes are on their third soles.

choices.text: Add a stone to every cairn

effects.log: Thousands of stones, and after a while you start to recognise the hands that stacked them: a careful one, a hurried one, one that always picks white.

choices.text: Carry a lame pilgrim's pack as well as your own

effects.log: Your shoulders never forgive you, and the old pilgrim never stops telling the company you are a saint, which is worse.

choices.text: Take the shortcut over the pass

ok.log: The pass is clear. You reach the next town two weeks early, sunburnt and smug, and wait for the others with your feet in a horse trough.

fail.log: Snow. You come down the far side three days later with two frostbitten toes and about as much new wisdom.

events.text: The Cradle at last. It is a valley, very green and very ordinary, with a temple at its mouth and pilgrims everywhere, weeping, singing, selling. In the middle is the Place: a ring of white posts around a patch of bare earth. Nothing grows there. Nothing ever has.

choices.text: Step over the posts when nobody is looking

effects.log: The bare earth is warm through your thin soles. You take up a pinch of it. It runs through your fingers as if it were still deciding what to be. You keep a little in a twist of cloth.

choices.text: Pray at the posts with everyone else

effects.log: The prayers of ten thousand pilgrims go up around you like a roar, and under the roar you feel something listening, very carefully, to all of it.

choices.text: Ask a priest why nothing grows

effects.log: 'Because it is finished,' the priest says. 'Everything else is still being made.' You chew on that all the way home.

events.text: Home. Your town comes out to meet you, because a returned pilgrim is good luck. Children want to touch your staff. Old people want to know if it was worth it. You notice you walk differently now, as if the ground were a friend.

choices.text: Tell them it was worth it

effects.log: They cheer and carry your bag and feed you for a week. You tell the story so often it grows a mountain it never had.

choices.text: Tell them the truth: it was only a valley

effects.log: Some are disappointed. One old man laughs until he cries, and says that is exactly what his grandmother said, and she was the holiest person he ever knew.

choices.text: Plant a seed in the earth you carried home

effects.log: You plant a pear seed in it, in a pot. In a week it is a little tree in full fruit, in the middle of winter. Your town calls it a miracle. You call it a hint.

events.text: On the pilgrim road every inn is named for a step of the making, and every inn keeps one bed empty for the Maker, in case. The Seventh Step, a crooked inn at a river crossing, is going cheap, because the last owner kept giving the Maker's bed to people who said they were the Maker.

choices.text: Buy the Seventh Step

effects.log: You own an inn, a leaking roof, an empty holy bed and a goat. The goat came with the deeds and will not discuss it.

choices.text: Work there as the cook

effects.log: The new owner, Mother Grisel, pays badly and feeds you well. You learn pilgrim soup, which is mostly onions and hope.

choices.text: Stay one night, as a pilgrim

effects.log: You sleep in a room with nine snoring pilgrims and wake rested, which feels like the first miracle of the road.

events.text: Pilgrim season. The Seventh Step is full to the rafters: a choir that will not stop rehearsing, a merchant who wants a discount for holiness, two runaway lovers, and, at midnight, a knock, and a small shabby stranger asking for the Maker's bed.

choices.text: Give the stranger the Maker's bed

effects.log: The stranger sleeps like a stone and leaves before dawn, and pays with a coin nobody in {pw_world} has ever seen, stamped with an open hand.

choices.text: Ask the stranger to prove it

effects.log: The stranger thinks about it, then looks at the leaking roof, and the leak stops. Or the rain does. It is hard to tell. You hand over the bed with a bow.

choices.text: Give the bed to the runaway lovers

effects.log: An angry uncle finds them by morning, and they are married in the yard on the spot. The goat attends. It is the best wedding the inn has ever had.

choices.text: Put the stranger in the stable

effects.log: The stranger sleeps with the goat and leaves no coin. You charge the goat rent. The goat does not pay either.

events.text: Years of pilgrims. The Seventh Step has a name on the road now: the inn where they leave the light on. One night, the season over and the inn empty, you sit down on the Maker's bed yourself, for the first time, just to see.

choices.text: Lie down on it

effects.log: You sleep better than you ever have. In the morning the bed is made, very neatly, the way you have never once made a bed in your life.

choices.text: Lay the stranger's coin on the pillow

effects.log: The coin warms, and for a moment it shows not a hand but your own face, younger and older at once. Then it is a coin again, and you sit very still until dawn.

choices.text: Get up and keep it empty, as is right

effects.log: You smooth the blanket and leave the lamp burning. Pilgrims say the Seventh Step is the only inn on the road where the empty bed feels occupied.

events.text: On the pilgrim road a stranger falls into step beside you: {npc}, who has walked to the Cradle eleven times and back ten, is going for the twelfth, and talks about feet the way poets talk about the moon.

choices.text: Walk with {npc}

effects.log: By the end of the week you know three hundred things about blisters and one or two about the stars. {npc} walks exactly one pace behind you, always.

choices.text: Ask {npc} why eleven times

effects.log: 'I keep missing something,' {npc} says. 'Every time I get there, it feels as if it has just left.'

choices.text: Walk faster

effects.log: You lose {npc} at a ford. Two days later {npc} catches you up again, unhurried, holding out a pear.

events.text: Fever on the road. {npc} is burning up in a barn at the edge of a village that wants no sick strangers, and says between shivers that you should go on. 'The road is the point. Not the walker.'

choices.text: Stay and nurse {npc}

effects.log: You stay nine days. On the tenth {npc} sits up, eats a whole loaf, and says you have the bedside manner of a goat, which from {npc} is high praise.

choices.text: Run to the next town for a healer

ok.log: You run eleven miles and come back in a cart with a complaining healer. {npc} is up in three days.

fail.log: You get lost and come back with only willow bark. It works, slowly. {npc} says the bark was the right choice all along.

choices.text: Go on, as {npc} said

effects.log: At the Cradle you light a candle for {npc}. A month later {npc} walks up behind you at the posts, thin and grinning.

events.text: The Cradle. {npc} stands at the white posts for a long time, then turns and looks at you instead of at the bare earth. 'Huh,' says {npc}. 'Twelve times. It was walking next to me.'

choices.text: Ask {npc} what that means

effects.log: 'Nothing,' says {npc}. 'Everything. I will tell you on the way home.' {npc} never quite does, but all the way home {npc} keeps a pace behind you, the way people walk behind what they have followed a long way.

choices.text: Tell {npc} it needs a thirteenth try

effects.log: {npc} laughs so loudly the priests turn round. 'Thirteen, then. You are coming.' You both know you will.

choices.text: Give {npc} your walking staff

effects.log: {npc} holds it like a relic. You both know it is a stick. It is the most precious stick in {pw_world} from that day on.

events.text: Years later a message comes: {npc} has walked the road one last time, slowly, and will not be coming back from the Cradle, and would like you to have a pair of very old boots.

choices.text: Wear the boots

effects.log: They fit. They have walked twelve times to the end of the world, and they take you to market and back without a word of complaint. You think of {npc} with every step.

choices.text: Walk the road once more, for {npc}

effects.log: You walk it in the old boots. At the posts you say the name {npc} out loud, and a wind goes through the valley, warm, like someone answering.

choices.text: Hang the boots by your door

effects.log: Passing pilgrims touch them for luck. You never tell them whose boots they were. They were {npc}'s.

events.text: Past the last village on the eastern road, past where the pilgrim road officially ends, there is said to be another holy place: the Seat. Not a temple. A stone. The god sat on it once, after the making, to rest. The priests do not mention it. Old pilgrims will tell you the way for a drink.

choices.text: Buy an old pilgrim a drink

effects.log: The old pilgrim drinks it slowly and draws you a map on the table in spilled cider: a hill, a stone, and an arrow that says up.

choices.text: Look for it with no directions

effects.log: You wander the hills for a week and find a hundred stones. Any of them could be it. You sit on all of them, to be sure, and none of them is right.

choices.text: Decide some places should stay unfound

effects.log: You go home. But you find yourself, on quiet evenings, looking east, the way you look toward a room someone has just left.

events.text: You find it, in the end. The Seat is a plain grey stone at the top of a bare hill, knee-high, flat on top, worn a little in the middle. No carving, no altar, no priest. Someone has left a wildflower on it. The view is of the whole of {pw_world}, or feels like it.

choices.text: Sit on it

effects.log: It is exactly the right height, and the hollow is exactly the right shape. You sit until dark, looking at everything, feeling that it is good.

choices.text: Leave a flower too

effects.log: You pick a blue one from the slope and lay it beside the other. On the way down you meet three strangers coming up, each carrying a flower, none of them saying why.

choices.text: Count the smoke of the towns below

effects.log: You count the smoke of forty towns and lose count. Every one of them is cooking supper. You feel, absurdly, proud of them.

events.text: You come back to the Seat more often than you can explain. One spring a goatherd girl is sitting on it, eating cheese. She looks up at you, unbothered. 'Oh,' she says. 'Is this yours? It feels like somebody's.'

choices.text: Say it is everyone's

effects.log: She shuffles over. You share the stone and the cheese and the view. A seat for one, it turns out, holds two quite well.

choices.text: Say yes, it is yours

effects.log: She gets up at once and brushes off the crumbs, the way you would for a host. As you sit, the hill sighs under you, very softly, like a dog that has waited a long time by a door.

choices.text: Leave her to it

effects.log: You walk back down. It is a good stone. Somebody should be sitting on it, and today it is her.

events.text: In the back room of a dyer's shop meets a small forbidden heresy called the Footfolk. Their belief is simple: the god is not on the throne. The god climbed down, and was born, and is walking among us as somebody's neighbour, not knowing. They meet to look at each other's faces, hopefully.

choices.text: Go to a meeting

effects.log: They are dyers, mostly, with blue hands. They look at your face with such hope that you feel you are letting them down by being only you.

choices.text: Report them to the temple

effects.log: The temple pays you a small reward and fines the dyer. The heresy grows by forty people that week, out of spite.

choices.text: Laugh it off

effects.log: A god who does not know it is a god, you say to a friend. Ridiculous. Your friend says that is exactly what such a god would say. You have no answer.

events.text: The Footfolk have a test. Not a holy one: they made it up. They ask every newcomer three questions. What did you dream the night you were born? What does the world smell like when you are sad? Why does the river bend at the old mill?

choices.text: Answer honestly

ok.log: You answer the third without thinking: because the first miller liked to sleep late, and the bend slows the water. The room goes silent. Then the eldest dyer starts to cry.

fail.log: You say you do not know, and they nod kindly: nobody ever knows. They give you a cup of blue tea.

choices.text: Make up answers to cheer them up

effects.log: Your answers are wonderful and completely invented. The Footfolk are thrilled for a week, then suspicious, then sad.

choices.text: Ask what their own answers were

effects.log: Every one of them took the test once, hoping. They tell you their answers. Some are beautiful. None of them is right, and all of them are true.

events.text: The temple raids the dyer's shop. The Footfolk scatter through the back door, and the eldest, old Ama Teague, is caught on the step. She looks at you across the yard. She does not say a word. She does not have to.

choices.text: Walk over and stand beside her

effects.log: The temple guards look at you, at Ama, and at you again. The youngest lowers his staff without being told. Ama is let go. She never says why. She only bows to you in the street, every day, for the rest of her life.

choices.text: Speak for her to the priests

effects.log: You plead that she is old and harmless. She is fined a bolt of blue cloth, and sends you a scarf cut from it.

choices.text: Look away

effects.log: Ama is fined and released and never speaks to you again, and you see her blue hands in your sleep.

events.text: A philosopher named Dorrow Pike stands on a barrel in the market every morning and proves there is no god. He has eleven proofs. People pay to hear them, because they are funny, and because Dorrow is so happy about it. Today it is proof four: if there were a god, why would there be wasps?

choices.text: Heckle him

effects.log: 'Wasps eat the flies,' you shout. Dorrow beams, delighted to be argued with, and the market has its best morning in years.

choices.text: Tell him why there are wasps

effects.log: You hear yourself explain, quite precisely, why there are wasps: something to do with figs. You have no idea where it came from. Dorrow writes it down.

choices.text: Pay a coin and hear all eleven

effects.log: They are good proofs. You go home nearly convinced, and a sparrow lands on your windowsill and stares at you as if personally offended.

events.text: Dorrow Pike is in trouble. The temple has charged him with heresy, the serious kind: he must recant on the temple steps or leave the city. He does not seem worried. He asks you to come and watch, and to bring a cushion, since recanting takes a long time.

choices.text: Go and stand by him

effects.log: You stand by him on the steps with a cushion. He recants for two hours, at length and with footnotes, and the crowd applauds.

choices.text: Help him write a recantation that is secretly proof twelve

effects.log: It is so clever the priests accept it, and only realise a week later that it proved them wrong. They are far too embarrassed to say so.

choices.text: Stay home

effects.log: You hear later that he recanted beautifully, with eleven reasons, and everyone cried, and he winked at the high priest.

events.text: Dorrow is old now, and ill, and has run out of proofs. He sends for you. 'I have been thinking,' he says from his narrow bed. 'If there were a god, and it heard me all those years, mocking it from a barrel. Would it mind?'

choices.text: Tell him the god would have loved it

effects.log: Dorrow laughs, and coughs, and laughs. 'Good. I would have hated a god with no sense of humour.' He goes that week, unconverted and content.

choices.text: Tell him there is a god, and it listened, and took notes

effects.log: He looks at you a long time. 'You,' he says. 'Of course. You always argued as if you had made the thing.' He holds your hand and is not afraid at all.

choices.text: Tell him there is no god, to comfort him

effects.log: 'Liar,' says Dorrow fondly. 'But a kind one.' He sleeps, smiling.

events.text: A weaver named Lysette Orm is on trial in the temple court. Her crime: a hanging that showed the god as a mortal on a doorstep, mending a shoe. It has been burned, and the court needs witnesses who saw it. You saw it. You remember it was beautiful, and that the face on the doorstep looked tired and kind.

choices.text: Agree to bear witness

effects.log: You give your name to the clerk. That night you try to remember the face exactly, and find it is easy, much too easy.

choices.text: Pretend you never saw it

effects.log: The summons goes to your neighbour, who saw it too and remembers it as ugly. You realise you will have to go anyway, if only to correct him.

choices.text: Weave a copy from memory before you forget

effects.log: You are no weaver. Your copy is a lumpy rag. But the doorstep is right, and the shoe, and the face.

events.text: The court: three priests in grey, a crowd at the back, Lysette at the rail with her hands folded. The question put to you is simple. Did the hanging show the god as a mortal?

choices.text: Say yes: it was the truest picture of the god you have ever seen

effects.log: The crowd gasps. The eldest priest asks, drily, how many pictures of the god you have seen. 'Enough,' you say, and somehow it lands like a stone in a pond.

choices.text: Say the figure could have been anyone

effects.log: It is true, and it is a way out, and the court seizes it. Lysette looks at you with relief and a little disappointment.

choices.text: Unroll your lumpy copy before the court

effects.log: Your rag is so bad the court laughs, and the laugh breaks the solemnity. The eldest priest stops laughing first, staring at the face. 'Who sat for this?' Nobody answers.

events.text: The verdict: guilty. Lysette is sentenced to weave a new hanging for the temple, the god as the priests describe it, enthroned in glory. She comes to you afterwards with one question. What does the god look like, really?

choices.text: Sit for her

effects.log: You sit on her doorstep for a week, mending a shoe. The hanging she weaves shows the god enthroned in glory, with your tired face. The priests think it a marvel and hang it above the altar.

choices.text: Tell her to weave whatever she likes

effects.log: She weaves the god enthroned in glory, with one bare foot and a shoe beside it, half mended. Nobody notices but the two of you.

choices.text: Tell her to do as the priests say

effects.log: It is a fine hanging and a dull one. She is paid well. She never weaves a face again.

events.text: Beyond the river stands a school the temple pretends not to see: the Lantern House. It teaches that the god was not born a god, but was once a person who learned, and that the first law, that {pw_law}, is not a command but a lesson left behind. Its best teacher, {npc}, is lecturing nine students and a cat when you wander in by mistake.

choices.text: Stay and listen

effects.log: You stay three hours. {npc} teaches as if every idea were a lamp being passed hand to hand, and you leave with your head full of light.

choices.text: Argue with {npc} from the back

mem.note: argued with me from the back

effects.log: {npc} loves being argued with. The lecture runs two hours over, and the cat leaves in disgust, and neither of you notices.

choices.text: Slip out quietly

effects.log: At the door you hear {npc} say, to the cat, 'That one will be back.' You are annoyed to find that it is true.

events.text: A year of evenings at the Lantern House. {npc} has a theory that the world has mistakes in it on purpose, so the people would have something to mend. You have a strange certainty about which mistakes were meant and which were not.

choices.text: Tell {npc} which mistakes were real

effects.log: {npc} writes down every word, staring at you. 'How do you know the marsh was an accident?' You do not know how you know.

choices.text: Walk with {npc} by the river at night

effects.log: You talk about nothing at all, for hours. It is the best nothing you have ever talked about.

choices.text: Teach a class yourself

mem.note: taught a class at my school

effects.log: Your class is about why the hills are the shape they are. It is wildly popular and slightly frightening. {npc} sits at the back and does not take notes.

events.text: The temple sends word: the Lantern House is to close, and {npc} is to be sent to the far end of {pw_land} with whichever students will follow. {npc} comes to your door at night with a lantern and one bag.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to marry you, and go together

effects.log: You are married by lantern light by a ferryman who turns out to be a heretic too. You take the school to the far end of the world in a cart, with the cat.

choices.text: Hide {npc} and the books in your cellar

effects.log: {npc} lives in your cellar among four hundred forbidden books for a season, until the temple forgets. It is the happiest cellar in {pw_world}.

choices.text: Go to the temple and argue for the school

ok.log: You argue for three hours. In the end the high priest, worn out, lets the school stay, on condition that the cat is registered as a priest.

fail.log: They close it anyway. You walk with {npc} to the edge of town, and then further than you meant to.

events.text: You have started dreaming of the making. Not every night: on nights before rain. In the dream there is nothing, and it is not dark, because there is no dark yet either, and you are bored, and lonely, and you put out a hand.

choices.text: Write the dream down in the morning

effects.log: You write it in a cheap notebook. Reading it back at breakfast, you notice you wrote I, and not you, all the way through.

choices.text: Tell the temple priest

effects.log: The priest says many of the faithful dream of the making, and gives you a herb tea to stop it. The tea is pleasant and does nothing.

choices.text: Ignore it

effects.log: You ignore the dreams. The dreams do not ignore you.

events.text: The dreams go on. Last night you made {pw_gift}, and it was harder than the songs say: it came out wrong twice, and you laughed at it, and started again. You woke with your hands warm, smelling of something that has no name in any tongue spoken in {pw_world}.

choices.text: Try to dream on purpose

effects.log: You lie down at noon with the curtains drawn. You dream of the first people waking and looking at you, and of not knowing what to say to them. You wake with a headache and a lump in your throat.

choices.text: Draw what you made

effects.log: You draw it on the kitchen wall in charcoal. Your neighbour sees it and goes pale: it is the exact shape in the oldest temple window, which you have never seen.

choices.text: Go for a long walk instead

effects.log: You walk until the smell fades from your hands. It takes all day. The world, on the way, looks oddly like a finished piece of work.

events.text: The last dream. The making is done. You sit down somewhere high, tired and pleased, and look at all of it, and then you do the thing the songs never mention: you get up and leave without saying goodbye. In the dream you know why. You wake before you can remember.

choices.text: Go back to sleep and make yourself remember

effects.log: You remember. You left so that they could grow without you watching. You came back because they did, and you missed them. You dress, walk to the oldest temple, and look up past its roof at a stair you have never seen before.

choices.text: Get up and say goodbye to someone, properly

effects.log: You visit an old friend to say goodbye before a journey you are not taking. They are puzzled and touched. You feel lighter, as if an old debt had been paid.

choices.text: Let it go

effects.log: It was a dream, mostly. You make breakfast. The bread rises unusually well.

events.text: It starts at market. You are haggling over turnips and you say, in a voice that is not quite yours, deep as a well: Let it be. The turnip seller sits down hard on the cobbles. Every turnip on the stall is suddenly perfect.

choices.text: Help the seller up and pretend it was a cough

effects.log: You cough theatrically for a week to keep the story straight. Nobody believes you, and everybody wants your turnips.

choices.text: Try the voice again at home, alone

ok.log: You say Let it be to a wilted plant. It stands up. You sit down.

fail.log: You say Let it be to a wilted plant in your own ordinary voice. It stays wilted. You feel foolish and relieved.

choices.text: Buy all the perfect turnips

effects.log: You eat the best turnips of your life for a month. They taste of the first harvest, the one in the songs.

events.text: The voice comes when it likes. At a funeral it says Rest, and the mourners sleep through the night for the first time in weeks. At a quarrel it says Enough, and both sides forget what it was about. People have started crossing the street to stand near you, or to avoid you.

choices.text: Learn to keep it in

effects.log: You learn to hum when you feel it rising, low, like holding a lid on a pot. People think you are very musical.

choices.text: Use it on purpose, for small good things

effects.log: A stuck cart rolls free. A lost child turns round and walks home. You keep it small. Even small, it makes your throat ache like a held song.

choices.text: Use it to win an argument with your landlord

effects.log: Your landlord lowers your rent for a year and cannot remember why, and keeps lowering it, puzzled, out of habit.

events.text: A priest from the great temple comes to hear the voice for herself, sceptical. She asks you to say the oldest prayer, the one whose ending nobody knows. You open your mouth to tell her you do not know it either.

choices.text: Let the voice finish it

effects.log: The voice says the prayer, and then the end of it, which is not a prayer at all but an answer: I hear you. I am coming up the stair. The priest is on her knees before the last word. She tells you where the stair is.

choices.text: Say in your own voice that you do not know

effects.log: The priest looks oddly relieved. 'Good,' she says. 'It would be a great deal of trouble if you did.'

choices.text: Hum instead

effects.log: You hum. The priest weeps, without knowing why, and leaves a coin on your step on the way out.

events.text: Every child in {pw_world} learns the first law: that {pw_law}. It is carved over every temple door and stitched on every cradle cloth. You have read it ten thousand times. Today, passing a temple door, you read it again, and for the first time it sounds like something you said.

choices.text: Stop and read it again

effects.log: You read it until the doorkeeper asks if you are ill. The words sit in your mouth like your own name.

choices.text: Hurry past, unsettled

effects.log: You hurry past. All day the law follows you, quietly, like a dog that has decided you are its person.

choices.text: Ask the doorkeeper who wrote it

effects.log: The doorkeeper says nobody wrote it: it was simply true one morning. 'Like a name,' the doorkeeper says, 'before anyone has called you by it.'

events.text: The law has started to show itself to you. In small things: the market, the road, the way rain falls. You see it working the way a carpenter sees the joints in a table, and you see where it was hard to make it fit, and where you cheated a little.

choices.text: Look for the place where it was cheated

ok.log: You find it in an old orchard: one tree where the law bends, where long ago you made an exception out of pity. You remember the pity. You remember whose tree it was.

fail.log: You look for a year and find nothing but the law, everywhere, holding.

choices.text: Leave it alone

effects.log: Some things should not be looked at too long, the way you should not stare at your own handwriting until it turns strange.

choices.text: Explain the law to a child

effects.log: You explain it so well that the child explains it back to you, better. You feel, oddly, that you have been graded.

events.text: At the temple school a teacher asks the pupils, as always, why the first law says that {pw_law}. As always, the pupils answer: because the Maker said so. You are at the back by chance, and you hear yourself answer instead.

choices.text: Give the real reason

effects.log: You tell them the real reason. It is short and not very grand, and the pupils nod, because it makes sense. The teacher, white to the lips, closes the school for the day and takes you by the arm to the oldest temple, and shows you the stair.

choices.text: Say: because the Maker said so

effects.log: It is true, after all. Just not all of it. The teacher nods and moves on, and you keep the rest.

choices.text: Say: because it seemed a good idea at the time

effects.log: The pupils laugh. The teacher does not. You acquire a reputation, and a small, devoted following of eight-year-olds.

events.text: The Maker's Stair is steeper than anything in the songs, and you are a mortal with mortal knees. On a landing halfway up, a woman sits mending a net: a priest of the stair, she says, who has never seen the top. She asks you, without looking up, why you want it back.

choices.text: Say: because it is yours

effects.log: 'Mine,' she repeats, knotting. 'A child's reason. But children are often right.' She moves over to make room on the step.

choices.text: Say: you are not sure that you do

effects.log: She looks up for the first time. 'Good,' she says. 'Sit. Help with the net.'

choices.text: Say: because they pray, and nobody answers

effects.log: She is quiet a long while. 'Somebody hears,' she says. 'Hearing is not the hard part.'

events.text: Her test is not the one the priests below promised. She asks you to mend the net, and that is all. It takes you all day, and your fingers bleed. When you finish, she cuts a hole in it with a little knife and asks you to mend it again.

choices.text: Mend it again

effects.log: You mend it again, and again, for three days. On the third she stops cutting, and you understand: a world is a net, always torn somewhere, and whoever made it does not get to stop.

choices.text: Refuse, and climb on

effects.log: You climb past her. She does not stop you. Behind you she says, to the net, 'That one will be back.'

choices.text: Ask her to show you how she does it

effects.log: She shows you a knot that cannot slip. Your mending improves a great deal. Your doubts do not.

events.text: Night on the stair. Below you every lamp in {pw_world} is lit, a field of small fires. You could go down. Nobody would know. You would live a short mortal life and die of something ordinary, and be mourned by a few people who knew your face, which is more than the god ever was.

choices.text: Go on up

effects.log: You go on up. It is not courage. It is that the lamps below look as if they are waiting.

choices.text: Go on up, carrying the net

effects.log: You climb with the torn net over your shoulder. It will need mending at the top, too. That, it turns out, is the reason, and it is enough.

choices.text: Sit and watch the lamps until dawn

effects.log: You watch them go out one by one into morning. You love them. That settles it, more or less.

events.text: You are not alone on the Maker's Stair. Three flights above you a man in white robes is climbing and singing hymns about himself. He is Aurel Vantine. He has two hundred followers camped below and a certificate from a country temple that says he is the Returned.

choices.text: Catch him up and introduce yourself

effects.log: 'Ah, a pilgrim,' Aurel says warmly, and gives you his blessing, and a pamphlet about himself with a very flattering drawing.

choices.text: Let him go on ahead

effects.log: Let him reach the top first. You want to see what the stair does with a wrong one.

choices.text: Race him

ok.log: You pass him on the forty-ninth flight, which is very undignified for you both. He reaches the next landing purple and furious.

fail.log: He is fitter than he looks. You reach the landing to find him eating a pear, smug.

events.text: The stair tests Aurel. You watch it happen: the steps under his feet grow, one by one, until each is as high as a wall, and he is climbing them with his hands, weeping, still singing. The steps under yours stay ordinary steps.

choices.text: Help him up

effects.log: You haul Aurel up three steps the height of a house. He weighs a great deal for a god. He thanks you through tears, and whispers to ask why your steps are small.

choices.text: Tell him gently to go home

effects.log: 'It does not want you,' you say, as kindly as you can. Aurel sits on a giant step and looks down at his two hundred, very far below, very small.

choices.text: Climb on past him

effects.log: You climb on. His singing follows you for a long time, thinner and thinner, and then stops.

events.text: You find Aurel Vantine sitting on a landing. He has stopped climbing. His robes are torn, and without the hymns he looks younger. 'I wanted it to be me,' he says. 'Not the throne. Just, for something to be me.'

choices.text: Tell him the world is already his, like everyone's

effects.log: He laughs, a real laugh, and wipes his face on his sleeve. He goes down to his two hundred and tells them the truth, and most of them stay with him anyway, which surprises him more than anything.

choices.text: Promise to send him a sign one day

effects.log: 'You can do that?' he asks. You do not know yet. You promise anyway, and he goes down the stair holding the promise like a lamp.

choices.text: Leave him to his thoughts

effects.log: Some people need to go down a stair alone. You go up.

events.text: Since the throne, you hear the prayers. All of them. They come like rain on a roof: soft, constant, and mostly about weather, money and goats. You are still a mortal with a body that needs sleep, and you have not slept well in a month.

choices.text: Learn to hear them one at a time

effects.log: It is like learning to hear one voice in a crowded hall. The first you hear clearly is a girl in the south, praying for her goat to come home.

choices.text: Ask them, in your sleep, to pray more quietly

effects.log: Next morning priests all over {pw_world} announce a revelation: the god prefers whispering. The temples go hushed. You sleep like a stone.

choices.text: Stuff your ears with wax

effects.log: It does nothing, of course. But you feel you have taken a stand.

events.text: The goat girl again. Every evening, the same prayer: please bring Bramble home. You know where Bramble is: stuck on a ledge above a gorge two valleys over, alive and bleating. You could move a stone, or a wind, or a dream.

choices.text: Send the girl a dream of the ledge

effects.log: She wakes, runs two valleys at dawn and carries Bramble home on her shoulders. Her prayer that night is two words, thank you, and it is very loud.

choices.text: Walk two valleys over and fetch the goat yourself

effects.log: You climb down with a rope, like any mortal, and haul a furious goat up by the horns. You leave it at her gate with no note. Some answers should have mud on them.

choices.text: Do nothing

effects.log: Bramble finds the way home alone three days later, thin and proud. The girl stops praying for goats and starts praying for courage. You are not sure that was better. You are not sure it was worse.

events.text: You understand now why the god was silent so long. For every prayer you could answer there are ten thousand more, and every answer changes the next ten thousand. Tonight one town prays for rain and the next town prays for a dry harvest.

choices.text: Give both what they want: rain at night, sun by day

effects.log: It takes all your attention and a kind of arithmetic you had forgotten you could do. Both towns are happy. You sleep until noon.

choices.text: Answer neither, and let the world keep its own weather

effects.log: The weather does what weather does. Both towns grumble, and both survive. Silence that is chosen, you find, feels nothing like silence that is only absence.

choices.text: Go to both towns as a mortal and help them share the water

effects.log: You spend a summer arguing about ditches in two village halls. In the end they dig a channel together, and nobody prays about it at all. It is your best miracle yet.

events.text: The Feast of the Maker comes round, as it has for {pw_years} years. Every one of the {pw_temples} temples will carry a giant painted figure of you through the streets, and your neighbours expect you to come along and throw petals at yourself.

choices.text: Go, and throw petals

effects.log: You throw petals at a figure of yourself twenty feet high, with a beard you never had and a stern look you hope you never wear. A child beside you says it does not look much like the god. You agree warmly.

choices.text: Volunteer to help carry the figure

effects.log: You carry your own left foot down the high street with eleven other people. It is heavier than you deserve.

choices.text: Stay home and pretend to be ill

effects.log: The whole procession passes your window singing your praises, and you hide under a blanket, mortified.

events.text: The play. Every year the temple players act out the god's real deeds from the scrolls. Tonight the herald unrolls the oldest and announces that {pw_deed}. Then an actor in a gold mask does it all again, badly, with a drum.

choices.text: Heckle the actor

effects.log: 'It was not like that,' you shout, before you can stop yourself. The whole square turns. You add, weakly, that you read it differently. The actor, offended, does it again, slower.

choices.text: Watch, and remember how it really was

effects.log: You remember the real day. It was raining, and you were tired, and you very nearly did not. The play leaves that out. Plays always do.

choices.text: Go backstage and show the actor how you held your hands

effects.log: The next night the actor does it your way, and an old priest in the front row bursts into tears and cannot say why.

events.text: At the end of the feast the priests choose one ordinary person from the crowd to light the great lamp, standing in for the Maker. They choose by lot. They choose you.

choices.text: Light it

effects.log: The lamp catches before the taper even touches it. Somebody gasps. You say loudly that it must be a very well-trimmed wick, and everyone agrees, relieved.

choices.text: Light it, and tell them the truth

effects.log: You say it plainly: it is me. The square is silent for one long breath, and then a grandmother at the front says, 'Well, sit down, then, you must be tired,' and gives you her stool. It is the finest throne you have ever had.

choices.text: Hand the taper to a child

effects.log: The child lights the lamp with tremendous seriousness. The priests are annoyed: the god, they say, does not delegate. You do.

events.text: Being a god in a mortal body is lonely in ways no hymn mentions. Friends tell you their troubles and you can see how every one of them ends. A neighbour pours you tea and you can hear the whole life of the tea plant. You laugh at the wrong moments.

choices.text: Tell one friend the truth

effects.log: You tell your oldest friend, Pell, over a game of stones. Pell looks at you for a long time, then moves a stone. 'Your turn. God or no god, you still play badly.' You have never loved anyone more.

choices.text: Pretend you cannot see the endings

effects.log: You learn to be surprised on purpose. It is the hardest thing you have ever learned, harder than making a world.

choices.text: Move to a small house on a hill

effects.log: You keep bees and talk to them. Bees do not pray. It is very restful.

events.text: A night of stars. You go out and look up at the sky you made, and notice for the first time that there is nobody up there making anything. It was always you, and now you are down here. The sky is very large, and very quiet, and entirely yours.

choices.text: Talk to it anyway

effects.log: You talk to the sky the way your people talk to you. It does not answer. You understand them a great deal better after that.

choices.text: Put one new star in it

effects.log: You set a small new star low in the south. By morning every stargazer in {pw_world} is shouting. Privately, you call it Company.

choices.text: Go back inside and sleep

effects.log: You sleep, and the sky gets on without you, as it was built to. That is a comfort too.

events.text: You are old now, in this body. Somewhere in {pw_world} people are being born who will pray to you all their lives and never know that you once bought turnips. Sitting on your step in the evening sun, you find you do not mind being unknown. You mind only being alone.

choices.text: Play one more game of stones with Pell

effects.log: Pell is old too. You play until dark, and lose, as always. 'Same time tomorrow,' Pell says, and for once you do not look ahead to see whether there will be one.

choices.text: Walk down to the village and sit where people are

effects.log: You sit in the corner of the tavern and listen to people being people. Nobody knows you. Everybody nods. That, it turns out, is a kind of company, and the oldest kind.

choices.text: Write it all down for whoever comes next

effects.log: You write a short book: what it is like to make a world and then live in it. You leave it unsigned in a temple. The priests will argue about it for a thousand years.
